<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{shifts of R-complexes}
We follow Ekedahl's convention \cite[Section~0, p.~188]{Ek1}; see
also \cite[Chapter~0]{Ek3}. For \(i,j\in\mathbb{Z}\), write \(M(i)[j]\) for
the shift by \(i\) in the internal \(R\)-grading and by \(j\) in
cohomological degree. If \(M=(M^{k,\ell},d,\delta)\), then
\[
    M(i)[j]^{k,\ell}=M^{k+i,\ell+j},\qquad
    d_{M(i)[j]}=(-1)^i d_M,\qquad
    \delta_{M(i)[j]}=(-1)^j\delta_M.
\]
In particular,
\(\mathrm{H}^q(M(i)[j])^k\simeq\mathrm{H}^{q+j}(M)^{k+i}\).
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{reduction by R_n}
For a graded \(R\)-module \(M\), its standard filtration is
\[
    \operatorname{Fil}^nM^i:=V^nM^i+dV^nM^{i-1}
    \qquad(n\geqslant0).
\]
The operators \(W,d,V\) preserve this filtration, whereas
\(F(\operatorname{Fil}^{n+1}M)\subseteq\operatorname{Fil}^nM\).
For \(n\geqslant1\), put \(W_n=W/p^nW\) and define the graded right
\(R\)-module
\[
    R_n:=R/(V^nR+dV^nR).
\]
The denominator is a right ideal, and \(R_n\) is understood as a
quotient of right \(R\)-modules. Left multiplication by \(W\) and \(d\)
descends to \(R_n\), and \(p^nR_n=0\). Thus \(R_n\) is a graded
\((W_n[d]/(d^2),R)\)-bimodule, with \(d\) in degree \(1\).
Quotienting by the standard filtration is tensoring with \(R_n\):
\[
    (R_n\otimes_R M)^i\cong M^i/\operatorname{Fil}^nM^i.
\]
For \(M\in D(R)\), define its derived reduction by
\[
    R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M
    \in D\bigl(W_n[d]/(d^2)\bigr).
\]
The target is the derived category of graded modules: internal and
cohomological degrees remain separate, with no totalization. For
\(n=1\), the target is \(D(k[d]/(d^2))\).

For a \(K\)-flat resolution \(P^\bullet\to M\), the derived reduction
is represented by \(P^\bullet/\operatorname{Fil}^nP^\bullet\).
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{Ekedahl completion}
The quotient maps \(R_{n+1}\to R_n\) form a tower. Following Ekedahl,
define
\[
    \widehat M
    :=R\varprojlim_{n\geqslant1}
       \bigl(R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M\bigr).
\]
The limit is taken before totalization in complexes of graded
\(W[d]/(d^2)\)-modules. It has a natural \(R\)-action and a natural
map \(M\to\widehat M\). We call \(M\) complete when this map is a
quasi-isomorphism.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{R1 detects vanishing of complete complexes}
Let \(M\in D(R)\) be complete and bounded from either of the four directions
in the sense of \Cref{derived category of R-modules of level I}.
If \(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M=0\), then \(M=0\).
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By \Cref{Ek2I.1.1}, applied with \(A=0\) and varying \(r,s\),
we have \(R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M=0\) for every \(n\geqslant1\).
Thus completeness gives
\(M\simeq R\varprojlim_n(R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)=0\).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{Nygaard modification}
Let \(\varphi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\) have finite support, and let \(M\) be a
graded left \(R\)-module. Its Nygaard modification
\(M(\varphi)\) has graded pieces
\[
    M(\varphi)^i=\sigma_*^{s_i}M^i,
    \qquad
    s_i=-\sum_{j\geqslant i+1}\varphi(j),
\]
with the induced operators \(F,V\) and differential
\[
    d(\varphi):M(\varphi)^{i-1}\longrightarrow M(\varphi)^i,
    \qquad
    d(\varphi)=
    \begin{cases}
        F^{\varphi(i)}d,&\varphi(i)\geqslant0,\\
        dV^{-\varphi(i)},&\varphi(i)<0.
    \end{cases}
\]
The scalar twists make \(d(\varphi)\) \(W\)-linear, and the relation
\(FdV=d\) makes \(M(\varphi)\) an \(R\)-module. We use
\(F^{\varphi(i)}d=dV^{-\varphi(i)}\) when \(\varphi(i)<0\); this
does not mean that \(F\) is inverted.

The construction is functorial and exact. Moreover, for
finitely supported functions \(\varphi,\psi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\),
\[
    M(0)=M,\qquad
    (M(\varphi))(\psi)=M(\varphi+\psi).
\]
Thus \((\mathrm{Fun}_c(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}),+)\) acts on graded \(R\)-modules by
exact autoequivalences, with \((-)(-\varphi)\) inverse to
\((-)(\varphi)\). Applied termwise, the same construction defines
exact autoequivalences of \(D(R)\).
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{completion commutes with Nygaard modification}
Let \(M\in D(R)\), and let \(\varphi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\) have finite support.
Then completion commutes with Nygaard modification:
\[
\widehat M(\varphi)\simeq\widehat{M(\varphi)}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
As in \cite[Proposition~0.2.1]{Ek3}, the identity
\[
(-)(\varphi)(\psi)=(-)(\varphi+\psi)
\]
reduces the claim to \(\varphi=\pm\delta_i\), where \(\delta_i\) is
the characteristic function of \(\{i\}\). By d\'evissage and free
resolutions, it then suffices to treat \(R(1-i)\), the only shifted
free module whose differential is changed. This is the explicit
free-module calculation there.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{coherent R-modules}
Following Ekedahl, an elementary graded \(R\)-module is one
of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item A finite free \(W\)-module in degree \(0\), with \(F\)
    bijective.
    \item A finite free \(W\)-module in degree \(0\), with both
    \(F\) and \(V\) topologically nilpotent for the \(p\)-adic topology.
    \item A finitely generated \(W\)-module in degree \(0\), killed
    by \(p\), with \(F\) bijective.
    \item The module \(k\) in degree \(0\), with \(F=V=d=0\).
    \item An elementary domino \(U_i\), for \(i\in\mathbb{Z}\), concentrated
    in degrees \(0\) and \(1\):
    \[
        U_i=\left(
        \prod_{n\geqslant0}kV^n
        \xrightarrow{\ d\ }
        \prod_{n\geqslant0}k\,dV^{n+i}
        \right).
    \]
    Here \(dV^{-j}\) means \(F^jd\) for \(j\geqslant0\).
    In degree \(0\), \(F=0\) and \(V\) is the usual semilinear
    shift; in degree \(1\), \(V=0\) and \(F\) sends \(dV^t\)
    to \(dV^{t-1}\), with the term below the lower bound \(i\)
    set equal to zero. The differential sends \(V^n\) to \(dV^n\)
    if \(n\geqslant i\), and to zero otherwise.
\end{enumerate}
A graded \(R\)-module is coherent if it has a finite filtration by
graded \(R\)-submodules whose successive quotients are grading shifts
of elementary modules. This is not the usual notion of finite
presentation over \(R\); elementary dominos are included by definition.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{coherent derived categories of R}
Let \(D_c(R)\) be the full subcategory of \(D(R)\) consisting of
complexes \(M\) such that every \(\mathrm{H}^q(M)\) is a coherent graded
\(R\)-module, and set
\[
    D_c^\ast(R):=D_c(R)\cap D^\ast(R),
    \qquad \ast\in\{-,+,b\}.
\]
The superscripts \(-\), \(+\), and \(b\) mean that the cohomology
vanishes in sufficiently large degrees, in sufficiently small degrees,
and outside a finite range, respectively.
Each coherent cohomology module is supported in finitely many internal
degrees, but objects of \(D_c(R)\) need not be cohomologically bounded.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{stable cycles boundaries and dominos}
Let \(M\) be a graded \(R\)-module. Following \cite{IR}, put
\[
F^\infty BM^i
 :=\bigcup_{j\geqslant0}F^j\bigl(dM^{i-1}\bigr),
\qquad
V^{-\infty}ZM^i
 :=\bigcap_{j\geqslant0}
 \ker\bigl(dV^j:M^i\longrightarrow M^{i+1}\bigr).
\]
Thus \(F^\infty BM^i\) is the \(F\)-saturation of the boundaries,
and \(V^{-\infty}ZM^i\) consists of those \(x\in M^i\) for which
\(dV^j x=0\) for every \(j\geqslant0\).
Define the diagonal truncations of \(M\) by
\[
\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}M
 :=
 \bigl(\cdots\xrightarrow{d}M^{i-1}\xrightarrow{d}M^i
 \xrightarrow{d}F^\infty BM^{i+1}\longrightarrow0\bigr),
\qquad
\widetilde{\tau}_{\geqslant i+1}M:=M/\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}M.
\]
The displayed terms retain their original module degrees.
Finally, define
\[
\mathrm{dom}^i(M)
 :=
 \bigl(M^i/V^{-\infty}ZM^i
       \xrightarrow{\ \bar d\ }F^\infty BM^{i+1}\bigr),
\]
with the two terms in module degrees \(i\) and \(i+1\), respectively,
and with \(\bar d\) induced by \(d\).
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{R-modules of level I}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\). An \(R\)-module of level \(\mathrm{I}\) is a graded
left \(R\)-module of the form
\[
M^m\xrightarrow{d}M^{m+1}\xrightarrow{d}\cdots\xrightarrow{d}M^n
\]
with \(F\) bijective on \(M^n\). Equivalently, the top term carries
an action of \(R^{\mathrm{top}}=W_{\sigma}[F,F^{-1}]\) extending its
\(R^0\)-action. Morphisms are grading-preserving \(R\)-linear maps.
We denote this abelian category by \(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{radical filtration}
Let \(D\) be a triangulated category endowed with a \(t\)-structure
whose heart is \(D^0\). A radical filtration on \((D,D^0)\) is an
increasing sequence
\[
\cdots\subseteq T^i\subseteq T^{i+1}\subseteq\cdots
\subseteq\mathrm{id}_{D^0}
\]
of subfunctors \(T^i:D^0\to D^0\) of the identity functor, satisfying the following conditions.

{\rm (1)} For every \(M\in D^0\), one has \(T^i(M)=0\) for
\(i\ll0\) and \(T^i(M)=M\) for \(i\gg0\).

{\rm (2)} For all \(i,j\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(M,N\in D^0\),
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_D^{j-i}\bigl(T^i(M),N/T^j(N)\bigr)=0.
\]

{\rm (3)} For all \(i<j\) and \(M,N\in D^0\),
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_D^{j-i+1}\bigl(T^i(M),N/T^j(N)\bigr)=0.
\]

Here
\(\mathrm{Hom}_D^r(M,N):=\mathrm{Hom}_D(M,N[r])\).
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The orthogonality conditions can also be read on the successive
layers of the filtration. Set \(S^i(M)=T^i(M)/T^{i-1}(M)\). By d\'evissage,
conditions (2) and (3) are together equivalent to the layerwise
vanishing
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_D^r\bigl(S^i(M),S^j(N)\bigr)=0
\]
whenever \(r\leqslant j-i-1\) or
\(2\leqslant r\leqslant j-i\).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{example:radical-filtration}
The motivating example is the ordinary heart of \(D_c^b(R)\). For a
coherent \(R\)-module \(M\), set
\[
\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}M
 =\bigl(\cdots\xrightarrow dM^{i-1}\xrightarrow dM^i
   \xrightarrow dF^\infty BM^{i+1}\longrightarrow0\bigr)
\]
and
\[
\widetilde{\tau}_{\geqslant i+1}M:=M/\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}M
 \simeq
 \bigl(0\longrightarrow M^i/F^\infty BM^i
   \xrightarrow dM^{i+1}\xrightarrow d\cdots\bigr).
\]
The Ext calculations in
\Cref{Ekedahl vanishing over any perfect field} show that the
subfunctors \(\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}\) form a radical filtration. The
associated \(t\)-structure is the diagonal \(t\)-structure.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{diagonal t-structure}
Let \((D^{\leqslant0},D^{\geqslant0})\) be a \(t\)-structure on a
triangulated category \(D\), with heart \(D^0\), and suppose that it
is bounded: every object has finite cohomological amplitude.
Write \(\mathrm{H}^i\) for its cohomology functors.

{\rm (1)} A radical filtration \(T^\bullet\) on \((D,D^0)\) defines
a bounded \(t\)-structure by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}
 &=\bigl\{X\in D\mid
      T^{-i}(\mathrm{H}^i(X))=\mathrm{H}^i(X)\text{ for every }i\bigr\},\\
\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}
 &=\bigl\{X\in D\mid
      (\mathrm{id}/T^{-i})(\mathrm{H}^i(X))=\mathrm{H}^i(X)
      \text{ for every }i\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the lower half consists of objects whose \(i\)-th cohomology is
entirely contained in filtration step \(-i\); the upper half consists
of those for which this step is zero. This \(t\)-structure commutes
with the original one: each of its truncation functors commutes, up
to natural isomorphism, with every truncation functor of the original
\(t\)-structure.

{\rm (2)} Conversely, let \(\widetilde{\tau}\) denote the truncation functors of
any bounded \(t\)-structure commuting with the original one.
Restricting these functors to the heart \(D^0\) gives a radical
filtration
\[
\cdots\subseteq\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}
 \subseteq\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i+1}
 \subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathrm{id}_{D^0}.
\]

{\rm (3)} These constructions are inverse to one another. In particular,
a bounded commuting \(t\)-structure is determined by the filtration
that its truncations induce on the original heart.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Throughout the proof,
\(D^{[m,n]}\) and \(\mathrm{H}^q\) refer to the original \(t\)-structure,
and \((\mathrm{id}/T^a)(A)=A/T^a(A)\).

We first prove orthogonality. Let \(X\in\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}\) and
\(Y\in\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}\).
By definition, for every \(r,s\in\mathbb{Z}\),
\[
    \mathrm{H}^r(X)=T^{-r}(\mathrm{H}^r(X)),\qquad
    \mathrm{H}^s(Y)\simeq(\mathrm{id}/T^{-s})(\mathrm{H}^s(Y)).
\]
Condition (2) of \Cref{radical filtration}, with indices
\(-r\) and \(-s\), therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{Hom}_D\bigl(\mathrm{H}^r(X)[-r],\mathrm{H}^s(Y)[-s]\bigr)\\
&\qquad=
\mathrm{Hom}_D^{r-s}\bigl(
T^{-r}(\mathrm{H}^r(X)),(\mathrm{id}/T^{-s})(\mathrm{H}^s(Y))
\bigr)=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The original \(t\)-structure is bounded, so \(X\) and \(Y\) are
finite successive extensions of their ordinary cohomology
objects with the indicated shifts. Applying the long exact
Hom sequences to these truncation filtrations, first in \(Y\)
and then in \(X\), proves
\[
    \mathrm{Hom}_D(X,Y)=0.
\]
We next construct the truncation triangle. Since the filtration
\(T^\bullet\) is increasing, the defining
conditions immediately imply
\[
    \widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}[1]\subseteq\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0},
    \qquad
    \widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}[-1]\subseteq\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}.
\]
We also need the identities
\[
    T^a(T^a(A))=T^a(A),\qquad
    T^a\bigl((\mathrm{id}/T^a)(A)\bigr)=0
    \qquad(A\in D^0).
\]
To see this, condition (2) with equal indices says that
\(\mathrm{Hom}_D(T^a(M),(\mathrm{id}/T^a)(N))=0\) for all \(M,N\in D^0\).
Taking \(M=A\), \(N=T^a(A)\), the quotient map
\[
    T^a(A)\twoheadrightarrow
    (\mathrm{id}/T^a)(T^a(A))
\]
is zero; being an epimorphism in \(D^0\), it has zero target.
Taking \(M=(\mathrm{id}/T^a)(A)\), \(N=A\), the inclusion
\[
    T^a\bigl((\mathrm{id}/T^a)(A)\bigr)
    \hookrightarrow(\mathrm{id}/T^a)(A)
\]
is zero; being a monomorphism, it has zero source.
These identities ensure that the subobject and quotient at a
single filtration step belong to the required new halves.

For \(X\in D^{[m,n]}\), we construct a distinguished triangle
\[
Y\longrightarrow X\longrightarrow Z\longrightarrow Y[1],
\qquad Y\in\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0},\quad Z\in\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1},
\]
with both \(Y,Z\in D^{[m,n]}\).
We induct on \(n-m\). If \(m=n\), set \(A=\mathrm{H}^m(X)\);
the required triangle is the shift by \([-m]\) of
\[
0\longrightarrow T^{-m}(A)\longrightarrow A
 \longrightarrow (\mathrm{id}/T^{-m})(A)\longrightarrow0.
\]

Otherwise choose \(m\leqslant c<n\), and put
\(X'=\tau_{\leqslant c}X\), \(X''=\tau_{\geqslant c+1}X\).
Induction gives triangles
\[
Y'\longrightarrow X'\longrightarrow Z'\longrightarrow Y'[1],
\qquad
Y''\longrightarrow X''\longrightarrow Z''\longrightarrow Y''[1],
\]
where \(Y',Z'\in D^{[m,c]}\), \(Y'',Z''\in D^{[c+1,n]}\),
the \(Y\)-terms lie in \(\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}\), and the \(Z\)-terms
lie in \(\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}\).

The obstruction to lifting the composite
\(Y''[-1]\to X''[-1]\to X'\) through \(Y'\to X'\)
lies in \(\mathrm{Hom}_D(Y''[-1],Z')\). This group vanishes.
Indeed, by ordinary cohomological d\'evissage its relevant groups
are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{Hom}_D\bigl(T^{-a}(A)[-a-1],(\mathrm{id}/T^{-b})(B)[-b]\bigr)\\
&\hspace{2em}=
\mathrm{Hom}_D^{a-b+1}\bigl(T^{-a}(A),(\mathrm{id}/T^{-b})(B)\bigr)=0,
\qquad a\geqslant c+1,\quad b\leqslant c.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(-a<-b\), so the last equality is exactly condition (3)
of \Cref{radical filtration}.
Choose a lift \(Y''[-1]\to Y'\).
The octahedral axiom, in its \(3\times3\) form, completes the
resulting square to a diagram of distinguished triangles
commuting up to the usual signs:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
Y' \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &
Y \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &
Y'' \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d] & {}\\
X' \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &
X \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &
X'' \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d] & {}\\
Z' \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"+1"'] &
Z \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"+1"'] &
Z'' \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d,"+1"'] & {}\\
{} & {} & {} & {}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The separated ordinary amplitudes give
\[
\mathrm{H}^q(Y)\simeq
\begin{cases}
\mathrm{H}^q(Y'),&q\leqslant c,\\
\mathrm{H}^q(Y''),&q\geqslant c+1,
\end{cases}
\]
and the analogous formula for \(Z\).
Thus \(Y\in\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}\), \(Z\in\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}\), and
both retain amplitude \([m,n]\). This proves the truncation axiom.

By orthogonality, the constructed triangle is the new truncation triangle.
The same diagram and the amplitude bounds identify
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{\leqslant c}\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}X
 &\simeq Y'\simeq\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}\tau_{\leqslant c}X,\\
\tau_{\geqslant c+1}\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}X
 &\simeq Y''\simeq\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}\tau_{\geqslant c+1}X,
\end{aligned}
\]
and similarly for \(\widetilde{\tau}_{\geqslant1}\), using \(Z',Z''\).
By shifting, all ordinary and new truncations commute.
Finally, every \(X\) has finitely many ordinary cohomology objects,
and the filtration on each is eventually zero and eventually
the whole object. The defining formulas therefore place \(X\)
in a finite interval for the new \(t\)-structure as well.

Conversely, suppose that a bounded \(t\)-structure
\((\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0},\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1})\) commutes with the original one.
Its truncations preserve \(D^0\), so for \(A\in D^0\) they give
short exact sequences in \(D^0\)
\[
0\longrightarrow T^a(A):=\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant a}A
 \longrightarrow A\longrightarrow
 \widetilde{\tau}_{\geqslant a+1}A\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus \(\widetilde{\tau}_{\geqslant a+1}A\simeq(\mathrm{id}/T^a)(A)\).
The subfunctors \(T^a\) form an increasing filtration.
Boundedness gives condition (1) of \Cref{radical filtration}.
Moreover, \(T^a(A)[a]\in\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}\) and
\((\mathrm{id}/T^b)(B)[b]\in\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}\); orthogonality gives condition (2).

For condition (3), we first show that
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_D(X[-1],Y)=0
\quad\text{if}\quad
X\in D^{\geqslant c+1}\cap\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0},\qquad
Y\in D^{\leqslant c}\cap\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}.
\]
Given \(f:X[-1]\to Y\), complete it to a triangle
\[
Y\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow X\xrightarrow{\,f[1]\,}Y[1].
\]
The ordinary truncations of \(E\) are \(Y\) and \(X\).
Commutation of the two truncation systems gives
\[
\tau_{\leqslant c}\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}E
 \simeq\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}Y=0,\qquad
\tau_{\geqslant c+1}\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}E
 \simeq\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}X=X.
\]
Consequently the natural composite
\(\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}E\to E\to X\) is an isomorphism.
It supplies a section of \(E\to X\), so the triangle splits and
\(f=0\).
Apply this with
\[
X=T^a(A)[a],\qquad Y=(\mathrm{id}/T^b)(B)[b],\qquad c=-b,\qquad a<b.
\]
The ordinary degrees of \(X,Y\) are \(-a>-b\) and \(-b\),
respectively. The resulting vanishing is
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_D^{b-a+1}(T^a(A),(\mathrm{id}/T^b)(B))=0,
\]
which is condition (3).

It remains to show that the two constructions are inverse. Commutation
implies that each \(\mathrm{H}^q(X)[-q]\) belongs to
\(\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}\), respectively \(\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}\), whenever
\(X\) does. Conversely, the finite ordinary truncation filtration
and extension closure recover membership of \(X\) from these pieces.
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
X\in\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}
 &\Longleftrightarrow
 T^{-q}(\mathrm{H}^q(X))=\mathrm{H}^q(X)\quad\text{for every }q,\\
X\in\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant1}
 &\Longleftrightarrow
 T^{-q}(\mathrm{H}^q(X))=0\quad\text{for every }q.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are precisely the formulas in (1).
In the other direction, the single-cohomology construction of the
truncation triangle recovers \(T^a(A)\) as
\(\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant a}A\) for \(A\in D^0\).
Thus the two constructions are inverse, proving (3).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{graded Hom}
For graded left \(R\)-modules \(M,N\), define the graded Hom group by
\[
    \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,N):=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,N)^i,
    \qquad
    \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,N)^i
       :=\mathrm{Hom}_{R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}_{\mathrm{gr}}}(M,N(i)).
\]
Thus \(\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,N)^i\) consists of the grading-preserving
\(R\)-linear maps \(M\to N(i)\).

For \(M,N\in D(R)\), similarly set
\[
    \mathrm{Hom}_{D(R)}(M,N)
       :=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{Hom}_{D(R)}(M,N)^i,
    \qquad
    \mathrm{Hom}_{D(R)}(M,N)^i
       :=\mathrm{Hom}_{D(R)}(M,N(i)),
\]
where the right-hand side is computed in the derived category of
graded \(R\)-modules. This internal grading is independent of the
cohomological shift \([j]\); its degree-zero part is the usual
morphism group.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
For graded left \(R\)-modules \(M,N\), define
\[
\mathrm{Ext}_R^j(M,N)^i:=\mathrm{Hom}_{D(R)}(M,N[j])^i.
\]
Equivalently,
\(\mathrm{Ext}_R^j(M,N)^i\simeq R^j\mathrm{Hom}_R(M,N)^i\).
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{completed resolution of elementary domino}
For \(t\in\mathbb{Z}\), define homogeneous elements of degree \(1\) by
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &t\leqslant0&t\geqslant1\\ \hline
 w_t&F^{1-t}d&dV^{t-1}\\
 h_t&F^{-t}dV&dV^{t+1}.
\end{array}
\]
Then the elementary domino \(U_t\) has the exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{elementary domino completed resolution sequence}
0\longrightarrow\widehat R(-1)
 \xrightarrow{\;\alpha_t\;}
 \widehat R\oplus\widehat R(-1)
 \xrightarrow{\;\beta_t\;}
 \widehat R
 \xrightarrow{\;\epsilon_t\;}U_t
 \longrightarrow0,
\end{equation}
where
\[
 \alpha_t(z)=(zh_t,-zV),\qquad
 \beta_t(x,y)=xF+yw_t.
\]
The augmentation \(\epsilon_t\) sends \(1\) to \(1\in U_t^0=k[[V]]\).
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
All products in the displayed maps are on the right.
The Raynaud relations give
\(h_tF=Vw_t\) and \(w_tV=Fh_t,\)
thus \(\beta_t\alpha_t=0\).

We first identify the cokernel of \(\beta_t\). In degree \(0\), it is
\(\widehat R^0/\widehat R^0F=k[[V]].\)
In degree \(1\), right multiplication by \(F\) has image
\(p\widehat R^1\), since right multiplication by \(V\) is
bijective. Modulo \(p\), elements of \(\widehat R^1\) have unique
expansions in the symbols \(dV^j\), bounded below in \(j\);
negative exponents mean \(dV^{-j}=F^jd\).
The element \(w_t\) is the symbol \(dV^{t-1}\), so its
left \(F\)-multiples remove precisely the symbols with index
less than \(t\). Consequently
\[
    \operatorname{coker}(\beta_t)^1
       \simeq\prod_{j\geqslant t}k\,dV^j.
\]
The induced differential and the actions of \(F,V\) are those
of \(U_t\). This identifies the cokernel and the augmentation
in \eqref{elementary domino completed resolution sequence}.

It remains to check exactness at the two terms on the left.
The unique \(F\)-\(V\) expansions give the divisibility criterion
\[
    y\,d\in p\widehat R^1
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
    y\in\widehat R^0V
    \qquad(y\in\widehat R^0).
\]
Indeed, \(V^nd=p^ndV^n\), whereas the terms \(F^jd\) carry no \(p\)-factor. 
The same criterion holds with \(d\) replaced by \(w_tV\):
for \(t\geqslant1\), this is \(dV^t\), and for \(t\leqslant0\),
it is \(dV^t=F^{-t}d\). Right multiplication by any integral
power of \(V\) is an automorphism of \(\widehat R^1\) preserving
\(p\widehat R^1\).

In internal degree \(0\), the middle kernel is zero because
right multiplication by \(F\) on \(\widehat R^0\) is injective.
In internal degree \(1\), suppose
\[
    xF+yw_t=0,\qquad x\in\widehat R^1,\quad y\in\widehat R^0.
\]
Multiplying on the right by \(V\) gives
\(px+yw_tV=0\). The preceding criterion implies \(y=zV\)
for some \(z\in\widehat R^0\). Since \(Vw_tV=ph_t\) and
\(\widehat R^1\) is \(p\)-torsion-free, it follows that
\(x=-zh_t\). Thus \((x,y)=\alpha_t(-z)\).
In degree \(2\), the middle term is \(\widehat R^1\), its
map to \(\widehat R\) is zero, and \(\alpha_t\) maps onto it
by right multiplication by \(-V\).
Finally, \(\alpha_t\) is injective because right multiplication
by \(V\) is injective on \(\widehat R^0\) and bijective on
\(\widehat R^1\). This proves exactness in every internal degree.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
In the statements below we use the convention of \Cref{graded Hom}:
\(\mathrm{Ext}_R^j(P,Q)^i=\mathrm{Hom}_{D(R)}(P,Q(i)[j])\).
In particular,
\[
 \mathrm{Hom}_{D(R)}(P(-a),Q(-b)[j])=\mathrm{Ext}_R^j(P,Q)^{a-b}.
\]
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{cyclic devissage of Dieudonne modules}
Let \(k\) be perfect. Every finite-type \(V\)-complete Dieudonn\'e module
admits a finite filtration whose successive quotients are of the form
\[
 E_P,\qquad k_0,\qquad N_Q.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
First separate the finite \(p\)-power torsion submodule. Its
\(p\)-adic filtration reduces us to a finite-dimensional Dieudonn\'e
module killed by \(p\). The simple complete factors are \(k_0\) and
the simple \'etale modules: a nonzero vector generates any simple
\'etale factor, and its annihilator is an irreducible skew polynomial
\(Q(F)\) with nonzero leading and constant coefficients. These
give the modules \(N_Q\). Completeness excludes the
\(V\)-bijective simple factor.

It remains to treat a \(W\)-torsion-free module \(M\). Choose a simple
constituent of \(M[1/p]\) and a cyclic vector. The Newton-polygon
inequalities normalize its minimal skew relation to an \(F\)-\(V\)
relation \(P\) as above when the slope is positive, and to an
\(F\)-only relation \(P(F)\) with unit leading and constant
coefficients when the slope is zero. After multiplying the vector by a power of \(p\),
the corresponding cyclic lattice \(E_P\) lies in \(M\).
The quotient has smaller \(W\)-rank and finite torsion, so induction
on the rank completes the filtration.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{Ekedahl vanishing over any perfect field}
Let \(k\) be a perfect field. All Dieudonn\'e modules below are of finite
type and concentrated in internal degree \(0\).

{\rm (1)} For Dieudonn\'e modules \(M,N\),
\[
 \mathrm{Ext}_R^j(M,N)^i=0
 \quad\text{unless}\quad i=0,\quad 0\leqslant j\leqslant2.
\]

{\rm (2)} For a Dieudonn\'e module \(M\) and \(t\in\mathbb{Z}\),
\[
 \mathrm{Ext}_R^j(U_t,M)^i=0
 \quad\text{unless}\quad
 \begin{cases}
 i=-1,&1\leqslant j\leqslant2,\\
 i=0,&0\leqslant j\leqslant1,
 \end{cases}
\]
whereas
\[
 \mathrm{Ext}_R^j(M,U_t)^i=0
 \quad\text{unless}\quad i\in\{0,1\},\quad
 0\leqslant j\leqslant2.
\]

{\rm (3)} For \(t,s\in\mathbb{Z}\),
\[
 \mathrm{Ext}_R^j(U_t,U_s)^i=0
 \quad\text{unless}\quad
 \begin{cases}
 i=-1,&j=2,\\
 i=0,&0\leqslant j\leqslant2,\\
 i=1,&j=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let \(M\) be a Dieudonn\'e module. By
\Cref{cyclic devissage of Dieudonne modules}, it has a finite
filtration with successive quotients \(E_P\), \(k_0\), or
\(N_Q\). Their completed \(\widehat R\)-resolutions have lengths at
most two and compute \(R\mathrm{Hom}_R\) against every complete target.

If the target is a Dieudonn\'e module \(N\), concentrated in internal
degree \(0\), the resulting Hom complexes occur only in internal
degree \(0\) and cohomological degrees \(0,1,2\). If the target is
\(U_t\), they occur only in internal degrees \(0,1\), again in
cohomological degrees \(0,1,2\). The long exact Ext sequences along
the filtration prove (1) and the second assertion of (2).

The assertions with domino source follow directly from
\Cref{completed resolution of elementary domino}. For target \(N\),
its two relevant components are
\[
 [\,N\xrightarrow{F}N\,]\quad (i=0),\qquad
 [\,N\xrightarrow{-V}N\,]\quad (i=-1),
\]
in cohomological degrees \(0,1\) and \(1,2\), respectively. For target
\(U_s\), the injectivity of \(V\) on \(U_s^0\) and the surjectivity of
\(F\) on \(U_s^1\) give exactly the ranges in (3).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{diagonal t-structure on coherent R-complexes}
The diagonal \(t\)-structure on \(D_c^b(R)\) is the
\(t\)-structure associated, as in \Cref{diagonal t-structure},
to the radical filtration \(\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}\) on coherent
\(R\)-modules. Explicitly, its two halves are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde{D}_{\leqslant0}
 &=\bigl\{M\in D_c^b(R)\mid
   \widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant-j}\mathrm{H}^j(M)=\mathrm{H}^j(M)
   \text{ for every }j\bigr\},\\
\widetilde{D}_{\geqslant0}
 &=\bigl\{M\in D_c^b(R)\mid
   \widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant-j-1}\mathrm{H}^j(M)=0
   \text{ for every }j\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\mathrm{H}^j\) denotes ordinary cohomology, and the truncations
applied to \(\mathrm{H}^j(M)\) are those of graded \(R\)-modules.
We write
\[

}}

  \end{tikzpicture}}}

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}}

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\,

<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{Basic Vanishing}
Let \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\,

  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}}

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\).

{\rm (1)} One has \(\mathrm{H}^i(\mathrm{Tot}(M))=0\) for \(i\notin\{0,1\}\), and
\(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\) is a finite-length torsion \(W\)-module.

{\rm (2)} If \(D\) is one of \(R_n,B_n,Z_n,R_1/B_n\), then
\[
\mathrm{H}^j(D\otimes_R M)^i=0
\qquad\text{for }i+j\notin\{-1,0,1\}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For (1), use the finite filtration of \(M\) by its ordinary
truncations. Its successive quotients are twists \(N(j)[-j]\), with
\(N\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\!\cap R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\), and twists do not change
totalization. We may therefore reduce to such an \(N\).

The module \(N\) is an extension of a finite-type Dieudonn\'e module
by a coherent domino. The former contributes only to
\(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(N))\), while the latter has a finite filtration by
elementary dominos, whose total cohomology has finite length and is
concentrated in degrees \(0\) and \(1\). The long exact sequences
associated with the two finite filtrations prove
(1).

For (2), d\'evissage, together with homotopy limits and colimits,
reduces to an elementary coherent \(R\)-module. Use the resolutions

    \[\begin{aligned}
        &0\rightarrow R(-1)\xrightarrow{(F,-Fd)\cdot} R(-1)\oplus R\xrightarrow{(dV,V)\cdot} R\rightarrow R_1\rightarrow 0,\\
        &0\rightarrow R(-1) \xrightarrow{(V,-F)\cdot } R(-1)\oplus R(-1) \xrightarrow{(F,V)\cdot} R(-1)\rightarrow B_1 \rightarrow 0,\\
        &0\rightarrow R(-1) \xrightarrow{(F,-d)\cdot } R(-1)\oplus R \xrightarrow{(dV^2,V)\cdot} R\xrightarrow{C^{-1}} \sigma_*(Z_1) \rightarrow 0,\\
        &0\rightarrow R(-1) \xrightarrow{(V^n,-d)\cdot} R(-1)\oplus R \xrightarrow{(F^{n-1}d,V)\cdot} R\rightarrow R_1/B_n \rightarrow 0.
    \end{aligned}\]

For \(B_1\), the claimed range is immediate for a finite-type
Dieudonn\'e module; for a domino it follows from the surjectivity of
left multiplication by \(F\) in degree \(1\). The remaining cases
follow inductively from

    \[\begin{aligned}
          &0\rightarrow B_1\rightarrow B_{n+1}\xrightarrow{C}\sigma_*^{-1}B_n\rightarrow 0,\\
        &0\rightarrow B_1\rightarrow Z_{n+1}\xrightarrow{C}\sigma^{-1}_*Z_n\rightarrow 0,
    \end{aligned}\]
and the corresponding long exact cohomology sequences. Frobenius
twists do not alter the stated vanishing range.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{Totsubquo}
Let \(M\in D_c^b(R)\).

{\rm (1)} For every \(i\), there is a natural short exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{i-1}(M)))
\longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^i(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
\longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^i(M)))
\longrightarrow0.
\]

{\rm (2)} If \(D\) is one of \(R_n,B_n,Z_n,R_1/B_n\), then
\(\mathrm{H}^i(D\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M))^{-i}\) is a subquotient of
\(\mathrm{H}^{i+j}(D\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^{-i}\).
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The diagonal Postnikov filtration of \(M\), whose graded pieces are
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M)[-j]\), gives after totalization the spectral sequence
\[
E_2^{i,j}=\mathrm{H}^i\bigl(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M))\bigr)
 \Longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^{i+j}(\mathrm{Tot}(M)).
\]
By \Cref{Basic Vanishing}(1), it has only two adjacent columns, which
gives (1). Applying \(D\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}-\) to the same filtration
gives
\[
E_2^{i,j}=\mathrm{H}^i\bigl(D\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M)\bigr)
 \Longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^{i+j}(D\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M).
\]
In internal degree \(-i\), \Cref{Basic Vanishing}(2) leaves no
incoming or outgoing differential. Thus the indicated \(E_2\)-term
survives to \(E_\infty\), proving (2).
<!-- end proof-8 -->

<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For (1), let \(Q\) be the cokernel of \(N\hookrightarrow M\) in
\(

  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\). The resulting distinguished triangle gives
\[
\mathrm{H}^{q-1}(Q)^{-q}\longrightarrow
\mathrm{H}^q(N)^{-q}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^q(M)^{-q}.
\]
The first term vanishes because \(Q\) is diagonal. Thus the second map
is injective. For \(q\neq0\), its target is zero; since
\(\mathrm{H}^q(N)\) is generated by its component of internal degree \(-q\),
we obtain \(\mathrm{H}^q(N)=0\). Hence \(N\) is an actual \(R\)-module, and
the case \(q=0\) gives the asserted injection \(N^0\hookrightarrow
M^0\).

For (2), let \(K=\ker_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\,

  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);

}}

}(f)\). By (1), \(K\) is an actual diagonal
\(R\)-module and \(K^0\hookrightarrow N^0\). Since \(N^0\to\mathrm{H}^0(M)^0\) is injective,
we have \(K^0=0\). Every diagonal \(R\)-module is generated by its

<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{homomorphism between U_i}
Let \(U_a,U_b\) be the elementary dominos of types \(a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\).
Then
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_R(U_a,U_b)^0=0\qquad\text{if }a>b,
\]
and every nonzero grading-preserving \(R\)-endomorphism of \(U_a\) is
an isomorphism. The superscript \(0\) denotes internal grading degree;
see \Cref{graded Hom}.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let \(\varphi:U_a\to U_b\) be a nonzero grading-preserving
\(R\)-homomorphism. Since \(U_a\) is generated in degree \(0\),
\(\varphi^0:U_a^0\to U_b^0\) is nonzero. Both degree-zero parts are
\(k[[V]]\), and every nonzero map compatible with scalars and \(V\)
is injective. Hence \(\varphi^0\) is injective.

Apply the Nygaard modification \((-)(\psi)\), where
\(\psi(n)=-b\delta_{1n}\).
It sends \(U_a,U_b\) to \(U_{a-b},U_0\), respectively, without
changing Hom groups. We may therefore assume \(b=0\). The induced map
\[
\ker(d:U_a^0\to U_a^1)
 \longrightarrow
\ker(d:U_0^0\to U_0^1),
\]
is injective. For \(a>0\), however, its source is nonzero and its
target is zero. This proves the vanishing.

For endomorphisms, the same modification reduces to
\(\varphi:U_0\to U_0\). Its restriction to
\[
\ker(Fd:U_0^0\longrightarrow U_0^1)
\]
is bijective because this kernel is one-dimensional over \(k\). It
generates \(U_0\) as an \(R\)-module, so \(\varphi\) is surjective and
\(\varphi^0\) is an isomorphism. Since \(d:U_0^0\to U_0^1\) is an
isomorphism and \(\varphi^1d=d\varphi^0\), so is \(\varphi^1\).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{diagonal category is Noetherian}
The abelian category \(

}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) is Noetherian.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The ordinary truncation filtration of \Cref{diagonal t-structure on coherent R-complexes},
together with the structure theorem for coherent \(R\)-modules, reduces
the assertion by twists and d\'evissage to a finite-type Dieudonn\'e
module or an elementary domino \(U_j\).

For a finite-type Dieudonn\'e module, \Cref{subobjects of diagonal modules}
identifies every ascending chain of subobjects in \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) with an
ascending chain of \(W\)-submodules. It stabilizes because the module is
finitely generated over the Noetherian ring \(W\).

Now let
\[
N_0\subseteq N_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_j
\]
be an ascending chain. Every nonzero \(N_a\) is an actual
one-dimensional domino, hence \(N_a\simeq U_{r_a}\) for some
\(r_a\in\mathbb{Z}\). By \Cref{homomorphism between U_i}, the inclusions give
\[
r_a\leqslant r_{a+1}\leqslant j.
\]
The sequence \((r_a)\) therefore stabilizes. Once
\(r_a=r_{a+1}\), the inclusion \(N_a\hookrightarrow N_{a+1}\) is an
isomorphism, again by \Cref{homomorphism between U_i}. Thus the chain
stabilizes.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{dcDegen}
{\rm (1)} The canonical exact sequence
\(0\to\text{\rm {c\oe ur}}(M)\to M\to\operatorname{dom}(M)\to0\)
for \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice

}}           
    {\,

}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\!\cap R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\) induces
\[
\begin{gathered}
0\longrightarrow\text{\rm {c\oe ur}}(M)\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
 \longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(\operatorname{dom}(M)))
 \longrightarrow0,\\
\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
 \xrightarrow{\sim}
 \mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(\operatorname{dom}(M))).
\end{gathered}
\]

{\rm (2)} Let \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\). If \(i\) and \(j\) are respectively
the smallest and largest integers for which \(\mathrm{H}^i(M)\) and
\(\mathrm{H}^j(M)\) are nonzero, then
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{H}^0\bigl(\mathrm{Tot}(\mathrm{H}^i(M)(-i))\bigr)
 \hookrightarrow\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M)),\\
\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
 \twoheadrightarrow
\mathrm{H}^1\bigl(\mathrm{Tot}(\mathrm{H}^j(M)(-j))\bigr).
\end{gathered}
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Part (1) is the long exact sequence of total cohomology. For (2), use
the \(E_2\)-page of the slope spectral sequence
\[
E_2^{a,b}=\mathrm{H}^a(\mathrm{Tot}(\mathrm{H}^b(M)))
 \Longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^{a+b}(\mathrm{Tot}(M)).
\]
At the two extremal nonzero cohomological degrees, the relevant edge
terms admit no possible incoming or outgoing differential. They
therefore survive to \(E_\infty\), giving the asserted subobject and
quotient.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{dcamplitude}
{\rm (1)} The subcategories
\(\widetilde D_c^b(R)_{\leqslant0}\) and
\(\widetilde D_c^b(R)_{\geqslant0}\) are stable under every Nygaard
modification \((-)(\varphi)\), with
\(\varphi\in\mathrm{Fun}_c(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})\).

{\rm (2)} Let \(M\in D_c^b(R)\), and choose
\(\mathrm{I}_1=[m_1,n_1]\) such that
\(M\in D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{I}_1)\) (see \Cref{derived category of R-modules of level I}). For another interval
\(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\), the complex \(M\) has diagonal amplitude \([m,n]\) if
and only if there exists \(N\in\mathbb{Z}\) such that
\(\mathrm{Tot}(M(\varphi))\) has ordinary amplitude \([m,n]\) whenever
\[
\varphi(k)\geqslant N
\qquad(m_1+1\leqslant k\leqslant n_1).
\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For a coherent \(R\)-module \(A\), one has
\[
\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}(A(\varphi))
 =\bigl(\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant i}A\bigr)(\varphi),
\]
which proves (1).

Suppose first that \(M\) has diagonal amplitude \([m,n]\). The domino
parts of the finitely many modules
\(\mathrm{H}^i(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M))\), with \(m\leqslant j\leqslant n\) and
\(-n_1+1\leqslant i\leqslant-m_1\), are iterated extensions of
finitely many \(U_t\). Choose \(N\) so large that
\(t+N>0\) for every such constituent. If \(\varphi\geqslant N\) on
\([m_1+1,n_1]\), Nygaard modification replaces these constituents by
\(U_{t+\varphi(-i+1)}\). Their indices are positive, so their
totalizations have the expected single degree. The spectral sequence
of \Cref{Totsubquo} now gives ordinary amplitude \([m,n]\) for
\(\mathrm{Tot}(M(\varphi))\).

Conversely, assume the stated uniform amplitude condition and suppose
that \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M)\neq0\) for some maximal \(j>n\). By
\Cref{Totsubquo}(1), both total cohomology groups of
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M(\varphi))\) must vanish. Let \(j'\) be its smallest ordinary
cohomological degree. The heart part would survive by
\Cref{dcDegen}(2), so this extremal term must be a domino and
\(j'+1\in[m_1+1,n_1]\). Taking \(\varphi(j'+1)\) sufficiently large
makes
\[
\mathrm{H}^{-j'}\!\left(\mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\mathrm{H}^{j'}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M(\varphi)))\bigr)\right)
\neq0.
\]
Again by \Cref{dcDegen}(2), this injects into the vanishing group
\(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M(\varphi))))\), a contradiction. The argument at
the lower endpoint is dual.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->

Let \(M\in

    {\,

    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);

    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\).

{\rm (1)} The object \(M\) is finite torsion if \(t^1(M)=M\).

{\rm (2)} It is without finite torsion if \(t^1(M)=0\).
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{without finite torsion implies artinian}
Let \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\).

{\rm (1)} The object \(\widetilde D^1(M)\) is finite torsion, whereas
\(\widetilde D^0(M)\) is without finite torsion. Moreover, \(t^1(M)\)
is the maximal finite-torsion subobject of \(M\), and \(t^0(M)\) is its
maximal quotient without finite torsion.

{\rm (2)} Every descending chain of subobjects
\[
M\supseteq M_1\supseteq M_2\supseteq\cdots
\]
for which each \(M/M_i\) is without finite torsion eventually
stabilizes.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Apply the biduality sequence to \(\widetilde D^1(M)\). Its \(t^0\)-term
vanishes because \(\widetilde D^0\widetilde D^1=0\); hence
\[
t^1(\widetilde D^1(M))\simeq\widetilde D^1(M).
\]
Thus \(\widetilde D^1(M)\) is finite torsion. Similarly,
\[
t^1(\widetilde D^0(M))
 =\widetilde D^1\widetilde D^1\widetilde D^0(M)=0,
\]
so \(\widetilde D^0(M)\) is without finite torsion. Applying these
statements once more shows that \(t^1(M)\) is finite torsion and
\(t^0(M)\) is without finite torsion.

If \(A\) is finite torsion and \(B\) is without finite torsion, then
every morphism \(A\to B\) vanishes. Indeed, this follows from the
naturality of \(t^1(X)\to X\), since \(t^1(A)=A\) and \(t^1(B)=0\).
Consequently, every finite-torsion subobject \(A\hookrightarrow M\)
maps trivially to \(t^0(M)\) and therefore lies in \(t^1(M)\).
Likewise, every quotient \(M\twoheadrightarrow B\) without finite
torsion kills \(t^1(M)\) and hence factors through \(t^0(M)\). This
proves (1).

For (2), apply the contravariant functor \(\widetilde D^0\) to the
quotient tower. It gives an ascending chain
\[
\cdots\hookrightarrow\widetilde D^0(M/M_i)
 \hookrightarrow\widetilde D^0(M/M_{i+1})
 \hookrightarrow\cdots\hookrightarrow\widetilde D^0(M).
\]
By \Cref{diagonal category is Noetherian}, this chain stabilizes. Biduality on
objects without finite torsion then shows that the quotients
\(M/M_i\), and hence the subobjects \(M_i\), stabilize as well.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{elementary finite-torsion objects}
Let \(N\) be a finite-type Dieudonn\'e module.

{\rm (1)} If \(N\) has finite \(W\)-length, then \(N\) is finite
torsion.

{\rm (2)} If \(N\) is finite free over \(W\), then \(N\) is without
finite torsion.

{\rm (3)} Every elementary domino \(U_i\) is without finite torsion.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
A Dieudonn\'e module is unchanged by Nygaard modification. If \(N\)
has finite \(W\)-length, then
\[
R\mathrm{Hom}_W(N,W)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_W(N,K/W)[-1]
\]
is concentrated in cohomological degree \(1\). Hence total duality
shows that \(\mathrm{Tot}(D(N)(\varphi))\) has amplitude \([1,1]\) for every
Nygaard modification \(\varphi\). By \Cref{dcamplitude}, \(D(N)\) has
diagonal amplitude \([1,1]\). Thus \(\widetilde D^0(N)=0\), and the
biduality sequence reduces to \(t^1(N)\simeq N\). This proves (1).

If \(N\) is finite free over \(W\), then
\(R\mathrm{Hom}_W(N,W)=\mathrm{Hom}_W(N,W)\) is concentrated in degree \(0\). The
same argument shows that \(D(N)\) has diagonal amplitude \([0,0]\).
Consequently, \(\widetilde D^1(N)=0\) and \(t^1(N)=0\), proving (2).

We first show that no elementary domino \(U_r\) is finite torsion.
Suppose otherwise. Since
\(U_r=t^1(U_r)=\widetilde D^1\widetilde D^1(U_r)\), the cross-vanishing
\(\widetilde D^0\widetilde D^1=0\) gives
\(\widetilde D^0(U_r)=0\). Hence
\[
D(U_r)\simeq\widetilde D^1(U_r)[-1].
\]
Choose a Nygaard modification \(\varphi\) such that
\(U_r(\varphi)\simeq U_s\) with \(s<0\). Then
\(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(U_r(\varphi)))\neq0\). This group has finite
\(W\)-length, so total duality gives
\[
\mathrm{H}^0\!\left(\mathrm{Tot}(D(U_r(\varphi)))\right)\neq0.
\]
On the other hand, compatibility of duality with Nygaard modification
gives
\[
D(U_r(\varphi))
 \simeq\widetilde D^1(U_r)(\text{-}\varphi\text{-})[-1].
\]
The object \(\widetilde D^1(U_r)(\text{-}\varphi\text{-})\) lies in \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\), so
its total complex has amplitude \([0,1]\). After shifting by \([-1]\),
it has no cohomology in degree \(0\), a contradiction.

Finally, suppose that \(t^1(U_i)\neq0\). It is a finite-torsion
subobject of \(U_i\). By \Cref{subobjects of diagonal modules}, it is
an actual diagonal \(R\)-module; the classification of subobjects of a
one-dimensional domino identifies it with some \(U_r\). This
contradicts the preceding paragraph. Thus \(t^1(U_i)=0\).
<!-- end proof-15 -->

{\rm (1)} The object \(M\) is finite torsion if and only if every
\(\mathrm{H}^i(M)(-i)\) is a finite-length Dieudonn\'e module. In this case,
\[
M\cong\bigoplus_i\mathrm{H}^i(M)[-i].
\]

{\rm (2)} If \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}}

\!\cap R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\), then \(M\) is
without finite torsion if and only if \(\text{\rm {c\oe ur}}(M^0)\) is torsion free.

{\rm (3)} The object \(M\) is without finite torsion if and only if
every \(\mathrm{H}^i(M)(-i)\) is without finite torsion.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By \Cref{without finite torsion implies artinian}(1), finite-torsion
objects are closed under quotients, extensions, and direct summands,
whereas objects without finite torsion are closed under subobjects and
extensions.

We first prove (1). Suppose that \(M\) is finite torsion, and let \(r\)
be the largest integer for which \(\mathrm{H}^r(M)\neq0\). Since the ordinary
and diagonal truncations commute, the canonical map
\(M\twoheadrightarrow\mathrm{H}^r(M)[-r]\) is an epimorphism in \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\).
Hence
\[
N_r:=\mathrm{H}^r(M)(-r)\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\!\cap R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}
\]
is finite torsion.

The diagonal module \(N_r\) is an extension of a finite-type
Dieudonn\'e module by a coherent domino. If its domino quotient were
nonzero, it would have an elementary domino \(U_i\) as a quotient.
That quotient would be finite torsion, contradicting
\Cref{elementary finite-torsion objects}(3). Thus \(N_r\) is a
Dieudonn\'e module.

If \(N_r\) were not of finite \(W\)-length, its quotient by its
\(W\)-torsion would be a nonzero finite free Dieudonn\'e module. This
would again be a finite-torsion quotient of \(N_r\), contradicting
\Cref{elementary finite-torsion objects}(2). Consequently, \(N_r\) is
a finite-length Dieudonn\'e module.

The cohomology of \(M\) is now cut at the boundary between internal
degrees \(-r\) and \(1-r\). The two grading blocks in the cut category
therefore separate the ordinary truncation triangle, giving
\[
M\simeq\tau_{\leqslant r-1}M
 \oplus\mathrm{H}^r(M)[-r].
\]
The first summand is again finite torsion. Induction on the ordinary
cohomological amplitude gives
\[
M\simeq\bigoplus_i\mathrm{H}^i(M)[-i],
\]
and every \(\mathrm{H}^i(M)(-i)\) is a finite-length Dieudonn\'e module.

Conversely, suppose that every \(\mathrm{H}^i(M)(-i)\) is a finite-length
Dieudonn\'e module. Repeating the same cut argument splits the ordinary
cohomology filtration and gives the displayed decomposition. Each
summand is finite torsion by
\Cref{elementary finite-torsion objects}(1), and hence so is \(M\).
This proves (1).

We next prove (3). If every \(\mathrm{H}^i(M)(-i)\) is without finite torsion,
then so is \(M\), because such objects are closed under extensions.

Conversely, suppose that \(M\) is without finite torsion, and let \(r\)
be its largest nonzero ordinary cohomological degree. The subobject
\(\tau_{\leqslant r-1}M\subseteq M\) is without finite torsion, so
induction treats all lower cohomology objects. After a twist, we may
assume \(r=0\) and write
\[
0\longrightarrow\tau_{\leqslant-1}M\longrightarrow M
\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^0(M)\longrightarrow0.
\]
For an object \(X\) without finite torsion, one has
\(\widetilde D^1(X)=0\): indeed, \(\widetilde D^1(X)\) is finite
torsion and
\(t^1(\widetilde D^1(X))=\widetilde D^1(t^1(X))=0\). Thus the long
exact sequence for the dual contains
\[
\widetilde D^0(M)\xrightarrow{\phi}
\widetilde D^0(\tau_{\leqslant-1}M)\longrightarrow\widetilde D^1(\mathrm{H}^0(M))
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Put \(T=\operatorname{im}(\phi)\) and
\(N=\widetilde D^0(T)\). Naturality and biduality give a monomorphism
\(N\hookrightarrow\widetilde D^0\widetilde D^0(M)\simeq M\) and an
exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow\tau_{\leqslant-1}M\longrightarrow N
 \longrightarrow t^1(\mathrm{H}^0(M))\longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular, \(N\) is without finite torsion.

The object \(t^1(\mathrm{H}^0(M))\) is a subobject of the actual diagonal module
\(\mathrm{H}^0(M)\). By \Cref{subobjects of diagonal modules}, it is itself an actual
diagonal module, and by (1) it is a finite-length Dieudonn\'e module.
It follows that \(N\) is cut at internal degree \(0\), so the last exact
sequence splits. Thus \(t^1(\mathrm{H}^0(M))\) is a direct summand of the object \(N\)
without finite torsion. Since it is itself finite torsion, it must
vanish. Hence \(\mathrm{H}^0(M)\) is without finite torsion, completing the induction
and proving (3).

Finally, let \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\!\cap R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\). By
\Cref{subobjects of diagonal modules}, every finite-torsion subobject
of \(M\) is an actual diagonal \(R\)-module. Part (1) shows that these
are precisely the finite-length Dieudonn\'e submodules of \(M\). They
all lie in
\[
V^{-\infty}ZM^0=\text{\rm {c\oe ur}}(M^0),
\]
and every \(W\)-torsion element of \(\text{\rm {c\oe ur}}(M^0)\) generates a
finite-length Dieudonn\'e submodule. Therefore \(M\) contains no
nonzero finite-torsion subobject if and only if \(\text{\rm {c\oe ur}}(M^0)\) is
torsion free. This proves (2).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{R-modules cut at I}
Let \(\mathrm{I}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\). A graded \(R\)-module \(M\) is said to be
cut at \(\mathrm{I}\) if
\[
d:M^i\longrightarrow M^{i+1}
\]
is zero for every \(i\in\mathrm{I}\). We denote the abelian category of such
modules, with grading-preserving morphisms, by
\(R\text{-}\mathrm{Cut}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\).
A complex in \(D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Cut}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) is called coherent if its
image in \(D(R)\) is coherent. We write
\(D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{Cut}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) for the bounded coherent subcategory.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{D_c^b(R-Cut-I)}
The natural functor
\[
D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{Cut}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\longrightarrow D_c^b(R)
\]
is fully faithful. Its essential image consists of those complexes
\(M\) for which every cohomology module \(\mathrm{H}^q(M)\) is cut at \(\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By d\'evissage along
cohomological truncations, full faithfulness reduces to comparing the
grading-preserving derived Hom complexes of coherent modules \(M,N\)
cut at \(\mathrm{I}\).

Partition the grading indices into maximal consecutive blocks
\(\mathrm J_\alpha\) by cutting between \(i\) and \(i+1\) for every
\(i\in\mathrm{I}\). Since the differentials across these cuts vanish, we have
decompositions into \(R\)-submodules
\[
M=\bigoplus_\alpha M_\alpha,\qquad
N=\bigoplus_\alpha N_\alpha,
\]
where \(M_\alpha\) and \(N_\alpha\) are supported in
\(\mathrm J_\alpha\). Only finitely many summands are nonzero. Within
each block, imposing the cuts does not change the degree-preserving
derived Hom complex:
\[
R\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}\mathrm{Cut}\text{-}\mathrm{I}}
 (M_\alpha,N_\alpha)^0
 \simeq
R\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_\alpha,N_\alpha)^0.
\]
Between distinct blocks, derived Hom vanishes in the cut category, and
\[
R\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_\alpha,N_\beta)^0=0
\qquad(\alpha\neq\beta)
\]
follows by d\'evissage from Ekedahl's calculation \cite[Proposition~0.4.1]{Ek3},
as in the proof of \cite[Proposition~0.5.1]{Ek3}. Here \(0\) denotes
internal, not cohomological, degree. Summing over the blocks proves
full faithfulness.

Cohomology preserves the cut condition, so every object in the image
has the stated property. Conversely, let \(M\in D_c^b(R)\) have
cohomology cut at \(\mathrm{I}\), and argue by induction on its cohomological
amplitude \([a,b]\). The case \(a=b\) follows from
\(M\simeq\mathrm{H}^a(M)[-a]\). Otherwise, choose \(a\leqslant q<b\) and
consider
\[
\tau_{\leqslant q}M\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow
\tau_{\geqslant q+1}M
\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }(\tau_{\leqslant q}M)[1].
\]
By induction, the two truncations come from objects \(M_1,M_2\) of
\(D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{Cut}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\). Full faithfulness lifts \(\varphi\)
to \(\widetilde\varphi:M_2\to M_1[1]\), and
\[
M'=\operatorname{Cone}(\widetilde\varphi)[-1]
\]
maps to an object isomorphic to \(M\). This proves the assertion about
the essential image.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
We henceforth identify \(D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{Cut}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) with its
essential image in \(D_c^b(R)\). Thus a coherent complex is cut at
\(\mathrm{I}\) when its cohomology modules are, or equivalently when it has a
representative cut at \(\mathrm{I}\) termwise.
<!-- end remark-3 -->

complexes cut at \(\mathbb{Z}\) form a triangulated subcategory. For an actual diagonal module \(A\), the structure
theorem shows that \(A\) is Hodge--Witt precisely when \(A^0\) is
finitely generated over \(W\): a nonzero domino quotient contains a
copy of \(k[[V]]\) in degree zero.

{\rm (1)} The object \(M\) is Hodge--Witt if and only if its
\(p\)-torsion subobject
\({}_pM:=\ker_{

<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
For (1), closure under subobjects gives the forward implication.
For the converse, first suppose \(N\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\,

  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\!\cap R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\). Here
\(p:N\to N\) is the scalar map \(p\operatorname{id}_N\) in \(D(R)\),
so it induces multiplication by \(p\) on ordinary cohomology. Write
\(P=\operatorname{im}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(p)\). By
\Cref{subobjects of diagonal modules}, both \({}_pN\) and \(P\) are actual diagonal
modules, and \(P^0\hookrightarrow N^0\). Ordinary cohomology of
\(0\to{}_pN\to N\to P\to0\), together with the factorization
\(p:N\twoheadrightarrow P\hookrightarrow N\), therefore gives
\(({}_pN)^0=\ker(N^0\to P^0)=\ker(p:N^0\to N^0)\).

Set \(C=V^{-\infty}ZN^0\). If \({}_pN\) is Hodge--Witt, then \(({}_pN)^0\)
has finite \(W\)-length. The finite-type Dieudonn\'e module \(C\) also
has \(C/pC\) of finite length, so the snake lemma applied to
\(0\to C\to N^0\to N^0/C\to0\) makes
\(\ker(p:N^0/C\to N^0/C)\) finite. If \(N^0/C\neq0\), its domino
filtration places a copy of \(k[[V]]\) in this kernel, a contradiction.
Thus \(C=N^0\), and \(N\) is Hodge--Witt.

For general \(M\), induct on its ordinary cohomological amplitude and
let \(r\) be maximal with \(\mathrm{H}^r(M)\neq0\). Since
\({}_p(\tau_{\leqslant r-1}M)\) is a subobject of \({}_pM\), induction
shows that \(\tau_{\leqslant r-1}M\) is Hodge--Witt. The snake lemma
for \(0\to\tau_{\leqslant r-1}M\to M\to\mathrm{H}^r(M)[-r]\to0\), together
with the preceding proposition, shows that
\({}_p(\mathrm{H}^r(M)[-r])\) is Hodge--Witt. The actual-module case, after shifting both gradings, shows that
\(\mathrm{H}^r(M)[-r]\) is Hodge--Witt. Closure under extensions completes
the induction.

For (2), if \(M\) is Hodge--Witt, choose a representative cut at
\(\mathbb{Z}\) using \Cref{D_c^b(R-Cut-I)}. Nygaard modification only
Frobenius-twists its columns, and diagonal support gives
\(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(M(\varphi)))=0\) for every \(\varphi\).

Conversely, first take \(N\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\!\cap R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\). If \(N\)
is not Hodge--Witt, its nonzero domino quotient has an elementary
quotient \(U_t\). Exactness of Nygaard modification, the long exact
sequence of total cohomology, and \Cref{Basic Vanishing}(1) give a
surjection \(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(N(\varphi)))\twoheadrightarrow
\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(U_t(\varphi)))\). Taking \(\varphi_n=-n\delta_1\) gives
\(U_t(\varphi_n)\simeq U_{t-n}\), whose degree-one total
cohomology has length \(\max\{0,n-t\}\). Thus the lengths for
\(N\) are unbounded.

For general \(M\), let \(r\) again be its largest nonzero ordinary
cohomological degree. Applied to \(M(\varphi)\), \Cref{dcDegen}(2)
passes the uniform bound to the modifications of \(\mathrm{H}^r(M)(-r)\), up
to reindexing \(\varphi\) under the twist. The actual-module case makes
\(\mathrm{H}^r(M)[-r]\) Hodge--Witt. The cut between internal degrees \(-r\)
and \(1-r\) then gives
\(M\simeq\tau_{\leqslant r-1}M\oplus\mathrm{H}^r(M)[-r]\). The lower summand
inherits the bound, and induction completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{derived Hodge--Witt criterion}
Let \(M\in D_c^b(R)\). Then \(M\) is Hodge--Witt if and only if the
torsion lengths of \(\mathrm{H}^*(\mathrm{Tot}(M(\varphi)))\) are uniformly bounded in
\(\varphi\).
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
If \(M\) is Hodge--Witt, choose a representative cut at \(\mathbb{Z}\) using
\Cref{D_c^b(R-Cut-I)}. Nygaard modification only Frobenius-twists its
horizontal columns, so the torsion lengths of its total cohomology are
unchanged.

Conversely, \Cref{dcamplitude}(1) identifies
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M(\varphi))\) with \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M)(\varphi)\), while
\Cref{Totsubquo}(1) gives injections
\(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M)(\varphi)))\hookrightarrow
\mathrm{H}^{j+1}(\mathrm{Tot}(M(\varphi)))\). The sources are torsion by
\Cref{Basic Vanishing}(1), so their lengths are uniformly bounded.
By \Cref{Hodge--Witt criterion}(2), every \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^j(M)\) is therefore
Hodge--Witt, and so is \(M\) by its diagonal cohomology filtration.
<!-- end proof-20 -->

<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{HW of cohomology equals cohomology of HW}
For every \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]

}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{
