\). Taking dimensions gives the stated formulas.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{two fundamental filtrations}
For every \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\), there are two canonical functorial filtrations
\[
\begin{aligned}
0\subseteq F^1\subseteq F^2\subseteq F^3=M,\\
0\subseteq G^1\subseteq G^2\subseteq G^3=M,
\end{aligned}
\]
characterized as follows.

{\rm (i)} \(F^1\) is the largest \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion subobject of
\(M\), and \(M/F^2\) is the largest \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient
of \(M/F^1\).

{\rm (ii)} \(M/G^2\) is the largest \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient
of \(M\), and \(G^1\) is the largest \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion subobject
of \(G^2\).

Here a largest quotient means a quotient through which every quotient
of the specified kind factors. The filtrations satisfy:

{\rm (1)} \(G^1=F^1\cap G^2\) and \(F^2=F^1+G^2\).

{\rm (2)} There are canonical isomorphisms
\[
F^2/F^1\simeq G^2/G^1,\qquad F^1/G^1\simeq F^2/G^2.
\]
The first object is Mazur--Ogus, and the second is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic.

{\rm (3)} There is a canonical decomposition
\[
F^2/G^1\simeq (F^2/F^1)\oplus(F^1/G^1).
\]
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
By \Cref{sub and quotient object of Tot-torsion objects}, the
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion objects are closed under quotients and extensions,
so their subobjects in \(M\) are closed under finite sums.
Noetherianity therefore gives a largest such subobject \(F^1\).
Similarly, the kernels of \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotients are closed
under finite intersections, since this class is closed under subobjects
and extensions. These quotients are without finite torsion, so
\Cref{without finite torsion implies artinian}(2) gives a smallest
such kernel \(G^2\). Thus \(M/G^2\) is the largest
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient of \(M\).
Applying the same constructions to \(M/F^1\) and \(G^2\) gives
\(F^2\) and \(G^1\). Functoriality follows from the defining
properties: morphisms preserve \(F^1\) because its images are
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion, and preserve \(G^2\) because the image in
any \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient is again \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion.

Put \(C=F^1/(F^1\cap G^2)\). As a quotient of \(F^1\) and a
subobject of \(M/G^2\), it is both \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion and
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion, hence \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic.
Thus \(\mathrm{Tot}(F^1\cap G^2)\simeq\mathrm{Tot}(F^1)\), so
\(F^1\cap G^2\subseteq G^1\). The reverse inclusion follows from
\(G^1\subseteq F^1\), giving \(G^1=F^1\cap G^2\).
Likewise, quotienting \(M/G^2\) by \(C\) does not change its
totalization, so \(M/(F^1+G^2)\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion.
The defining property of \(M/F^2\) gives \(F^2\subseteq F^1+G^2\).
Conversely, \(M/F^2\) is a \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient of
\(M\), so \(G^2\subseteq F^2\), proving \(F^2=F^1+G^2\).
This proves (1), the isomorphisms in (2), and the acyclicity of
\(F^1/G^1\).

By maximality of \(F^1\), the quotient \(M/F^1\) has no nonzero
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion subobject: its inverse image would be a
larger such subobject of \(M\). Similarly, \(G^2\) has no nonzero
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient, since any such quotient
\(G^2/K\) would make \(M/K\) a larger \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion
quotient of \(M\). Here both assertions use closure under extensions.
Consequently, for every \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic object \(N\), any map
\(N\to F^2/F^1\) or \(G^2/G^1\to N\) has zero image.
By \Cref{Mazur-Ogus objects}, the common quotient
\(F^2/F^1\simeq G^2/G^1\) is Mazur--Ogus, completing (2).

Finally, (1) shows that \(G^2/G^1\) and \(F^1/G^1\) have zero
intersection and sum to \(F^2/G^1\). Their inclusions give the
canonical decomposition in (3), using
\(G^2/G^1\simeq F^2/F^1\).
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{total cohomology of the two fundamental filtrations}
For the filtrations of \Cref{two fundamental filtrations}, there are
canonical isomorphisms
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(F^1))
  &\simeq \operatorname{tors}\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
   \simeq \mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(G^1)),\\
\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(F^2/F^1))
  &\simeq \mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))/\operatorname{tors}
   \simeq \mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(G^2/G^1)),\\
\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(F^3/F^2))
  &\simeq \mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
   \simeq \mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(G^3/G^2)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\operatorname{tors}\) denotes the \(W\)-torsion submodule.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{The t-structure: G}
Let \((\widetilde D_g^{\leqslant0},\widetilde D_g^{\geqslant0})\) be the t-structure on \(D_c^b(R)\) associated
with this radical filtration, and let
\[
 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
_g:=\widetilde D_g^{\leqslant0}\cap\widetilde D_g^{\geqslant0}
\]
be its heart, and put \(\widetilde D_g^{[m,n]}:=\widetilde D_g^{\geqslant m}\cap\widetilde D_g^{\leqslant n}\). We write \(\tau^g_{\leqslant i}\) and
\(\tau^g_{\geqslant i}\) for its truncation functors and set
\[
\mathrm{H}_g^i(-)=
\tau^g_{\leqslant i}\tau^g_{\geqslant i}(-)[i].
\]
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{criteria for G-amplitude [m n]}
Let \(M\in D_c^b(R)\). Then \(M\in\widetilde D_g^{[m,n]}\) if
and only if \(\mathrm{Tot}(M)\) has amplitude \([m,n]\) and
\[
h^{i,j}:=\dim_k\mathrm{H}^j(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^i=0
\]
unless \(m-2\leqslant i+j\leqslant n\).
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By definition, \(M\in\widetilde D_g^{[m,n]}\) precisely when
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^q(M)=0\) for \(q\notin[m-1,n]\),
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{m-1}(M)\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion, and
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)\) has no nonzero \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient.
We compare these three conditions with the two bounds in the statement.

Suppose these conditions hold. The last condition and
\Cref{total cohomology of the two fundamental filtrations} give
\(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)))=0\), while
\(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{m-1}(M)))=0\). Thus \Cref{Totsubquo}(1) places
\(\mathrm{Tot}(M)\) in degrees \([m,n]\).
Every morphism from \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)\) to \(U_0[t](-t)\) is zero: its image
would be a \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient of \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)\).
Hence \Cref{Hodge numbers in degree plus minus 1} gives
\(h^{i,j}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M))=0\) for \(i+j=1\).
By \Cref{Basic Vanishing}(2), the reduction of each
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^q(M)[-q]\) has Hodge numbers only in total degrees
\([q-1,q+1]\), with the upper degree absent for \(q=n\).
The diagonal cohomology filtration therefore gives
\(h^{i,j}(M)=0\) outside \([m-2,n]\).

Conversely, assume the stated bounds on total cohomology and Hodge
numbers. By \Cref{Totsubquo}(1), \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^q(M)\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic for
\(q<m-1\) or \(q>n\), and
\(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{m-1}(M)))=\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)))=0\).
The first step is to show that the acyclic terms outside \([m-1,n]\)
actually vanish.
If \(M=0\), there is nothing to prove; otherwise let \(a\) and \(b\)
be its lowest and highest nonzero diagonal cohomological degrees.

If \(b>n\), choose a simple quotient
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^b(M)\twoheadrightarrow U_0[t](-t)\) using
\Cref{simple Tot acyclic objects are U_0^i}.
The composite \(M\to \widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^b(M)[-b]\to U_0[t-b](-t)\) is nonzero,
as its \(b\)-th diagonal cohomology is the chosen quotient.
By \Cref{Hodge numbers in degree plus minus 1}, this gives
\(h^{t+1,b-t}(M)\neq0\), contradicting the hypothesis since \(b+1>n\).
Similarly, if \(a<m-1\), a simple subobject
\(U_0[t](-t)\hookrightarrow \widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^a(M)\) gives a nonzero composite
\(U_0[t-a](-t)\to \widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^a(M)[-a]\to M\).
The same formula gives \(h^{t+1,a-t-2}(M)\neq0\), contradicting the hypothesis since \(a-1<m-2\). Thus \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^q(M)=0\) outside \([m-1,n]\), and
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{m-1}(M)\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion.

It remains to exclude a nonzero \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient
\(Q\) of \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)\). Since \(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)))=0\), the long exact
sequence gives \(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(Q))=0\); hence \(Q\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. A simple quotient of \(Q\) would give a nonzero
map \(M\to \widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^n(M)[-n]\to U_0[t-n](-t)\), and therefore
\(h^{t+1,n-t}(M)\neq0\), again a contradiction.
All three defining conditions are satisfied.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{simple Tot acyclic objects are U_0^i}
The \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic diagonal dominos form an abelian category in which every object has finite length.
Its simple objects are the \(U_0[i](-i)\).
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Each \(U_0[i](-i)\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic and has no proper nonzero
acyclic subobject, so it is simple. Closure under kernels and cokernels
follows from the long exact sequence of total cohomology. The category
is Noetherian because \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) is Noetherian, and Artinian by
\Cref{without finite torsion implies artinian}(2); thus it is a length
category.

Let \(M\) be simple. If every morphism between \(M\) and every shifted
\(U_0\) vanished, \Cref{Hodge numbers in degree plus minus 1} would
give \(h^{i,j}(M)=0\) whenever \(i+j=\pm1\). The Hodge--de Rham
spectral sequence and \(\mathrm{Tot}(M)=0\) would then force all Hodge groups,
and hence \(M\), to vanish. Therefore \(M\) has a nonzero morphism to
or from some \(U_0[i](-i)\); simplicity makes it an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{definition of F-gauge structure}
An \(F\)-gauge is a graded \(W\)-module
\(M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}M^i\), equipped with \(W\)-linear operators
\(\widetilde{F}\) and \(\widetilde{V}\) of degrees \(1\) and \(-1\), respectively, such
that \(\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=p\), together with a \(\sigma\)-linear
isomorphism
\[
\tau:M^\infty\xrightarrow{\sim}M^{-\infty}.
\]
For an interval \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\), the gauge \(M\) has level \(\mathrm{I}\) if
\(\widetilde{F}:M^i\to M^{i+1}\) is an isomorphism for \(i\geq n\) and
\(\widetilde{V}:M^i\to M^{i-1}\) is an isomorphism for \(i\leq m\).

We denote the category of \(F\)-gauges over \(k\) by \({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\), and
its full subcategory of gauges of level \(\mathrm{I}\) by \({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{definition of G_r}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\). The evaluation functor
\[
T^r:{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ab},\qquad T^r(M)=M^r,
\]
is represented by a projective \(F\)-gauge \(G_r\).
The object \(G_r\) is generated by an element \(\alpha_r\in G_r^r\), together with all of its iterated images under \(\widetilde{F}\), \(\widetilde{V}\), \(\tau\), and \(\tau^{-1}\). More explicitly,
\[
G_r^r=\bigoplus_{l=0}^{\infty}W\left(\widetilde{F}^{\,r-m}\tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-r}\right)^l\alpha_r+\bigoplus_{l=1}^{\infty}W\left(\widetilde{V}^{\,n-r}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{\,r-m}\right)^l\alpha_r.
\]

For \(m\leqslant i<r\),
\[
G_r^i=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{\infty}W\widetilde{F}^{\,i-m}\tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-r}\left(\widetilde{F}^{\,r-m}\tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-r}\right)^{l-1}\alpha_r+\bigoplus_{l=0}^{\infty}W\widetilde{V}^{\,r-i}\left(\widetilde{V}^{\,n-r}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{\,r-m}\right)^l\alpha_r.
\]

For \(r<i\leqslant n\),
\[
G_r^i=\bigoplus_{l=0}^{\infty}W\widetilde{F}^{\,i-r}\left(\widetilde{F}^{\,r-m}\tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-r}\right)^l\alpha_r+\bigoplus_{l=1}^{\infty}W\widetilde{V}^{\,n-i}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{\,r-m}\left(\widetilde{V}^{\,n-r}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{\,r-m}\right)^{l-1}\alpha_r.
\]
The operators \(\widetilde{F}\) and \(\widetilde{V}\) act on these generators as indicated
by their expressions. The identification
\(\tau:G_r^\infty\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}G_r^{-\infty}\)
completes the gauge structure. By construction, for every
\(M\in {F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}{\mathrm{I}}\), \(\mathrm{Hom}_{{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}{\mathrm{I}}}(G_r,M)\cong M^r\):
a morphism \(G_r\to M\) is determined uniquely by the image of
\(\alpha_r\).
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{definition of FG}
For a graded left \(R\)-module \(M\), let \(F\mathsf{G}(M)\) be the following
complex of \(F\)-gauges:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[
  row sep=large, column sep=large,
  execute at end picture={
    \foreach \r/\degree in {2/{i+1},3/i,4/{i-1}} {
      \draw[blue!55!gray, thin, rounded corners=2pt]
        ([xshift=-6pt,yshift=15pt]\tikzcdmatrixname-\r-1.center)
        rectangle
        ([xshift=6pt,yshift=-15pt]\tikzcdmatrixname-\r-5.center);
      \node[anchor=west, text=blue!55!gray, font=\small]
        at ([xshift=12pt]\tikzcdmatrixname-\r-5.center)
        {complex degree \(\degree\)};
    }
    \foreach \c/\degree in {2/{i-1},3/i,4/{i+1}} {
      \draw[orange!75!black, thin, rounded corners=2pt]
        ([xshift=-27pt,yshift=10pt]\tikzcdmatrixname-1-\c.center)
        rectangle
        ([xshift=27pt,yshift=-10pt]\tikzcdmatrixname-5-\c.center);
      \node[anchor=north, text=orange!75!black, font=\small,
            align=center]
        at ([yshift=-16pt]\tikzcdmatrixname-5-\c.center)
        {\(F\)-gauge\\degree \(\degree\)};
    }
  }
]
& \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \\
\cdots \arrow[r,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
& M^{i+1} \arrow[u,"d"] \arrow[l,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
& M^{i+1} \arrow[u,"d"] \arrow[l,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
& M^{i+1} \arrow[u,"d"] \arrow[l,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"F",shift left=0.6ex]
& \cdots \arrow[l,"V",shift left=0.6ex] \\
\cdots \arrow[r,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
& M^i \arrow[u,"d"] \arrow[l,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
& M^i \arrow[u,"d"] \arrow[l,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"F",shift left=0.6ex]
& \sigma_*M^i \arrow[u,"dV"] \arrow[l,"V",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex]
& \cdots \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex] \\
\cdots \arrow[r,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
& M^{i-1} \arrow[u,"d"] \arrow[l,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"F",shift left=0.6ex]
& \sigma_*M^{i-1} \arrow[u,"dV"] \arrow[l,"V",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex]
& \sigma_*M^{i-1} \arrow[u,"d"] \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex] \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}",shift left=0.6ex]
& \cdots \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex] \\
& \vdots \arrow[u,"dV"] & \vdots \arrow[u,"d"] & \vdots \arrow[u,"d"] &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Here the rightward arrows are \(\widetilde{F}\), the leftward arrows are
\(\widetilde{V}\), and the upward arrows are the cohomological differential.
More explicitly:

\smallskip
\noindent{\rm (1)} In gauge degree \(i\) and cohomological degree \(j\), set
\[
F\mathsf{G}(M)^{i,j}=
\begin{cases}
M^j,&i\leqslant j,\\
\sigma_*M^j,&i>j.
\end{cases}
\]

\noindent{\rm (2)} In each row \(j\), the maps
\(\widetilde{F}:F\mathsf{G}(M)^{i,j}\toF\mathsf{G}(M)^{i+1,j}\) and
\(\widetilde{V}:F\mathsf{G}(M)^{i+1,j}\toF\mathsf{G}(M)^{i,j}\) are
\[
(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})=
\begin{cases}
(p,\mathrm{id}),&i<j,\\
(F,V),&i=j,\\
(\mathrm{id},p),&i>j.
\end{cases}
\]

\noindent{\rm (3)} In each column \(i\), the complex \(F\mathsf{G}(M)^i\) is
\[
\cdots\longrightarrow\sigma_*M^{i-2}
\xrightarrow{d}\sigma_*M^{i-1}
\xrightarrow{dV}M^i\xrightarrow{d}M^{i+1}
\longrightarrow\cdots.
\]
Thus \(F\mathsf{G}(M)^i=\mathrm{Tot}(M(\varphi^i))\), where
\(\varphi^i(a)=-\delta_{i,a}\), as in \Cref{Nygaard modification}.
The vertical maps commute with \(\widetilde{F}\) and \(\widetilde{V}\) by the Raynaud relations.

\smallskip
\noindent{\rm (4)} The limiting complexes are
\(F\mathsf{G}(M)^\infty=\sigma_*\mathrm{Tot}(M)\) and
\(F\mathsf{G}(M)^{-\infty}=\mathrm{Tot}(M)\).
The operator \(\tau:F\mathsf{G}(M)^\infty\toF\mathsf{G}(M)^{-\infty}\) is the
canonical semilinear identification, given by the identity on the
underlying complexes.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{definition of FG^Tot}
For a fixed interval \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\), the functor \(F\mathsf{G}\) restricts to
\[
F\mathsf{G}:R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I}
\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ch}_{\mathrm{I}}({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}).
\]
Its totalization therefore induces
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}:D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})
\longrightarrow D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}).
\]
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{Nygaard filtration and Hodge filtration}
Let \(M\in D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).
There is a natural diagram in \(D(W)\), commuting up to signs, whose rows and columns are distinguished triangles:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small,row sep=large]
{F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i,\bullet}}
 \arrow[r,"\widetilde{F}"] \arrow[d,"\widetilde{V}"'] &
{F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i+1,\bullet}}
 \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\widetilde{V}"'] &
{(t_{\geqslant i+1}\mathrm{Hod}(M))^\bullet}
 \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d] & {}\\
{F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i-1,\bullet}}
 \arrow[r,"\widetilde{F}"] \arrow[d] &
{F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i,\bullet}}
 \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &
{(t_{\geqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(M))^\bullet}
 \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d] & {}\\
{\sigma_*(\tau_{\leqslant i-1}\mathrm{Hod}(M))^\bullet}
 \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"+1"'] &
{\sigma_*(\tau_{\leqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(M))^\bullet}
 \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"+1"'] &
{(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^{i,\bullet}[-i]}
 \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d,"+1"'] & {}\\
{} & {} & {} & {}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The rightmost triangle is the first triangle of
\eqref{Hodge filtration triangles}; the bottom triangle is
\(\sigma_*\) applied to its second triangle.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
We make the comparison maps of \cite[Proposition~II.3.4]{Ek3} explicit.
Choose a common semi-free resolution \(P\to M\) in complexes of
graded \(R\)-modules. Its terms are \(p\)-torsion-free and flat over
\(R\), so both \(R_1\otimes_RP\) and \(Z_1\otimes_RP\) compute
derived tensor products. All maps below are defined before
totalization and commute with the differential of \(P\).
It therefore suffices to describe them on a graded free
\(R\)-module \(L\), a term of \(P\).

Since \(FV=VF=p\), the maps \(F,V\) on \(L\) are injective.
Consequently the two gauge maps are termwise injective, and their
ordinary quotient complexes represent their cones. Put
\[
Q_{F,i}(L):=\operatorname{coker}
 \bigl(\widetilde{F}:F\mathsf{G}(L)^{i-1,\bullet}\to F\mathsf{G}(L)^{i,\bullet}\bigr),\qquad
Q_{V,i}(L):=\operatorname{coker}
 \bigl(\widetilde{V}:F\mathsf{G}(L)^{i+1,\bullet}\to F\mathsf{G}(L)^{i,\bullet}\bigr).
\]
The definition of the gauge maps gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{F,i}(L)&=
 \bigl(0\longrightarrow \sigma_*L^{i-1}/F L^{i-1}
 \xrightarrow{dV} L^i/pL^i\xrightarrow{d}L^{i+1}/pL^{i+1}
 \longrightarrow\cdots\bigr),\\
Q_{V,i}(L)&=
 \bigl(\cdots\xrightarrow{d}\sigma_*(L^{i-1}/pL^{i-1})
 \xrightarrow{dV}L^i/V L^i\longrightarrow0\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the images of \(F:L^{i-1}\to\sigma_*L^{i-1}\) and
\(V:\sigma_*L^i\to L^i\) are understood with their indicated
scalar actions. The terms retain their original horizontal degrees.

Set \(A_L=R_1\otimes_RL\) and \(Z_L=Z_1\otimes_RL\).
The first comparison sends the degree \(i-1\) term to zero and is
the quotient map in every degree \(a\geqslant i\):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] &
{\sigma_*L^{i-1}/F L^{i-1}} \arrow[r,"dV"] \arrow[d] &
{L^i/pL^i} \arrow[r,"d"] \arrow[d] &
{L^{i+1}/pL^{i+1}} \arrow[r] \arrow[d] & \cdots\\
0 \arrow[r] & 0 \arrow[r] &
{A_L^i} \arrow[r,"d"] &
{A_L^{i+1}} \arrow[r] & \cdots .
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Indeed, \(A_L^a=L^a/(VL^a+dVL^{a-1})\), so the quotient maps
are well defined and kill the displayed \(dV\).
After totalization this is a map
\[
Q_{F,i}(L)\longrightarrow t_{\geqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(L).
\]

For the second comparison, recall that
\(Z_L^i=\ker(d:A_L^i\to A_L^{i+1})\), since \(L\) is flat.
The presentation of \(\sigma_*Z_1\) identifies
\(\sigma_*Z_L^i\cong L^i/(VL^i+dV^2L^{i-1})\), with \(F\otimes x\) corresponding to the class of \(x\). Consider the following comparison:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\cdots \arrow[r,"d"] &
{\sigma_*(L^{i-1}/pL^{i-1})}
 \arrow[r,"dV"] \arrow[d] &
{L^i/VL^i} \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"F"] & 0\\
\cdots \arrow[r,"d"] &
{\sigma_*A_L^{i-1}} \arrow[r,"\sigma_*\partial"] &
{\sigma_*Z_L^i} \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Under this identification, \(\sigma_*\partial\) sends \([y]\)
to \([dVy]\), since \(d\otimes y=F\otimes dVy\).
The vertical maps below degree \(i\) are the natural quotient maps.
The right vertical map sends \([x]\) to \(F\otimes x\);
it is well defined because \(F\in Z_1\) and \(FV=0\) in \(R_1\).
Equivalently, it is the quotient map
\(L^i/VL^i\to L^i/(VL^i+dV^2L^{i-1})\).
The last square therefore commutes.
This gives
\[
Q_{V,i}(L)\longrightarrow\sigma_*\tau_{\leqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(L).
\]

To check that these maps are quasi-isomorphisms, it suffices to take
\(L=R\), since the constructions commute with direct sums and grading
shifts. The four cases with nonzero kernels are shown below;
Frobenius twists are suppressed, and \(\pi\) denotes the natural
quotient map. The two nonzero positions have complex degrees \(0,1\).
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}c@{\hspace{24pt}}c@{}}
\(\widetilde{F},\quad i\leqslant0\) & \(\widetilde{F},\quad i=1\)\\[7pt]
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=10pt,row sep=15pt,ampersand replacement=\&]
0\arrow[r]\& {R^0/p}\arrow[r,"d"]\arrow[d,"\pi"']\& {R^1/p}\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"\pi"]\&0\\
0\arrow[r]\& R_1^0\arrow[r,"d"]\& R_1^1\arrow[r]\&0
\end{tikzcd}
&
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=10pt,row sep=15pt,ampersand replacement=\&]
0\arrow[r]\& {R^0/FR^0}\arrow[r,"dV"]\arrow[d]\& {R^1/p}\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"\pi"]\&0\\
0\arrow[r]\&0\arrow[r]\&R_1^1\arrow[r]\&0
\end{tikzcd}
\\[32pt]
\(\widetilde{V},\quad i=1\)&\(\widetilde{V},\quad i\geqslant2\)\\[7pt]
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=10pt,row sep=15pt,ampersand replacement=\&]
0\arrow[r]\& {R^0/p}\arrow[r,"dV"]\arrow[d,"\pi"']\& {R^1/p}\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"F"]\&0\\
0\arrow[r]\&R_1^0\arrow[r,"d"]\&R_1^1\arrow[r]\&0
\end{tikzcd}
&
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=10pt,row sep=15pt,ampersand replacement=\&]
0\arrow[r]\&{R^0/p}\arrow[r,"d"]\arrow[d,"\pi"']\&{R^1/p}\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"\pi"]\&0\\
0\arrow[r]\&R_1^0\arrow[r,"d"]\&R_1^1\arrow[r]\&0
\end{tikzcd}
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Here \(R^a/p=R^a/pR^a\), and the arrow labelled \(F\) sends
\([x]\) to \([Fx]\); in the third diagram we use
\(VR^1=pR^1\) and \(Z_1^1=R_1^1\).
Computing the kernels in these four diagrams shows that the
comparison maps are quasi-isomorphisms.
The remaining cases are isomorphisms, including
\(k[F]\xrightarrow{F}\sigma_*(Fk[F])\) for the
\(\widetilde{V}\)-comparison at \(i=0\).
These explicit maps therefore identify the two cones with the Hodge
truncations. Applying the calculation to the terms of \(P\) gives
the comparisons for bounded double complexes. For a semi-free
resolution the general case follows by its filtration by free
cells and filtered colimits; all displayed constructions use
direct sums and are compatible with that filtration.
We obtain the natural distinguished triangles
\[
\begin{aligned}
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i-1}\xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}}F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^i
 &\longrightarrow t_{\geqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(M)
 \longrightarrowF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i-1}[1],\\
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i+1}\xrightarrow{\widetilde{V}}F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^i
 &\longrightarrow\sigma_*\tau_{\leqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(M)
 \longrightarrowF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i+1}[1].
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, the upper left square commutes because
\(\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=p\).
The quotient maps just constructed are compatible with this square:
on the \(F\)-quotients the induced map is the inclusion of the
horizontal tail starting at \(i+1\) into the tail starting at \(i\);
on the \(V\)-quotients it is the map between consecutive truncated
complexes induced by \(Z_1\hookrightarrow R_1\).
Thus their cones are the rightmost and bottom triangles of
\eqref{Hodge filtration triangles}, the latter after applying
\(\sigma_*\). Cartier identifies their common final object with
\((R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^{i,\bullet}[-i]\).
The resulting \(3\times3\) diagram is the one in the statement;
the usual cone convention accounts for the possible signs.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
\label{rmt}
Let \(M\in{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\). The \(R\)-complex \(\mathrm{t}(M)\) is generated
by symbols \(\beta_i\otimes x\), with \(i\in\mathrm{I}\) and \(x\in M\), where
\(\beta_i\otimes x\) has internal degree \(i\) and cohomological degree
\(-i\):
    {\small \[\begin{tikzcd}
	{R^0(\beta_m\otimes m)} & {R^1(\beta_m\otimes m)} \\
	& {R^0(\beta_{m+1}\otimes m)} & {...} \\
	&& {...} & {...} \\
	&&& {R^0(\beta_{n-1}\otimes m)} & {R^1(\beta_{n-1}\otimes m)} \\
	&&&& {R^0(\beta_{n}\otimes m).} \\
	&&&& {}
	\arrow["d", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\delta", from=2-2, to=1-2]
	\arrow["d", from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\delta", from=3-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["d", from=3-3, to=3-4]
	\arrow["\delta", from=4-4, to=3-4]
	\arrow["d", from=4-4, to=4-5]
	\arrow["\delta", from=5-5, to=4-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]}
                                     
In cohomological degree \(-n\), the complex is generated over \(R^0\);
there is no component of bidegree \((n+1,-n)\).

The generators are subject to the following relations.

    {\rm (1)} For any \(\lambda\in W\), \(m_1,m_2\in M^j\), 
    \[\begin{aligned}
        \beta_i \otimes (\lambda m_1+m_2) =\lambda \beta_i\otimes m_1+ \beta_i \otimes m_2, \quad \text{if}\; j\leqslant i, \\
        \beta_i \otimes (\lambda m_1+m_2) =\lambda^\sigma \beta_i\otimes m_1+ \beta_i \otimes m_2, \quad \text{if}\; j\geqslant i+1.
    \end{aligned}\]

    {\rm (2)} If \(m_j\in M^j\) then 
    \[\begin{aligned}
        &\delta(\beta_{i}\otimes m_j)=0,\quad  \text{if}\;i=m;\\
        &(-1)^{i}\delta(\beta_{i}\otimes m_j)+d(\beta_{i-1}\otimes m_j)=0,\quad  \text{if}\; i\in [m+1,n],i\neq j,\\
        &(-1)^{j}\delta(\beta_{j}\otimes m_j)+dV(\beta_{j-1}\otimes m_j)=0, \quad  \text{if}\; j=i.
    \end{aligned}\] 

    {\rm (3)} If \(m_j\in M^j\) then 
    \[\beta_i\otimes \widetilde{F} m_j =\begin{cases}
            \beta_i\otimes m_j,\;&\text{if}\;j>i\\
            F(\beta_i\otimes m_j),\;&\text{if}\;j=i\\
            p(\beta_i\otimes m_j),\;&\text{if}\;j<i.
        \end{cases}\]
    \[\beta_i\otimes \widetilde{V} m_j =\begin{cases}
            \beta_i\otimes m_j,\;&\text{if}\;j<i+1\\
            V(\beta_i\otimes m_j),\;&\text{if}\;j=i+1\\
            p(\beta_i\otimes m_j),\;&\text{if}\;j>i+1.
        \end{cases}\]

  

{\rm (4)} If \(\tau(m_{\infty})=m_{-\infty}\), impose
    \[\beta_i\otimes m_{\infty}=\beta_i\otimes m_{-\infty}. \]
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{degree (n -n) component of t(M)}
For \(M\in{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\), the operator \(F\) is bijective on the
component of \(\mathrm{t}(M)\) in bidegree \((n,-n)\).
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
By relation \Cref{rmt}(3), it suffices to consider a generator
\(\beta_n\otimes x\) with \(x\in M^j\) and \(m\leq j\leq n\). Let
\(\bar x\in M^{-\infty}\) be its image. Choose
\(a_\infty\in M^\infty\) with \(\tau(a_\infty)=\bar x\), and represent
\(a_\infty\) by \(a_n\in M^n\). Relations (3) and (4) give
\[
F(\beta_n\otimes a_n)
=\beta_n\otimes\widetilde{F} a_n
=\beta_n\otimes a_\infty
=\beta_n\otimes\bar x
=\beta_n\otimes x.
\]
Thus \(F\) is surjective. Repeating the construction with
\(\tau^{-1}\) gives its inverse, so \(F\) is bijective.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{degree (n -n+1) component of t(M)}
For \(M\in{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\), the operator \(F\) is bijective on
\(\mathrm{t}(M)^{n,-n+1}\).
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
If \(m=n\), this component is zero. Suppose \(m<n\).
Left multiplication by \(F\) is bijective on \(R^1\): in the unique
\(F\)-\(V\) expansions, it shifts the string
\(\ldots,dV^2,dV,d,Fd,F^2d,\ldots\) and applies \(\sigma\) to
coefficients. Its inverse \(S\) commutes with right multiplication
by \(R^0\), so \(S(uq)=S(u)q\) for \(u\in R^1\), \(q\in R^0\).
Define
\[
S\bigl(u(\beta_{n-1}\otimes x)\bigr)
:=S(u)(\beta_{n-1}\otimes x).
\]
Right \(R^0\)-linearity shows that this respects the scalar and gauge
relations \Cref{rmt}(1),(3): a relation with coefficients \(u\) and
\(uq\) is sent to the same relation with coefficients \(S(u)\) and
\(S(u)q\). It also respects the endpoint identifications in (4).
Relation (2) specifies the differential, compatibly with these
relations, rather than imposing further relations within this
component. Thus \(S\) descends to \(\mathrm{t}(M)^{n,-n+1}\), where
\(FS=SF=1\).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{adjunction between FG and t}
For \(M\in\mathrm{Ch}(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) and
\(N\in{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\), there are natural isomorphisms
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_{{F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}}(N,Z^0F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M))
\cong
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ch}({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}})}(N,F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M))
\cong
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ch}(R)}(\mathrm{t}(N),M).
\]
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The first isomorphism regards \(N\) as a complex concentrated in degree
zero. For the second, suppose that \(x\in N^j\) maps to a cycle in
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^j\), represented by a compatible sequence
\((m_i)_i\), where
\[
m_i\in\sigma_*M^{i,-i}\quad(i<j),
\qquad
m_i\in M^{i,-i}\quad(i\geq j).
\]
Compatibility with the gauge operators means
\[\begin{aligned}
x&\longmapsto(\ldots,m_i,\ldots),\\
\widetilde{F} x&\longmapsto(\ldots,m_{j-1},F(m_j),pm_{j+1},\ldots),\\
\widetilde{V} x&\longmapsto(\ldots,pm_{j-2},Vm_{j-1},m_j,\ldots).
\end{aligned}\]

The cycle condition is
\[\begin{cases}
\delta(m_i)=0,&i=m,\\
dm_{i-1}+(-1)^i\delta(m_i)=0,
    &i\in[m+1,n],\ i\neq j,\\
dVm_{j-1}+(-1)^j\delta(m_j)=0,&i=j\neq m.
\end{cases}\]

Thus sending \(\beta_i\otimes x\) to \(m_i\) respects the relations
in \Cref{rmt} and defines a morphism
\(\mathrm{t}(N)\to M\). The construction is reversible and natural, which
proves the second isomorphism. Under it, the adjunction unit is
\[
x\longmapsto\sum_{i\in\mathrm{I}}\beta_i\otimes x.
\]
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{adjunction between FG^Tot and t^Tot}
The functor \(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) is left adjoint to
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}:\mathrm{Ch}(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})
\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ch}({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}).
\]
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Both categories are locally presentable. Since \(\mathrm{I}\) is finite,
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) is computed componentwise by finite direct sums and
scalar twists, so it preserves small limits and colimits. The adjoint
functor theorem therefore gives a left adjoint \(\mathrm{T}\).

Totalizing the units \(N^q\toF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(N^q))\) of
\Cref{adjunction between FG and t} gives a natural map
\[
N^\bullet\longrightarrow
\mathrm{Tot}\bigl(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(N^\bullet))\bigr)
\congF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N^\bullet)).
\]
The identification reorders the finite sums, with the signs required
when interchanging the complex directions. By adjunction, we obtain
\(\alpha:\mathrm{T}\to\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\). The preceding adjunction and
compatibility with shifts show that \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism
on complexes concentrated in one degree.

For bounded complexes, we proceed by induction on the length.
Choose \(a\) just above the lowest nonzero degree.
The stupid truncation sequence
\(0\to t_{\geqslant a}N^\bullet\to N^\bullet\to
 t_{<a}N^\bullet\to0\) is split in every degree, so
\(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) preserves its exactness. Right exactness of
\(\mathrm{T}\) gives a commutative diagram with exact rows:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
{} & \mathrm{T}(t_{\geqslant a}N^\bullet)
 \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\alpha"'] &
\mathrm{T}(N^\bullet) \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\alpha"] &
\mathrm{T}(t_{<a}N^\bullet) \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\alpha"] & 0\\
0 \arrow[r] & \mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(t_{\geqslant a}N^\bullet)
 \arrow[r] &
\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N^\bullet) \arrow[r] &
\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(t_{<a}N^\bullet) \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The outer vertical maps are isomorphisms by induction.
Since the bottom-left map is injective, so is the top-left map;
the short five lemma then shows that the middle vertical map is an
isomorphism.

Every complex is the filtered colimit of its bounded subcomplexes
\(t_{\geqslant a}\tau_{\leqslant b}N^\bullet\) as \(a\) decreases
and \(b\) increases, with \(\tau_{\leqslant b}\) denoting ordinary
truncation. Both functors preserve colimits: \(\mathrm{T}\) is a left
adjoint, while \(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) is the totalization of the left
adjoint \(\mathrm{t}\) applied termwise. Thus \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism
for every complex, proving the adjunction.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{definition of (Lt)^Tot}
For a fixed interval \(\mathrm{I}\), we use the notation
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}:=\mathrm{Tot}\circF\mathsf{G}:
D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\longrightarrow D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})
\]
and
\[
(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}:=\mathrm{Tot}\circ\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t}:
D^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\longrightarrow D^-(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I}).
\]
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{derived adjunction between FG^Tot and t^Tot}
The functor \((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) is left adjoint to
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) on the bounded-above derived categories.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Resolve \(N^\bullet\in D^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) by a bounded-above complex
\(P^\bullet\) of projective generators \(G_r\). The adjunction of
\Cref{adjunction between FG^Tot and t^Tot} descends to homotopy
categories and gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Hom}_{D^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})}(N^\bullet,F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M^\bullet))
&\cong
\mathrm{Hom}_{K^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})}(P^\bullet,F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M^\bullet))\\
&\cong
\mathrm{Hom}_{K^-(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})}
  (\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(P^\bullet),M^\bullet)\\
&\cong
\mathrm{Hom}_{D^-(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})}
  ((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N^\bullet),M^\bullet).
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{description of t(G_r)}
Let \(r\in\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\).
    
{\rm (1)} The complex \(\mathrm{t}(G_r)\), supported in cohomological degrees
\([-n,-m]\), is
                                                                                                                           
    \[\mathrm{t}(G_r)=\left(W_{\sigma}[F,F^{-1}](-n)\xrightarrow{\cdot d}R(1\!\!-\!\!n) \xrightarrow{\cdot d} ... \xrightarrow{\cdot d}R(-\!m)\right),\]
where every differential is right multiplication by \(d\), except for
\(R(-r)\xrightarrow{\cdot dV}R(-r-1)\).
Here \(R(i)\) denotes the complex
\(R^0(i)\xrightarrow{(-1)^id\cdot}R^1(i-1)\), as in
\Cref{shifts of R-complexes}.

{\rm (2)} The adjunction unit
\[
G_r\longrightarrowF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))
\]
is a canonical quasi-isomorphism in \(\mathrm{Ch}({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Fix \(i\in[m,n-1]\). We first show that the component of
\(\mathrm{t}(G_r)\) in cohomological degree \(-i\) is the free
\(R\)-module generated by \(\beta_i\otimes\alpha_r\).

By \Cref{definition of G_r}, every basis element of every \(G_r^j\) is
obtained from \(\alpha_r\) by iterating \(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V},\tau\), and
\(\tau^{-1}\). Relations \Cref{rmt}(3)--(4) reduce every generator
\(\beta_i\otimes x\) to an \(R\)-multiple of
\(\beta_i\otimes\alpha_r\): each occurrence of \(\widetilde{F}\) or \(\widetilde{V}\)
is replaced by the corresponding operator \(F,V,p\), or \(1\)
specified in (3), while (4) removes occurrences of
\(\tau^{\pm1}\) by identifying the endpoint generators. To see that no further relations occur, send
\(\beta_i\otimes\alpha_r\) to the generator \(e\) of \(R(-i)\)
and evaluate the remaining generators by (3)--(4).
This respects the defining relations of \(G_r\):
\(\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=p\) becomes \(FV=VF=p\) or \(p\cdot1=p\),
the endpoint identifications are inverse, and (1) accounts for
the scalar twists. Compatibility with (2) follows from \(FdV=d\).
The resulting map is inverse to
\(R(-i)\to\mathrm{t}(G_r)^{-i}\), proving freeness.

For the component in bidegree \((n,-n)\), put
\(b:=\beta_n\otimes\alpha_r\). Here we must also use gauge degree
\(n+1\): for \(x\in G_r^n\), relation \Cref{rmt}(3) gives
\(\beta_n\otimes\widetilde{F} x=F(\beta_n\otimes x)\).
Since \(\widetilde{F} x\) represents the positive-tail image of \(x\),
relation (4) identifies \(\beta_n\otimes\widetilde{F} x\) with
\(\beta_n\otimes\tau x\). Thus passing through \(\tau\) acts
by \(F\), and passing through \(\tau^{-1}\) acts by \(F^{-1}\).
Within gauge degrees \([m,n]\), each \(\widetilde{F}\) contributes \(p\)
and each \(\widetilde{V}\) acts as the identity. Consequently, for \(l\geqslant0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_n\otimes
\left(\widetilde{F}^{\,r-m}\tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-r}\right)^l\alpha_r
 &= (p^{\,n-m}F)^l b,\\
\beta_n\otimes
\left(\widetilde{V}^{\,n-r}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{\,r-m}\right)^l\alpha_r
 &= F^{-l}b.
\end{aligned}
\]
Conversely, evaluating the gauge generators by these rules in
\(W_\sigma[F,F^{-1}]b\) respects (1)--(4) and gives an inverse
to the natural map onto the top component, so no further relations occur.
Thus the top component is
freely generated by \(b\) over \(W_\sigma[F,F^{-1}]\). Finally, \Cref{rmt}(2), applied to \(\alpha_r\), gives
\(\delta(\beta_i\otimes\alpha_r)=(-1)^{i+1}d(\beta_{i-1}\otimes\alpha_r)\)
for \(i>m\), with \(d\) replaced by \(dV\) when \(i=r\),
and \(\delta(\beta_m\otimes\alpha_r)=0\). After the standard sign
adjustment of the generators, these are exactly the displayed
differentials, proving (1).


For (2), the identity of \(\mathrm{t}(G_r)\) corresponds under adjunction to
the canonical morphism
\(
\eta:G_r\longrightarrow F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r)).
\)
By \Cref{adjunction between FG and t}, this map is given, for \(x\in G_r^j\), by
\[
x\longmapsto \sum_{i\in\mathrm{I}}\beta_i\otimes x.
\]
Since \(G_r\) is concentrated in cohomological degree \(0\), it suffices,
in each gauge degree \(j\), to identify \(G_r^j\) with the kernel of
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))^{j,0}\longrightarrow F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))^{j,1},
\]
and to show that the displayed differential is surjective.

Surjectivity in degree \(1\) follows directly from (1): each copy of
\(R^1(\beta_i\otimes\alpha_r)\) is reached either from
\(dV\cdot R^0(\beta_i\otimes\alpha_r)\) or from
\(\delta(R^0(\beta_{i+1}\otimes\alpha_r))\).

The map \(x\mapsto\sum_i\beta_i\otimes x\) lands in the kernel. Indeed,
the total cycle condition for \((x_i)_{i\in\mathrm{I}}\) is
\[
\delta(x_m)=0,
\]
\[
d(x_{i-1})+(-1)^i\delta(x_i)=0,\qquad i\in[m+1,n],\ i\neq j,
\]
and at the wall,
\[
dV(x_{j-1})+(-1)^j\delta(x_j)=0.
\]
These are precisely the relations in \Cref{rmt}(2).

To identify the entire kernel, fix \(j\). For \(\lambda\in W\), let
\(\rho_\lambda:G_r\to G_r\) send
\(\alpha_r\) to \(\lambda\alpha_r\). Functoriality makes the adjunction
unit equivariant for the induced actions.

Grouping the canonical basis elements by their \(\sigma^f\)-weights
for the action of \(\rho_\lambda\), we obtain
\[
G_r^j=\bigoplus_{f\in\mathbb{Z}}Y_f^j,\qquad
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))^{j,\bullet}=\bigoplus_{f\in\mathbb{Z}}X_f^{j,\bullet},
\]
where \(\rho_\lambda\) acts on \(Y_f^j\) and \(X_f^{j,\bullet}\) by
multiplication by \(\lambda^{\sigma^f}\). If \(k\) is infinite,
these characters are distinct. If \(k\) is finite, they may coincide,
but the same basis decomposition remains direct and is preserved by
the differential and the unit: this can be checked after the faithfully
flat base change \(W(k)\to W(\bar k)\), where the characters are
distinct. It therefore suffices to prove that \(Y_f^j[0]\to X_f^{j,\bullet}\) is a
quasi-isomorphism for every \(f\).

The module \(Y_f^j\) is free of rank one over \(W\). To specify its
generator, define the two cycling operators
\[
\Phi:=\widetilde{F}^{\,r-m}\tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-r},
\qquad
\Psi:=\widetilde{V}^{\,n-r}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{\,r-m}.
\]
A basis of \(Y_f^j\) over \(W\) is given by the following canonical
vector.
\[
y_{f,j}:=
\begin{cases}
\widetilde{F}^{\,j-r}\Phi^f\alpha_r,
  & f\geqslant0,\ j\geqslant r,\\[3pt]
\left(\widetilde{F}^{\,j-m}\tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-r}\right)\Phi^{f-1}\alpha_r,
  & f\geqslant1,\ j<r,\\[3pt]
\widetilde{V}^{\,r-j}\Psi^{-f}\alpha_r,
  & f\leqslant0,\ j\leqslant r,\\[3pt]
\left(\widetilde{V}^{\,n-j}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{\,r-m}\right)\Psi^{-f-1}\alpha_r,
  & f\leqslant-1,\ j>r.
\end{cases}
\]

The complex \(X_f^{j,\bullet}\) is the \(\sigma^f\)-weight subcomplex of
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))^{j,\bullet}\). Let \(b_i\) denote the element of
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))^{j,0}\) corresponding to
\(\beta_i\otimes\alpha_r\). Then \(b_i\in X_{w_i}^{j,0}\), where
\[
w_i:=\mathbf{1}_{i<r}-\mathbf{1}_{i<j}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf{1}_P\) denotes the indicator of a condition \(P\).
Indeed, \Cref{rmt}(1) contributes \(\mathbf{1}_{i<r}\) to the weight,
while the \(\sigma_*\)-twist in \Cref{definition of FG}(1) subtracts
\(\mathbf{1}_{i<j}\). Put \(h_i:=f-w_i\).
Since multiplication by \(F\) raises the weight exponent by \(1\)
and multiplication by \(V\) lowers it by \(1\), a \(W\)-basis of
\(X_f^{j,0}\) is given by
\[
e_i=
\begin{cases}
F^{h_i}b_i,&h_i\geqslant0,\\
V^{-h_i}b_i,&h_i<0,
\end{cases}
\quad(m\leqslant i<n),
\qquad e_n=F^fb_n.
\]
At the top component, both indicators vanish and \(F\) is invertible,
so the last formula applies to every \(f\in\mathbb{Z}\).

Similarly, \(db_i\) has internal degree \(i+1\), so the twist
\(\sigma_*\) occurs when \(i+1<j\). Since \(d\) commutes with
scalars, set
\[
w_i':=\mathbf{1}_{i<r}-\mathbf{1}_{i+1<j},\qquad h_i':=f-w_i'.
\]
A \(W\)-basis of \(X_f^{j,1}\) is therefore
\[
u_i=
\begin{cases}
F^{h_i'}db_i,&h_i'\geqslant0,\\
dV^{-h_i'}b_i,&h_i'<0,
\end{cases}
\qquad m\leqslant i<n.
\]
In the negative branch, the order in \(dV^ab_i\) matters: using
\(V^adb_i\) would introduce the factor in \(V^ad=p^adV^a\).
Also, \(h_i'=h_i\) except at
\(i=j-1\), where \(h_i'=h_i-1\).

In these bases, the adjunction unit sends
\[
\eta(y_{f,j})=(a_i e_i)_{i=m}^n,\qquad a_i=p^{c_i}.
\]
The exponents count the powers of \(p\) contributed by the complete
cycles and the remaining path from \(r\) to \(j\).
Explicitly, for \(m\leqslant i<n\), we have
\[
c_i=
\begin{cases}
f(i-m)+\min(i,j)-\min(i,r),
 & f>0\text{ or }(f=0,\ j\geqslant r),\\[3pt]
-f(n-i-1)+\max(i+1,r)-\max(i+1,j),
 & f<0\text{ or }(f=0,\ j\leqslant r).
\end{cases}
\]
At \(i=n\), we have \(c_n=f(n-m)+j-r\) in the first case
and \(c_n=0\) in the second. Both formulas give \(c_i=0\)
when \(f=0\) and \(j=r\).

For each \(j\) and each \(f\), at least one coefficient \(a_i\) is a
unit. Thus the image of \(Y_f^j\) in \(X_f^{j,0}\) is a saturated
\(W\)-submodule. This will identify the image once the kernel of the
differential is known.

Let \(D:X_f^{j,0}\to X_f^{j,1}\) be the differential.
The definitions in \Cref{definition of FG}(3) and \Cref{rmt}(2), with
the totalization sign, give the following formulas, where
\(u_{m-1}=0\).

For \(m\leqslant i<n\),
\[
D(e_i)=
\begin{cases}
p^{h_i}u_i-u_{i-1},
 & f>0\text{ or }(f=0,\ j\geqslant r),\\[3pt]
u_i-p^{-h_i}u_{i-1},
 & f<0\text{ or }(f=0,\ j\leqslant r).
\end{cases}
\]
In both cases, \(D(e_n)=-u_{n-1}\).

The coefficients \(-1\) in the first case and \(1\) in the second
allow us to solve successively for every \(u_i\), so \(D\) is surjective. Since \(X_f^{j,0}\) and \(X_f^{j,1}\) have ranks \(n-m+1\)
and \(n-m\), its kernel is free of rank one. The nonzero saturated
image of \(Y_f^j\) is therefore exactly this kernel. If \(m=n\),
\(X_f^{j,1}=0\) and the same conclusion is immediate.

Thus \(Y_f^j[0]\to X_f^{j,\bullet}\) is a quasi-isomorphism for every
\(f\). Summing over the weights \(f\) shows that
\(G_r^j\to F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))^{j,\bullet}\) is a quasi-isomorphism
for every \(j\in\mathrm{I}\). Hence
\(G_r\to F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))\) is a quasi-isomorphism in
\(\mathrm{Ch}({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{M simeq FGLtM}
For every \(M\in D^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\), the adjunction unit is a natural
quasi-isomorphism
\[
M\xrightarrow{\sim}F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)).
\]
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The \(G_r\) form a family of projective generators of
\({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\). Choose a bounded-above projective resolution
\(P^\bullet\to M\) whose terms are direct sums of the \(G_r\).

By definition of the left derived functor,
\(
(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^\mathrm{Tot}(M)\simeq \mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(P^\bullet).
\)
Applying \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\), we get
\(
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M))\simeq F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(P^\bullet)).
\)
For each projective generator \(G_r\), the preceding proposition shows
that the adjunction unit
\(
G_r\longrightarrow F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}(G_r))
\)
is a quasi-isomorphism. Since both \(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) and \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) commute with direct sums and with bounded totalizations, the same holds for every bounded complex \(P^\bullet\) whose terms are direct sums of the \(G_r\). Thus the natural map
\(
P^\bullet\longrightarrow F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(P^\bullet))
\)
is a quasi-isomorphism. 
Composing with the quasi-isomorphism \(P^\bullet\to M\), we obtain a natural quasi-isomorphism
\[
M\simeq P^\bullet\xrightarrow{\sim}F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\mathrm{t}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(P^\bullet))
\simeq F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)).
\]
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{The first example}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[0,2]\), and consider the \(F\)-gauge \(M\) defined by
\[
M^0=We_1\oplus We_2,\qquad
M^1=pWe_1\oplus We_2,\qquad
M^2=p^2We_1\oplus We_2.
\]
For \(i=0,1\), the map \(\widetilde{V}:M^{i+1}\hookrightarrow M^i\) is the
inclusion and \(\widetilde{F}:M^i\to M^{i+1}\) is multiplication by \(p\). The
Frobenius-semilinear isomorphism \(\tau:M^2\to M^0\) is determined by
\[
\tau(p^2e_1)=e_2,\qquad \tau(e_2)=e_1.
\]
As usual, set \(\Phi=\tau\widetilde{F}^2\) and \(\Psi=\widetilde{V}^2\tau^{-1}\).
The projective gauge \(G_0\) surjects onto \(M\) by
\(\alpha_0\mapsto e_1\), since both \(\Phi(\alpha_0)\) and
\(\Psi(\alpha_0)\) map to \(e_2\). The resulting relation generates
the kernel, giving an exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow G_0\xrightarrow{\ \Phi-\Psi\ }G_0
\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.
\]

Applying \((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) gives
\((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\simeq \mathrm{Tot}\left[\mathrm{t}(G_0)\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{t}(\Phi-\Psi)\ }\mathrm{t}(G_0)\right],\)
with the left term in degree \(-1\). For \(\mathrm{I}=[0,2]\), the object
\(\mathrm{t}(G_0)\) is represented by the following \(R\)-complex:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
{R^0(\beta_0\otimes\alpha_0)} & {R^1(\beta_0\otimes\alpha_0)} \\
& {R^0(\beta_1\otimes\alpha_0)} & {R^1(\beta_1\otimes\alpha_0)} \\
&& {W_\sigma[F,F^{-1}](\beta_2\otimes\alpha_0)}
\arrow["{d\cdot}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
\arrow["{\cdot d}"', from=2-2, to=1-2]
\arrow["{d\cdot}", from=2-2, to=2-3]
\arrow["{\cdot(-d)}"', from=3-3, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Equivalently, Ekedahl's shifting notation identifies this complex with
\[
\mathrm{t}(G_0)=\left[W_\sigma[F,F^{-1}](-2)\xrightarrow{\cdot d}R(-1)\xrightarrow{\cdot d}R\right],
\]
where the left term lies in degree \(-2\); the shift \(R(-1)\) absorbs
the sign in the final differential.


The endomorphism \(\Phi-\Psi\) of \(G_0\) induces the following
endomorphism of \(\mathrm{t}(G_0)\):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
R \arrow[r,"\cdot(F-pV)"] & R \\
R(-1) \arrow[r,"\cdot(pF-V)"] \arrow[u,"\cdot d"] & R(-1) \arrow[u,"\cdot d"] \\
W_\sigma[F,F^{-1}](-2) \arrow[r,"\cdot(p^2F-F^{-1})"] \arrow[u,"\cdot d"] & W_\sigma[F,F^{-1}](-2) \arrow[u,"\cdot d"]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Its total complex represents \((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\). Indeed, if
\(b_i=\beta_i\otimes\alpha_0\), the defining relations of \(\mathrm{t}\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_0\otimes(\Phi-\Psi)\alpha_0&=(F-pV)b_0,\\
\beta_1\otimes(\Phi-\Psi)\alpha_0&=(pF-V)b_1,\\
\beta_2\otimes(\Phi-\Psi)\alpha_0&=(p^2F-F^{-1})b_2.
\end{aligned}
\]

In module degree \(0\), one obtains
\(
\mathrm{H}^0((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M))^0\cong 
 R^0/R^0(F-pV) \coloneqq Q. 
\)
Inside \(Q\), we have \(F=pV\). Using \(FV=p\), we obtain
\(
p(V^2-1)=0.
\)
Multiplying by \(V^{i-2}\) gives
\(
 p(V^i-V^{i-2})=0\qquad(i\geqslant 2).
\)
Hence every \(V^i\) for \(i\geqslant 2\) is \(p\)-torsion modulo lower terms. Therefore, as a \(W\)-module,
\(
Q\simeq W\oplus WV\oplus \bigoplus_{i\geqslant 2} k\cdot V^i.
\)
In particular, \(Q\) is the direct sum of a free \(W\)-module of rank \(2\), generated by \(1\) and \(V\), and a \(p\)-torsion module generated by \(V^i\) for \(i\ge2\). 
After \(V\)-adic completion,
\(
\widehat Q\simeq W[[V]]/(p(V^2-1)).
\)
Since \(V^2-1\) is a unit in \(W[[V]]\), we obtain
\(
\widehat Q\simeq W[[V]]/(p)\simeq k[[V]].
\)
Thus \(Q\), and hence \((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\), is not complete.

A direct calculation in module degree \(1\) gives
\[\mathrm{H}^0((\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M))^1\cong R^1/\left(R^1 d+R^1(F-pV)\right)\cong k[dV]_{>0}.\]
Indeed, consider \(R^1/(R^0d+R^1(F-pV))\).
Modulo \(R^0d\), the quotient is generated by
\(dV,\ dV^2,\ dV^3,\ldots .\)
For \(i\geqslant 1\), we have
\(dV^i(F-pV)=p\,dV^{i-1}-p\,dV^{i+1}.\)
Since \(d=dV^0\) vanishes modulo \(R^0d\), the case \(i=1\) gives
\(p\,dV^2=0,
\)
and for \(i\geqslant 2\),
\(
p(dV^{i+1}-dV^{i-1})=0.
\)
Hence
\(
R^1/(R^0d+R^1(F-pV))
\cong k[dV]_{>0}
\)
After \(V\)-adic completion,
\(
R^1/(R^0d+\widehat{R^1}(F-pV))
\simeq k[[dV]]_{>0}.
\)

A direct check shows that all other graded cohomology components vanish.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{completion of F-gauge structure}
For \(M\in D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\), define its derived \(p\)-completion by
\[
\widehat M:=
\mathbf R\varprojlim_\nu
\bigl((W/p^\nu)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}M\bigr).
\]
The object \(M\) is complete if the canonical map
\(M\to\widehat M\) is an isomorphism.
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{FG commutes with completion}
For a fixed finite interval \(\mathrm{I}\), the functor
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}:D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})
 \longrightarrow D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})
\]
commutes with completion: there is a natural isomorphism
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\widehat M)\simeq\widehat{F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)}.
\]
Here completion on the \(R\)-side is in the sense of Ekedahl
(\Cref{Ekedahl completion}), and completion on the gauge side is
derived \(p\)-completion (\Cref{completion of F-gauge structure}).
In particular, \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) takes complete complexes to complete
complexes.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Recall the compatibility
\(\mathrm{Tot}(\widehat N)\simeq\widehat{\mathrm{Tot}(N)}\) of totalization
with these completions. By \Cref{definition of FG}(3), gauge degree
\(i\) of \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\) is the total complex of the Nygaard
modification \(M(\varphi^i)\), where
\(\varphi^i(j)=-\delta_{i,j}\).
Using \Cref{completion commutes with Nygaard modification}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\widehat M)^i
 &=\mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\widehat M(\varphi^i)\bigr)\\
 &\simeq\mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\widehat{M(\varphi^i)}\bigr)\\
 &\simeq\widehat{\mathrm{Tot}(M(\varphi^i))}
 =\widehat{F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^i}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These natural identifications respect \(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V}\) and \(\tau\),
so they give the asserted isomorphism of complexes of \(F\)-gauge
structures. The assertion about complete complexes follows.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{definition of completed derived rmt}
Set
\[
\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}
:=\widehat{(-)}\circ(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}.
\]
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
\label{shifts and derived quotients of F-gauges}
For an \(F\)-gauge \(M\), define \(M(i)\) to be the \(F\)-gauge with
\(M(i)^j=M^{i+j}\) and the same operators \(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V},\tau\).
The operators \(\widetilde{F}\) and \(\widetilde{V}\) define morphisms of \(F\)-gauges
\(M\to M(1)\) and \(M\to M(-1)\), respectively. 
For \(M\in D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\), define the derived quotients of its
underlying gauge by
\[
\begin{aligned}
M/\widetilde{F}&:=\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(\widetilde{F}:M(-1)\to M\bigr),\\
M/\widetilde{V}&:=\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(\widetilde{V}:M(1)\to M\bigr),\\
M/(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})&:=(M/\widetilde{F})/\widetilde{V}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus these symbols do not denote ordinary cokernels unless the
relevant higher derived terms vanish.
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{distinguished triangle of M(F V)}
Let \(M\in D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).

{\rm (1)} In \(D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}})\)
there is a natural diagram, commuting up to the usual signs, whose
rows and columns are distinguished triangles:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
M \arrow[r,"\widetilde{F}"] \arrow[d,"\widetilde{V}"'] &
M(1) \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\widetilde{V}"'] &
{(M/\widetilde{F})(1)} \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d,"\widetilde{V}"'] & {}\\
M(-1) \arrow[r,"\widetilde{F}"] \arrow[d] &
M \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &
{M/\widetilde{F}} \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d] & {}\\
{(M/\widetilde{V})(-1)} \arrow[r,"\widetilde{F}"] \arrow[d,"+1"'] &
{M/\widetilde{V}} \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"+1"'] &
{M/(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})} \arrow[r,"+1"] \arrow[d,"+1"'] & {}\\
{} & {} & {} & {}
\end{tikzcd}
\]

{\rm (2)} There is a natural distinguished triangle
\begin{equation}\label{derived mod p triangle for gauges}
(M/\widetilde{F})(1)\xrightarrow{\ \widetilde{V}\ }
(W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}M
\longrightarrow M/\widetilde{V}
\longrightarrow (M/\widetilde{F})(1)[1].
\end{equation}
Here \((1)\) is a gauge-grading shift, whereas \([1]\) is a
cohomological shift.

{\rm (3)} If \(M=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\) for
\(N\in D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\), then the gauge-degree \(i\)
component of the diagram in (1) is naturally isomorphic to the
diagram of \Cref{Nygaard filtration and Hodge filtration}.
In particular,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(M/\widetilde{F})^i&\simeq t_{\geqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(N),\\
(M/\widetilde{V})^i&\simeq\sigma_*\tau_{\leqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(N),\\
\bigl(M/(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})\bigr)^i
 &\simeq(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}N)^i[-i].
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Choose a complex representing \(M\) and use the usual mapping cones.
The upper-left square commutes because \(\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=p\).
Taking its row and column cones gives (1): the bottom-right term is
\(\operatorname{Cone}(\widetilde{V}:(M/\widetilde{F})(1)\to M/\widetilde{F})\), which is
\(M/(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})\) by definition. Taking the cones in the opposite
order gives the same total complex, with the usual sign change.
This construction is functorial on complexes and preserves
quasi-isomorphisms, so it descends to the derived category.

For (2), apply the triangle of cones to
\(M\xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}}M(1)\xrightarrow{\widetilde{V}}M\), whose composite
is multiplication by \(p\). Its three terms are
\((M/\widetilde{F})(1)\), \(\operatorname{Cone}(p:M\to M)\), and
\(M/\widetilde{V}\). The middle term is naturally
\((W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}M\), since
\([W\xrightarrow{p}W]\) resolves \(W/p\).
The first map is induced by \(\widetilde{V}\) on targets and the identity
on sources, giving the displayed triangle.

For (3), \Cref{Nygaard filtration and Hodge filtration} identifies
the row and column cones with the stated Hodge truncations and the
iterated cone with \((R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}N)^i[-i]\).
The comparison maps there are compatible with the gauge operators,
so these identifications give the entire diagram.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{FG is conservative on complete objects}
For a fixed finite interval \(\mathrm{I}\), the functor
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}:D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\to D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\)
is conservative on complete objects.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Since complete objects are closed under cones, it suffices to show
that \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)=0\) implies \(M=0\) for complete \(M\).
The derived quotient triangles of \Cref{distinguished triangle of M(F V)},
together with the comparisons in \Cref{Nygaard filtration and Hodge filtration},
then give \((R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^{i,\bullet}=0\) for every \(i\).
As \(M\) has internal degrees in the finite interval \(\mathrm{I}\),
\Cref{R1 detects vanishing of complete complexes} gives \(M=0\).
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{completed adjunction unit and counit are isomorphisms}
For \(N\in D^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) and
\(M\in D^-(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\), both
\(\widehat\eta_N\) and \(\widehat\epsilon_M\) are isomorphisms.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Resolve by the projective generators \(G_r\). For each generator, the
completed counit is an isomorphism by
\Cref{description of t(G_r)}(2), hence so is
\(\widehat\epsilon_M\) for every bounded-above complex. Since
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) is conservative on complete objects by
\Cref{Ek2I.1.1,distinguished triangle of M(F V)}, the triangle
identity for the adjunction then implies that \(\widehat\eta_N\) is an
isomorphism as well.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{Ekedahl's equivalence theorem}
The completed derived functor has finite amplitude and yields the
following equivalence.

{\rm (1)} It has finite amplitude on \(D^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) and
therefore extends to \(D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).

{\rm (2)} The functors \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) and
\(\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}\) are inverse equivalences between
complete \(R\)-complexes of level \(\mathrm{I}\) and complete complexes of
\(F\)-gauges of level \(\mathrm{I}\). They preserve bounded objects.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
The finite-amplitude assertion follows from
\Cref{distinguished triangle of M(F V)} and the conservativity of
\(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}-\) on complete objects. The equivalence then
follows from \Cref{completed adjunction unit and counit are isomorphisms}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- definition-30: body_md -->
\label{coherence of F-gauge complexes}
An object \(M\in D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) is coherent if it is
derived \(p\)-complete and, for every \(i\in\mathrm{I}\), the complex
\[
\bigl((W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}M\bigr)^i
\]
has finite-dimensional \(k\)-cohomology in every degree.
Here derived \(p\)-completeness means that
\[
M\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}
R\varprojlim_{\nu}\bigl((W/p^\nu)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}M\bigr);
\]
see \Cref{completion of F-gauge structure}.
An \(F\)-gauge structure is coherent if it is coherent when placed
in cohomological degree zero.
We denote the full subcategory of coherent complexes by
\(D_c({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\), and its bounded and bounded-above parts by
\(D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) and \(D_c^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).
<!-- end definition-30 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{criteria for coherent F-gauge complexes}
{\rm (1)} An object \(M\in D^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) is coherent if and only if
\(\mathrm{H}^q(M)^i\) is a finitely generated \(W\)-module for every
\(q\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(i\in\mathrm{I}\).
In particular, an \(F\)-gauge structure \(M\) is coherent if and
only if every \(M^i\), \(i\in\mathrm{I}\), is finitely generated over \(W\).

{\rm (2)} A derived \(p\)-complete object \(M\in D({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\)
is coherent if and only if every gauge-degree component of
\[
M/(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})
\]
has finite-dimensional \(k\)-cohomology in every degree.
The quotient here is the derived quotient of
\Cref{distinguished triangle of M(F V)}.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
For (1), evaluation at any gauge degree commutes with derived
reduction and derived completion, so we work with a bounded-above
\(W\)-complex \(X=M^i\).

If all \(\mathrm{H}^q(X)\) are finitely generated over \(W\), then \(X\)
is derived \(p\)-complete. This follows from completeness of finite
\(W\)-modules, applied to the truncations of \(X\); equivalently,
one can use the derived completion spectral sequence over the
complete discrete valuation ring \(W\).
Moreover,
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^q(X)/p
 \longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^q\bigl((W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}X\bigr)
 \longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^{q+1}(X)[p]\longrightarrow0
\]
shows that its derived reduction has finite-dimensional cohomology.

Conversely, suppose \(X\) is derived complete and its reduction
has finite-dimensional cohomology. If \(r\) is the highest possible
cohomological degree, the bounded-above derived Nakayama argument
shows that \(\mathrm{H}^r(X)\) is finitely generated:
lift finitely many generators of
\(\mathrm{H}^r(X)/p=\mathrm{H}^r((W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}X)\) to obtain a map
\(W^{\oplus d}[-r]\to X\). Its cone is derived complete, and its
reduction has no cohomology in degrees at least \(r\).
Derived Nakayama gives the same upper bound for the cone, so the
map is surjective on \(\mathrm{H}^r\).
The finite module \(\mathrm{H}^r(X)\) is derived complete; hence
\(\tau_{\leqslant r-1}X\) is derived complete and still has coherent
reduction. Descending induction proves finite generation in
every degree.

For (2), we compare reduction modulo \(p\) with the
two gauge quotients. Put \(C=(W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}M\),
\(Q_F=M/\widetilde{F}\), \(Q_V=M/\widetilde{V}\), and \(K=M/(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})\).
The cone triangles of \Cref{distinguished triangle of M(F V)} give
\[
Q_F^{i+1}\xrightarrow{\widetilde{V}}Q_F^i\longrightarrow K^i
 \longrightarrow Q_F^{i+1}[1],
\qquad
Q_V^{i-1}\xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}}Q_V^i\longrightarrow K^i
 \longrightarrow Q_V^{i-1}[1].
\]
The level condition gives \(Q_F^i=0\) for \(i>n\) and
\(Q_V^i=0\) for \(i<m\), since the maps defining these cones are
isomorphisms. If every \(K^i\) has finite-dimensional cohomology,
descending induction for \(Q_F\) and ascending induction for \(Q_V\)
give the same finiteness for both quotients. The triangle
\(Q_F^{i+1}\to C^i\to Q_V^i\to Q_F^{i+1}[1]\) then gives
finite-dimensional cohomology for \(C^i\). Together with the assumed
completeness, this proves that \(M\) is coherent.

Conversely, suppose \(M\) is coherent. Then \(C^i\) has
finite-dimensional cohomology in every gauge degree, including the
tails. Derived reduction commutes with mapping cones, so
\[
(W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}K\simeq (C/\widetilde{F})/\widetilde{V}.
\]
The two successive cones on the right involve only shifts and finite
sums of \(C^{i-1},C^i,C^{i+1}\) in gauge degree \(i\), and hence
have finite-dimensional cohomology. On \(M/\widetilde{F}\), the operator
\(\widetilde{F}\) is null-homotopic by the standard cone homotopy. This
homotopy commutes with \(\widetilde{V}\), so it extends to \(K\); consequently,
\(p=\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}\) acts trivially on \(\mathrm{H}^q(K^i)\).
The reduction triangle therefore gives an injection
\(\mathrm{H}^q(K^i)\hookrightarrow
\mathrm{H}^q((W/p)\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}K^i)\).
Thus \(K^i\) has finite-dimensional cohomology, as required.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{Ekedahl equivalence for coherent complexes}
Fix a finite interval \(\mathrm{I}\).
The functors \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) and
\(\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}\) induce inverse equivalences
\[
D_c^-(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\simeq D_c^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}),
\qquad
D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\simeq D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I}).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
By \Cref{Ekedahl's equivalence theorem}, the functors are inverse
equivalences on complete objects. Their finite amplitude at fixed
level ensures that they preserve bounded-above and bounded objects.
It remains to check that the equivalence preserves coherence.
For \(N\in D^-(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) complete, put \(M=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\).
By \Cref{distinguished triangle of M(F V)}(3),
\[
\bigl(M/(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V})\bigr)^i
 \simeq (R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}N)^i[-i].
\]
By Ekedahl's bounded-above coherence criterion, \(N\) is coherent
if and only if its derived \(R_1\)-reduction has finite-dimensional
cohomology; see \cite[Proposition 2.32]{LY}.
By \Cref{criteria for coherent F-gauge complexes}(2), coherence of
\(M\) is tested by the same condition on the left-hand side.
This proves the first equivalence, and restriction to bounded objects
gives the second; compare \cite[Theorem~II.5.3]{Ek3}.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{coherent equivalence and boundedness}
For unbounded complexes, the same argument identifies coherent gauge
complexes with complete \(R\)-complexes whose derived
\(R_1\)-reduction has finite-dimensional cohomology in every
bidegree. We do not identify this condition with coherence of all
cohomology modules without an additional boundedness hypothesis.
For bounded-below complexes, the coherence criterion is provided by
Li--Yang \cite[Corollary 3.21]{LY}; the same argument therefore gives
\(D_c^+(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\simeq D_c^+({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{Ekedahl equivalence and the G t-structure}
Under the equivalence of
\Cref{Ekedahl equivalence for coherent complexes},
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) takes the \(t\)-structure \(\widetilde D_g\) on
\(D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) to the standard \(t\)-structure on
\(D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).
In particular, it induces an equivalence between
\( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
_g\cap D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) and the category of coherent
\(F\)-gauge structures of level \(\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Let \(N\in D_c^b(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) and suppose that
\(M=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\) is concentrated in cohomological degree zero.
We show that \(N\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]

_g\).
The negative tail of the gauge construction identifies
\[
\mathrm{Tot}(N)\simeq M^{-\infty},
\]
so \(\mathrm{Tot}(N)\) is concentrated in degree zero.
Moreover, the three-term free Koszul resolution of \(k\) over

Its identification with the shifted columns of

\mathrm{H}^j(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}N)^i=0
\qquad\text{unless }-2\leqslant i+j\leqslant0.
\]
Together with the assertion about \(\mathrm{Tot}(N)\),
\Cref{criteria for G-amplitude [m n]} with \(m=n=0\) yields \(N\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
