<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{resolution of coherent complexes}
Let \(k\) be perfect and \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\). Every \(M\in D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) admits a
bounded projective resolution whose terms are finite direct sums
of the \(G_r\), \(r\in\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
By \Cref{two-out-of-three finite sums of G_r}, it suffices to treat a
single coherent \(F\)-gauge. The statement for bounded complexes then
follows by d\'evissage along the standard truncation triangles.

Let \(\mathcal C\) be the full subcategory of coherent \(F\)-gauges of
level \(\mathrm{I}\) admitting such a resolution. The horseshoe lemma and
mapping cones make \(\mathcal C\) stable under the two-out-of-three
operations in short exact sequences. We will construct the objects
of \(\mathcal C\) needed for d\'evissage, treating positive rank and
finite length separately.

\begin{lemma}\label{two-out-of-three finite sums of G_r}
Let
\[0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0\]
be exact in \(\mathrm{Ch}^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\). If two of its terms admit finite
resolutions by finite direct sums of the \(G_r\), then so does the
third.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The horseshoe lemma treats the case of \(A^\bullet\) and \(C^\bullet\).
If \(B^\bullet\) and \(C^\bullet\) have the required resolutions, lift
\(B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\) to a map between them; its shifted cone
resolves \(A^\bullet\). Similarly, the cone of a lifted map resolving
\(A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\) resolves \(C^\bullet\). All terms remain
finite direct sums of the \(G_r\).
\end{proof}


\begin{lemma}\label{lowering the rank}
Let \(M\) be a coherent \(F\)-gauge of level \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\) and positive
rank. Then \(M\) contains a torsion-free positive-rank subgauge
\(L\) admitting a finite resolution by finite direct sums of the
\(G_r\), \(r\in\mathrm{I}\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We first reduce to the torsion-free case. Coherence and the level
condition imply that the torsion subgauge
\(M[p^\infty]\) is killed by some \(p^N\). Multiplication by \(p^N\)
then identifies \(M/M[p^\infty]\) with the subgauge \(p^NM\subseteq M\).
We henceforth assume that \(M\) is torsion free and put \(K=W[1/p]\).

Shifting the grading, we may also assume that \(\mathrm{I}=[0,n]\).

    For \(0\leqslant i\leqslant n\), write
    \[
        \Phi_i=\widetilde{F}^i\tau\widetilde{F}^{n-i},\qquad
        \Psi_i=\widetilde{V}^{n-i}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^i.
    \]
    These operators satisfy \(\Phi_i\Psi_i=\Psi_i\Phi_i=p^n\).
    We have \(\widetilde{F}\Phi_i=\Phi_{i+1}\widetilde{F}\) and \(\widetilde{V}\Phi_{i+1}=\Phi_i\widetilde{V}\).
    Since \(\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=p\), these maps identify the isocrystals
    \((M^i[1/p],\Phi_i)\). Their common slopes lie in \([0,n]\), since
    \(\Phi_i\Psi_i=p^n\) and both operators preserve \(M^i\).

    Choose a simple subisocrystal \(D\) of their common isocrystal,
    and write its slope as
    \[
        \lambda=l+\frac{r}{r+s}=\frac{e}{r+s},
    \]
    where \(l=\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\), \(r,s\) are integers with
    \(r\geqslant0\), \(s>0\), and \(r+s=\dim_KD\), and
    \(e=l(r+s)+r\). The integers \(r,s\) need not be coprime.

    If \(l<n\), choose \(j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and \(t\in\mathbb{Z}\)
    uniquely by \(j+nt=l-e\). If \(l=n\), put \(j=n\) and
    \(t=-(r+s)\); the same equality holds.
    Choose \(0\neq x\in D\cap M^l\), and let \(L\subseteq M\)
    be the subgauge of level \(\mathrm{I}=[0,n]\) generated by \(x\), equivalently,
    the image of the morphism \(G_l\to M\) sending \(\alpha_l\) to \(x\). It is coherent and torsion free.
    Simplicity of \(D\) makes \(x\) cyclic, so \(L\) has rank \(r+s>0\).
    We claim that the surjection \(\pi:G_l\to L\), \(\alpha_l\mapsto x\),
    fits into an exact sequence
    \[
        0\longrightarrow G_j\xrightarrow{\ u_P\ }G_l
        \xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }L\longrightarrow0.
    \]

    To construct \(u_P\) and compute its image, set
    \[
        \mathcal A:=W_\sigma[\Phi,\Phi^{-1}],\qquad
        \mathcal B:=\mathcal A[1/p],
    \]
    where \(\Phi a=\sigma(a)\Phi\), and let \(\Phi\) act on
    \(D\) as \(\Phi_l\).
    The cyclic vector \(x\) has a monic relation
    \[
        P(\Phi)=\Phi^{r+s}+\sum_{a=0}^{r+s-1}c_a\Phi^a.
    \]
    We have \(P(\Phi)x=0\) and \(D\cong\mathcal B/\mathcal B P\).
    The Newton polygon theorem for cyclic difference modules gives
    \[
        v_p(c_a)\geqslant (r+s-a)\lambda,\qquad
        v_p(c_0)=(r+s)\lambda=e.
    \]
    Here and below \(v_p(0)=+\infty\).
    This applies over any perfect \(k\): simplicity makes \(x\) cyclic, without assuming that \(k\) is algebraically closed.\footnote{For the cyclic-vector and Newton-polygon statements, see K. S. Kedlaya,
    \href{https://kskedlaya.org/18.787/difference.pdf}{\emph{A little difference algebra}}, Lemma 1 and Proposition 18.}

    To compute the kernel integrally, we describe the graded pieces of
    the projective generators as lattices in \(\mathcal B\).
    For \(B=\sum_q b_q\Phi^q\in\mathcal B\), define
    \[
        v_0(B)=\min_q v_p(b_q),\qquad
        v_n(B)=\min_q\{v_p(b_q)+nq\},
    \]
    with both valuations equal to \(+\infty\) at zero. Both are multiplicative.
    For \(v_0\), this follows by reduction modulo \(p\), since \(k_\sigma[\Phi,\Phi^{-1}]\) has no zero divisors;
    the assertion for \(v_n\) follows by substituting \(p^n\Phi\) for \(\Phi\).
    For every integer \(b\), put
    \[
        \Lambda_b=\{B\in\mathcal B:v_0(B)\geqslant0,\ v_n(B)\geqslant-b\}
        =\bigoplus_{q\in\mathbb{Z}}W p^{\max\{0,-nq-b\}}\Phi^q.
    \]

    The lattices \(\Lambda_i\) give coordinates for the projective
    generators. For \(G_a\), consider the map of right
    \(W_\sigma[\Phi,\Psi]\)-modules
    \[
        \widetilde{F}^{a-i}:G_a^i\longrightarrow G_a^a[1/p]\cong\mathcal B
        \qquad(0\leqslant i,a\leqslant n).
    \]
    Here the latter identification sends \(\Phi_a^q\alpha_a\) to \(\Phi^q\)
    for every \(q\in\mathbb{Z}\). This map identifies \(G_a^i\) with the
    lattice \(\Lambda_{i-a}\):
    \[
        \widetilde{F}^{a-i}:G_a^i\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_{i-a}\subseteq\mathcal B.
    \]
    To check this, if \(i\geqslant a\), the two strings of
    \Cref{definition of G_r}
    become \(\Phi^q\) for \(q\geqslant0\) and
    \(p^{-nq-(i-a)}\Phi^q\) for \(q<0\); if \(i\leqslant a\),
    they become \(\Phi^q\) for \(q>0\) and
    \(p^{-nq-(i-a)}\Phi^q\) for \(q\leqslant0\).
    Here \(\Psi=p^n\Phi^{-1}\). In these coordinates, \(\widetilde{F}\) is inclusion and \(\widetilde{V}\) is
    multiplication by \(p\).
    Thus the gauge \(G_a\) of level \(\mathrm{I}\) has the following lattice
    description:
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
        \Lambda_{-a}
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-a}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i+1-a}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-a}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex].
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    The endpoint identification is
    \(\tau:\Lambda_{n-a}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_{-a}\),
    \(Q\mapsto\Phi Q\).

    In these coordinates we can compute the kernel of \(\pi:G_l\to L\).
    Under the preceding identification, the kernel in gauge degree \(i\)
    of \(\pi^i:G_l^i\to L^i\) is \(\Lambda_{i-l}\cap\mathcal B P\).
    Indeed, if \(z\in G_l^i\) corresponds to \(Q\in\Lambda_{i-l}\),
    then \(\widetilde{F}^{l-i}\pi^i(z)=Q(\Phi_l)x\) after inverting \(p\).
    Since \(L^i\) is torsion free and \(D\cong\mathcal B/\mathcal B P\),
    this vanishes precisely when \(Q\in\mathcal B P\).
    The coefficient inequalities for \(P\) imply \(v_0(P)=0\) and \(v_n(P)=e\).
    Indeed, the first minimum is attained by \(\Phi^{r+s}\), and
    \(v_p(c_a)+na\geqslant e+(n-\lambda)a\), with equality at \(a=0\).
    Multiplicativity therefore gives, for every integer \(b\),
    \begin{equation}\label{lowering rank lattice kernel}
        \Lambda_b\cap\mathcal B P=\Lambda_{b+e}P.
    \end{equation}
    In fact, \(BP\in\Lambda_b\) if and only if \(v_0(B)\geqslant0\) and \(v_n(B)\geqslant-b-e\).
    As a result, the kernel gauge of \(\pi:G_l\to L\) is
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.8em]
        \Lambda_{-l+e}P
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-l+e}P
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-l+e}P
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex].
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    Its endpoint identification is left multiplication by \(\Phi\).
    This gauge is isomorphic to \(G_j\): since \(j+nt=l-e\),
    right multiplication by \(\Phi^tP\) gives isomorphisms
    \[
        \Lambda_{i-j}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_{i-l+e}P,
        \qquad Q\longmapsto Q\Phi^tP.
    \]
    Indeed, \(\Lambda_{i-j}\Phi^t=\Lambda_{i-j-nt}=\Lambda_{i-l+e}\),
    and multiplication by the nonzero element \(P\) is injective.
    These maps commute with inclusion, multiplication by \(p\),
    and left multiplication by \(\Phi\), hence respect all gauge operators.

    The resulting morphism of gauges is displayed below; every upward
    map is right multiplication by \(\Phi^tP\).
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.8em,row sep=large]
        G_l:\quad
        & \Lambda_{-l}
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-l}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-l}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
        \\
        G_j:\quad \arrow[u,"u_P"]
        & \Lambda_{-j}
          \arrow[u,"\cdot\Phi^tP"]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-j}
          \arrow[u,"\cdot\Phi^tP"]
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-j}
          \arrow[u,"\cdot\Phi^tP"]
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex].
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    It is injective, since \(\mathcal B\) has no zero divisors.
    Outside \([0,n]\), exactness follows from the level condition. Hence
    \[
        0\longrightarrow G_j\xrightarrow{\ u_P\ }G_l\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }L\longrightarrow0
    \]
    is the required finite projective resolution.

\end{proof}


The rank reduction leaves coherent \(F\)-gauges of finite length.
We describe the simple objects that occur as composition factors and
give their resolutions before proving the classification.

\begin{itemize}
    \item For the interior simple \(S_r\), with \(m<r<n\), let
\(S_r\) be the gauge with
\[S_r^r=k,\qquad S_r^a=0\quad(a\neq r).\]
The natural map \(G_r\to S_r\) sends \(\alpha_r\mapsto 1\in S_r^r\). Its kernel is generated by the two relations
\(
\widetilde{V}\alpha_r=0,\; \widetilde{F}\alpha_r=0,
\)
lying in degrees \(r-1\) and \(r+1\). The only syzygy is
\(
\widetilde{F}\beta_{r-1}-\widetilde{V}\beta_{r+1}=0,
\)
since both terms map to \(p\alpha_r\). Hence \(S_r\) has the resolution
\[
0\to G_r\xrightarrow{} G_{r-1}\oplus G_{r+1}\xrightarrow{} G_r\to S_r\to0.
\]
Thus \(S_r\in\mathcal C\).

    \item 
The boundary simple \(S_{\tau}\) is defined by
\[
S_{\tau}^m=k,\qquad S_{\tau}^n=k,\qquad S_{\tau}^a=0\quad(m<a<n),
\]
with \(\tau:S_{\tau}^n\cong S_{\tau}^m\). The map \(G_m\to S_{\tau}\) sends \(\alpha_m\mapsto 1\in S_{\tau}^m\). The kernel is generated by
\(
\widetilde{F}\alpha_m=0,\;\; \widetilde{V}\tau^{-1}\alpha_m=0.
\)
The unique overlap relation is
\(
\widetilde{V}\beta_{m+1}-\tau\widetilde{F}\beta_{n-1}=0,
\)
because both terms map to \(p\alpha_m\). Therefore \(S_{\tau}\) has a finite resolution
\[
0\to G_m\to G_{m+1}\oplus G_{n-1}\to G_m\to S_{\tau}\to0.
\]
Thus \(S_{\tau}\in\mathcal C\).

   \item 
For the cyclic case, let \(N\) be a \(k\)-vector space equipped with a bijective
semilinear operator \(\Phi\), and define the constant cyclic
\(k\)-gauge \(S_{\Phi,N}\) by
\[
S_{\Phi,N}^a=N\quad\text{for all }a\in[m,n],
\]
with return operator
\[
\tau\widetilde{F}^{n-m}:S_{\Phi,N}^m\longrightarrow S_{\Phi,N}^m
\]
identified with \(\Phi:N\to N\). If \(N\) is simple as a
\(\Phi\)-module, every nonzero \(x\in N\) is cyclic; let
\(P(\Phi)x=0\) be its minimal relation.
In this case
\(
S_{\Phi,N}\cong G_m/(p,P(\Phi))G_m.
\)
It therefore has the Koszul resolution
\[
0\to G_m\xrightarrow{\ d_2\ }G_m\oplus G_m\xrightarrow{\ d_1\ }G_m\to S_{\Phi,N}\to0,
\]
where
\(
d_1(a,b)=ap+bP(\Phi),
\)
and
\(
d_2(x)=(xP(\Phi),-xp).
\)
Hence \(S_{\Phi,N}\in\mathcal C\).

\item 
Similarly, consider the constant cyclic \(k\)-gauge \(S_{\Psi,N}\).
\end{itemize}




\begin{proposition}\label{finite length F-gauge structures}
Let \(M\) be a coherent \(F\)-gauge whose graded pieces have finite
\(W\)-length. Then \(M\) admits a composition series, and every simple
factor is of one of the following types:
\[
S_r,\qquad S_\tau,\qquad S_{\Phi,N},\qquad S_{\Psi,N},
\]
where \(N\) is simple for the indicated semilinear operator.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Since \(M\) is supported in finitely many degrees,
\[
    \ell(M):=\sum_{r\in \mathrm{I}} \ell_W(M^r)<\infty .
\]
Every sub-\(F\)-gauge structure \(N\subset M\) satisfies
\[
    \ell(N)=\sum_{r\in\mathrm{I}} \ell_W(N^r)\leq \ell(M),
\]
The bound \(\ell(M)\) therefore makes the category both Artinian and
Noetherian, and induction on \(\ell(M)\) gives a composition series.

It remains to identify the simple objects. Let \(M\) be simple. Since
multiplication by \(p\) is compatible with all the structure maps, \(pM\subset M\)
is a sub-\(F\)-gauge structure. By simplicity, either \(pM=0\) or \(pM=M\).
The second possibility is excluded because \(M\) has finite \(W\)-length.
Thus
\[
    pM=0.
\]
Hence a simple object is a finite-dimensional graded \(k\)-vector
space with induced operators
\[
    \widetilde{F},\ \widetilde{V},\tau,\tau^{-1}. 
\]
satisfying the reduced relations. Their images and kernels are
subgauges.

Every nonzero homogeneous element generates \(M\), so we can classify
the simple objects by the behavior of the structure maps on such an
element.

If all structure maps out of \(0\neq x\in M^r\) vanish, then
\(m<r<n\), \(\widetilde{F} x=\widetilde{V} x=0\), and simplicity forces
\[M=kx
\]
concentrated in degree \(r\). This is the simple object \(S_r\).

If \(M^m=0\), then the support of \(M\) is contained in a strictly smaller
interval. By induction on the length of the interval, \(M\) is one of the
skyscraper simples. Hence
\(
    M\cong S_r
\)
for some \(r\in [m+1,n]\).

Assume now that \(M^m\neq 0\). Consider the two structure maps out of \(M^m\),
namely
\(
    \tau\widetilde{F}^{n-m}:M^m\longrightarrow M^{m},\;\;
    \widetilde{V}^{n-m}\tau^{-1}:M^m\longrightarrow M^{m}.
\)
If both maps vanish, simplicity forces \(M\) to be concentrated at the
boundary; thus
\(
    M\cong S_{\tau}.
\)

Suppose now that at least one return map is nonzero. If
\(
    \Phi:M^m\longrightarrow M^{m}
\)
is nonzero, its image generates a nonzero subgauge and therefore all
of \(M\). The iterates of \(\widetilde{F}\), together with \(\tau\), identify the
graded pieces cyclically:
\[
    M^m \xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}} M^{m+1}
    \xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}} \cdots
    \xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}} M^n
    \xrightarrow{\tau} M^m .
\]
Consequently \(M\) is a constant cyclic \(k\)-gauge. Its monodromy around the
cycle is the semilinear automorphism
\(
    \tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-m}:M^m\longrightarrow M^m .
\)
Let
\(
    N:=M^m
\)
equipped with this semilinear operator. If \(N\) had a nontrivial
\(\Phi\)-stable subspace, then propagating it around the cycle would give a
nontrivial sub-\(F\)-gauge structure of \(M\), contradicting simplicity.
Therefore \(N\) is simple as a \(\Phi\)-module. Hence
\(
    M\cong S_{\Phi,N}.
\)
If \(\Phi=0\) but \(\Psi\neq0\), the same argument with \(\Psi\) gives
\(
    M\cong S_{\Psi,N}
\)
for some simple \(\Psi\)-module \(N\).

These cases exhaust the simple objects:
\[
    S_r,\qquad S_{\tau},\qquad S_{\Phi,N},\qquad S_{\Psi,N}.
\]
\end{proof}

Each simple finite-length coherent gauge lies in \(\mathcal C\), and
extension closure therefore puts every finite-length coherent gauge in
\(\mathcal C\). Combined with the positive-rank reduction, this proves
the assertion for coherent \(F\)-gauges.

Resolving the cohomology objects and assembling the resolutions along
the standard truncation triangles proves the statement for bounded
complexes.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{two-out-of-three finite sums of G_r}
Let
\[0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0\]
be exact in \(\mathrm{Ch}^-({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\). If two of its terms admit finite
resolutions by finite direct sums of the \(G_r\), then so does the
third.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
The horseshoe lemma treats the case of \(A^\bullet\) and \(C^\bullet\).
If \(B^\bullet\) and \(C^\bullet\) have the required resolutions, lift
\(B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\) to a map between them; its shifted cone
resolves \(A^\bullet\). Similarly, the cone of a lifted map resolving
\(A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\) resolves \(C^\bullet\). All terms remain
finite direct sums of the \(G_r\).
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lowering the rank}
Let \(M\) be a coherent \(F\)-gauge of level \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\) and positive
rank. Then \(M\) contains a torsion-free positive-rank subgauge
\(L\) admitting a finite resolution by finite direct sums of the
\(G_r\), \(r\in\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
We first reduce to the torsion-free case. Coherence and the level
condition imply that the torsion subgauge
\(M[p^\infty]\) is killed by some \(p^N\). Multiplication by \(p^N\)
then identifies \(M/M[p^\infty]\) with the subgauge \(p^NM\subseteq M\).
We henceforth assume that \(M\) is torsion free and put \(K=W[1/p]\).

Shifting the grading, we may also assume that \(\mathrm{I}=[0,n]\).

    For \(0\leqslant i\leqslant n\), write
    \[
        \Phi_i=\widetilde{F}^i\tau\widetilde{F}^{n-i},\qquad
        \Psi_i=\widetilde{V}^{n-i}\tau^{-1}\widetilde{V}^i.
    \]
    These operators satisfy \(\Phi_i\Psi_i=\Psi_i\Phi_i=p^n\).
    We have \(\widetilde{F}\Phi_i=\Phi_{i+1}\widetilde{F}\) and \(\widetilde{V}\Phi_{i+1}=\Phi_i\widetilde{V}\).
    Since \(\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=p\), these maps identify the isocrystals
    \((M^i[1/p],\Phi_i)\). Their common slopes lie in \([0,n]\), since
    \(\Phi_i\Psi_i=p^n\) and both operators preserve \(M^i\).

    Choose a simple subisocrystal \(D\) of their common isocrystal,
    and write its slope as
    \[
        \lambda=l+\frac{r}{r+s}=\frac{e}{r+s},
    \]
    where \(l=\lfloor\lambda\rfloor\), \(r,s\) are integers with
    \(r\geqslant0\), \(s>0\), and \(r+s=\dim_KD\), and
    \(e=l(r+s)+r\). The integers \(r,s\) need not be coprime.

    If \(l<n\), choose \(j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and \(t\in\mathbb{Z}\)
    uniquely by \(j+nt=l-e\). If \(l=n\), put \(j=n\) and
    \(t=-(r+s)\); the same equality holds.
    Choose \(0\neq x\in D\cap M^l\), and let \(L\subseteq M\)
    be the subgauge of level \(\mathrm{I}=[0,n]\) generated by \(x\), equivalently,
    the image of the morphism \(G_l\to M\) sending \(\alpha_l\) to \(x\). It is coherent and torsion free.
    Simplicity of \(D\) makes \(x\) cyclic, so \(L\) has rank \(r+s>0\).
    We claim that the surjection \(\pi:G_l\to L\), \(\alpha_l\mapsto x\),
    fits into an exact sequence
    \[
        0\longrightarrow G_j\xrightarrow{\ u_P\ }G_l
        \xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }L\longrightarrow0.
    \]

    To construct \(u_P\) and compute its image, set
    \[
        \mathcal A:=W_\sigma[\Phi,\Phi^{-1}],\qquad
        \mathcal B:=\mathcal A[1/p],
    \]
    where \(\Phi a=\sigma(a)\Phi\), and let \(\Phi\) act on
    \(D\) as \(\Phi_l\).
    The cyclic vector \(x\) has a monic relation
    \[
        P(\Phi)=\Phi^{r+s}+\sum_{a=0}^{r+s-1}c_a\Phi^a.
    \]
    We have \(P(\Phi)x=0\) and \(D\cong\mathcal B/\mathcal B P\).
    The Newton polygon theorem for cyclic difference modules gives
    \[
        v_p(c_a)\geqslant (r+s-a)\lambda,\qquad
        v_p(c_0)=(r+s)\lambda=e.
    \]
    Here and below \(v_p(0)=+\infty\).
    This applies over any perfect \(k\): simplicity makes \(x\) cyclic, without assuming that \(k\) is algebraically closed.\footnote{For the cyclic-vector and Newton-polygon statements, see K. S. Kedlaya,
    \href{https://kskedlaya.org/18.787/difference.pdf}{\emph{A little difference algebra}}, Lemma 1 and Proposition 18.}

    To compute the kernel integrally, we describe the graded pieces of
    the projective generators as lattices in \(\mathcal B\).
    For \(B=\sum_q b_q\Phi^q\in\mathcal B\), define
    \[
        v_0(B)=\min_q v_p(b_q),\qquad
        v_n(B)=\min_q\{v_p(b_q)+nq\},
    \]
    with both valuations equal to \(+\infty\) at zero. Both are multiplicative.
    For \(v_0\), this follows by reduction modulo \(p\), since \(k_\sigma[\Phi,\Phi^{-1}]\) has no zero divisors;
    the assertion for \(v_n\) follows by substituting \(p^n\Phi\) for \(\Phi\).
    For every integer \(b\), put
    \[
        \Lambda_b=\{B\in\mathcal B:v_0(B)\geqslant0,\ v_n(B)\geqslant-b\}
        =\bigoplus_{q\in\mathbb{Z}}W p^{\max\{0,-nq-b\}}\Phi^q.
    \]

    The lattices \(\Lambda_i\) give coordinates for the projective
    generators. For \(G_a\), consider the map of right
    \(W_\sigma[\Phi,\Psi]\)-modules
    \[
        \widetilde{F}^{a-i}:G_a^i\longrightarrow G_a^a[1/p]\cong\mathcal B
        \qquad(0\leqslant i,a\leqslant n).
    \]
    Here the latter identification sends \(\Phi_a^q\alpha_a\) to \(\Phi^q\)
    for every \(q\in\mathbb{Z}\). This map identifies \(G_a^i\) with the
    lattice \(\Lambda_{i-a}\):
    \[
        \widetilde{F}^{a-i}:G_a^i\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_{i-a}\subseteq\mathcal B.
    \]
    To check this, if \(i\geqslant a\), the two strings of
    \Cref{definition of G_r}
    become \(\Phi^q\) for \(q\geqslant0\) and
    \(p^{-nq-(i-a)}\Phi^q\) for \(q<0\); if \(i\leqslant a\),
    they become \(\Phi^q\) for \(q>0\) and
    \(p^{-nq-(i-a)}\Phi^q\) for \(q\leqslant0\).
    Here \(\Psi=p^n\Phi^{-1}\). In these coordinates, \(\widetilde{F}\) is inclusion and \(\widetilde{V}\) is
    multiplication by \(p\).
    Thus the gauge \(G_a\) of level \(\mathrm{I}\) has the following lattice
    description:
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
        \Lambda_{-a}
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-a}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i+1-a}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-a}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex].
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    The endpoint identification is
    \(\tau:\Lambda_{n-a}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_{-a}\),
    \(Q\mapsto\Phi Q\).

    In these coordinates we can compute the kernel of \(\pi:G_l\to L\).
    Under the preceding identification, the kernel in gauge degree \(i\)
    of \(\pi^i:G_l^i\to L^i\) is \(\Lambda_{i-l}\cap\mathcal B P\).
    Indeed, if \(z\in G_l^i\) corresponds to \(Q\in\Lambda_{i-l}\),
    then \(\widetilde{F}^{l-i}\pi^i(z)=Q(\Phi_l)x\) after inverting \(p\).
    Since \(L^i\) is torsion free and \(D\cong\mathcal B/\mathcal B P\),
    this vanishes precisely when \(Q\in\mathcal B P\).
    The coefficient inequalities for \(P\) imply \(v_0(P)=0\) and \(v_n(P)=e\).
    Indeed, the first minimum is attained by \(\Phi^{r+s}\), and
    \(v_p(c_a)+na\geqslant e+(n-\lambda)a\), with equality at \(a=0\).
    Multiplicativity therefore gives, for every integer \(b\),
    \begin{equation}\label{lowering rank lattice kernel}
        \Lambda_b\cap\mathcal B P=\Lambda_{b+e}P.
    \end{equation}
    In fact, \(BP\in\Lambda_b\) if and only if \(v_0(B)\geqslant0\) and \(v_n(B)\geqslant-b-e\).
    As a result, the kernel gauge of \(\pi:G_l\to L\) is
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.8em]
        \Lambda_{-l+e}P
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-l+e}P
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-l+e}P
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex].
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    Its endpoint identification is left multiplication by \(\Phi\).
    This gauge is isomorphic to \(G_j\): since \(j+nt=l-e\),
    right multiplication by \(\Phi^tP\) gives isomorphisms
    \[
        \Lambda_{i-j}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_{i-l+e}P,
        \qquad Q\longmapsto Q\Phi^tP.
    \]
    Indeed, \(\Lambda_{i-j}\Phi^t=\Lambda_{i-j-nt}=\Lambda_{i-l+e}\),
    and multiplication by the nonzero element \(P\) is injective.
    These maps commute with inclusion, multiplication by \(p\),
    and left multiplication by \(\Phi\), hence respect all gauge operators.

    The resulting morphism of gauges is displayed below; every upward
    map is right multiplication by \(\Phi^tP\).
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.8em,row sep=large]
        G_l:\quad
        & \Lambda_{-l}
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-l}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-l}
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
        \\
        G_j:\quad \arrow[u,"u_P"]
        & \Lambda_{-j}
          \arrow[u,"\cdot\Phi^tP"]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{i-j}
          \arrow[u,"\cdot\Phi^tP"]
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \cdots
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex]
          \arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{incl.}",shift left=0.6ex]
        & \Lambda_{n-j}
          \arrow[u,"\cdot\Phi^tP"]
          \arrow[l,"p",shift left=0.6ex].
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    It is injective, since \(\mathcal B\) has no zero divisors.
    Outside \([0,n]\), exactness follows from the level condition. Hence
    \[
        0\longrightarrow G_j\xrightarrow{\ u_P\ }G_l\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }L\longrightarrow0
    \]
    is the required finite projective resolution.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{finite length F-gauge structures}
Let \(M\) be a coherent \(F\)-gauge whose graded pieces have finite
\(W\)-length. Then \(M\) admits a composition series, and every simple
factor is of one of the following types:
\[
S_r,\qquad S_\tau,\qquad S_{\Phi,N},\qquad S_{\Psi,N},
\]
where \(N\) is simple for the indicated semilinear operator.
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Since \(M\) is supported in finitely many degrees,
\[
    \ell(M):=\sum_{r\in \mathrm{I}} \ell_W(M^r)<\infty .
\]
Every sub-\(F\)-gauge structure \(N\subset M\) satisfies
\[
    \ell(N)=\sum_{r\in\mathrm{I}} \ell_W(N^r)\leq \ell(M),
\]
The bound \(\ell(M)\) therefore makes the category both Artinian and
Noetherian, and induction on \(\ell(M)\) gives a composition series.

It remains to identify the simple objects. Let \(M\) be simple. Since
multiplication by \(p\) is compatible with all the structure maps, \(pM\subset M\)
is a sub-\(F\)-gauge structure. By simplicity, either \(pM=0\) or \(pM=M\).
The second possibility is excluded because \(M\) has finite \(W\)-length.
Thus
\[
    pM=0.
\]
Hence a simple object is a finite-dimensional graded \(k\)-vector
space with induced operators
\[
    \widetilde{F},\ \widetilde{V},\tau,\tau^{-1}. 
\]
satisfying the reduced relations. Their images and kernels are
subgauges.

Every nonzero homogeneous element generates \(M\), so we can classify
the simple objects by the behavior of the structure maps on such an
element.

If all structure maps out of \(0\neq x\in M^r\) vanish, then
\(m<r<n\), \(\widetilde{F} x=\widetilde{V} x=0\), and simplicity forces
\[M=kx
\]
concentrated in degree \(r\). This is the simple object \(S_r\).

If \(M^m=0\), then the support of \(M\) is contained in a strictly smaller
interval. By induction on the length of the interval, \(M\) is one of the
skyscraper simples. Hence
\(
    M\cong S_r
\)
for some \(r\in [m+1,n]\).

Assume now that \(M^m\neq 0\). Consider the two structure maps out of \(M^m\),
namely
\(
    \tau\widetilde{F}^{n-m}:M^m\longrightarrow M^{m},\;\;
    \widetilde{V}^{n-m}\tau^{-1}:M^m\longrightarrow M^{m}.
\)
If both maps vanish, simplicity forces \(M\) to be concentrated at the
boundary; thus
\(
    M\cong S_{\tau}.
\)

Suppose now that at least one return map is nonzero. If
\(
    \Phi:M^m\longrightarrow M^{m}
\)
is nonzero, its image generates a nonzero subgauge and therefore all
of \(M\). The iterates of \(\widetilde{F}\), together with \(\tau\), identify the
graded pieces cyclically:
\[
    M^m \xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}} M^{m+1}
    \xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}} \cdots
    \xrightarrow{\widetilde{F}} M^n
    \xrightarrow{\tau} M^m .
\]
Consequently \(M\) is a constant cyclic \(k\)-gauge. Its monodromy around the
cycle is the semilinear automorphism
\(
    \tau\widetilde{F}^{\,n-m}:M^m\longrightarrow M^m .
\)
Let
\(
    N:=M^m
\)
equipped with this semilinear operator. If \(N\) had a nontrivial
\(\Phi\)-stable subspace, then propagating it around the cycle would give a
nontrivial sub-\(F\)-gauge structure of \(M\), contradicting simplicity.
Therefore \(N\) is simple as a \(\Phi\)-module. Hence
\(
    M\cong S_{\Phi,N}.
\)
If \(\Phi=0\) but \(\Psi\neq0\), the same argument with \(\Psi\) gives
\(
    M\cong S_{\Psi,N}
\)
for some simple \(\Psi\)-module \(N\).

These cases exhaust the simple objects:
\[
    S_r,\qquad S_{\tau},\qquad S_{\Phi,N},\qquad S_{\Psi,N}.
\]
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rmt-tensor-product}
Using the preceding Morita equivalence, we also write \(M\) for the
left \(A\)-module associated to an \(F\)-gauge \(M\) of level \(\mathrm{I}\), with \(M^j=e_jM\).
The \(F\)-gauge \(\oplus_{r\in\mathrm{I}}G_r\) corresponds to \(A\) itself, regarded as a left \(A\)-module.
Thus \(\mathrm{t}(A)\) means that we first regard this module as
the \(F\)-gauge \(\oplus_{r\in\mathrm{I}}G_r\). Set
\[
\mathcal T:=\mathrm{t}(A)\cong\bigoplus_{j\in\mathrm{I}}\mathrm{t}(G_j).
\]
This is a complex of graded left \(R\)-modules. 

For \(a\in A\), right multiplication \(r_a:z\mapsto za\) is a
left \(A\)-linear endomorphism of \(A\). It then induces a right \(A\)-action
on \(\mathcal T\) by \(z\cdot a:=\mathrm{t}(r_a)(z)\). This action
commutes with the left \(R\)-action and the complex differential,
thus \(\mathcal T\) is a complex of graded left \(R\)-modules and
right \(A\)-modules with commuting actions. The tensor product
\(\mathcal T\otimes_A M\) is taken termwise:
its term in complex degree \(q\) is \(\mathcal T^q\otimes_A M\),
with the inherited left \(R\)-action and differential
\(\delta\otimes1\). It is therefore a complex of graded left
\(R\)-modules. As a matter of fact,
there is a natural isomorphism of \(R\)-complexes
\[
\theta_M:\mathcal T\otimes_A M\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{t}(M).
\]
Indeed, by the adjunction proved in \Cref{adjunction between FG and t},
\(\mathrm{t}\) preserves direct sums and cokernels. Apply it to a free
presentation
\[
A^{(S_1)}\longrightarrow A^{(S_0)}\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.
\]
Both \(\mathrm{t}(M)\) and \(\mathcal T\otimes_A M\) are the cokernel
of the same map \(\mathcal T^{(S_1)}\to\mathcal T^{(S_0)}\): its
matrix entries act by the right \(A\)-action just defined.

The description on generators explains how tensor balancing recovers
the defining relations of the functor.
Let \(\alpha_j\in G_j^j\) be the canonical generator, corresponding
to \(e_j\in Ae_j\), and write
\[
b_{i,j}:=\beta_i\otimes\alpha_j
\in\mathrm{t}(G_j)\cong\mathcal T e_j.
\]
Viewed inside \(\mathrm{t}(A)\), this is the symbol
\(\beta_i\otimes e_j\). For \(x\in M^j\), 
\begin{equation}\label{rmt-tensor-generators}
\theta_M(b_{i,j}\otimes_A x)=\beta_i\otimes x.
\end{equation}
More generally, let \(x\in M^s=e_sM\). Tensor balancing gives
\[
b_{i,j}\otimes_A x
=b_{i,j}\otimes_A e_sx
=(b_{i,j}e_s)\otimes_A x.
\]
Since \(\alpha_j\) corresponds to \(e_j\), we have
\(b_{i,j}e_s=\beta_i\otimes(\alpha_je_s)\).
The orthogonality of the idempotents makes this \(b_{i,j}\) if
\(j=s\) and zero otherwise. Hence
\[
\theta_M(b_{i,j}\otimes_A x)=
\begin{cases}
\beta_i\otimes x,&j=s,\\
0,&j\ne s.
\end{cases}
\]

Tensor balancing encodes the gauge relations. For
\(a\in e_\ell A e_j\), right multiplication gives
\(b_{i,\ell}a=\beta_i\otimes a\), and hence, for \(x\in M^j\),
\[
b_{i,\ell}\otimes_A(ax)
=(b_{i,\ell}a)\otimes_A x
=(\beta_i\otimes a)\otimes_A x.
\]
The defining relations of \(\mathrm{t}(A)\) express the last symbol in
terms of \(b_{i,j}\). For example, for \(m\leq i<n\), the arrow
\(\widetilde{F}_i\in e_{i+1}Ae_i\) satisfies
\[
b_{i,i+1}\widetilde{F}_i=F b_{i,i},
\]
so balancing recovers
\(\beta_i\otimes\widetilde{F}_i x=F(\beta_i\otimes x)\).
Likewise, the scalar relation is encoded by
\[
b_{i,j}(\lambda e_j)=
\begin{cases}
\lambda b_{i,j},&j\leq i,\\
\sigma(\lambda)b_{i,j},&j>i,
\end{cases}
\qquad \lambda\in W.
\]
The relations involving \(\widetilde{V}\), \(\tau\), and the differentials
are inherited in the same way from \(\mathcal T\); in particular,
\(\delta(z\otimes_A x)=(\delta z)\otimes_A x\).
Thus the inverse of \(\theta_M\) sends
\(\beta_i\otimes x\) to \(b_{i,j}\otimes_A x\) for \(x\in M^j\).
These tensors are taken in the whole \(\mathcal T\otimes_A M\):
the right \(A\)-action can move between the summands
\(\mathcal T e_j\), which are not generally right \(A\)-submodules.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{Exactness after completion}
The above termwise \(p\)-adic completion
is a resolution of \(M\) by finite direct sums of the completed projective generators \(\widehat{G}_r\).
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Let \(d:P_a\to P_{a-1}\) be a differential and set \(K=\ker(d)\).
It suffices to prove that the sequence
\(
0\to \widehat K\to \widehat{P_a}\to \widehat{\operatorname{im}(d)}\to0
\)
is exact. 

We use Artin--Rees in the following form. If \(B\) is left Noetherian,
\(p\in Z(B)\), \(P\) is a finitely generated left \(B\)-module, and
\(K\subseteq P\) is any submodule, then for some \(c\geq0\),
\[
K\cap p^{N+c}P=p^N(K\cap p^cP)\subseteq p^NK
\qquad(N\geq0).
\]
Indeed, the Rees ring
\[
\mathrm{Rees}_{(p)}(B)=\bigoplus_{N\geq0}p^NBt^N
\]
is a quotient of the central polynomial ring \(B[T]\), hence left
Noetherian. The Rees module \(\bigoplus_{N\geq0}p^NPt^N\) is generated
in degree zero by generators of \(P\). Its graded submodule
\(\bigoplus_{N\geq0}(K\cap p^NP)t^N\) therefore has finitely many
homogeneous generators \(x_\alpha t^{n_\alpha}\). Let
\(c=\max_\alpha n_\alpha\), taking \(c=0\) if \(K=0\). In degree
\(N+c\), these generators express every element as \(p^N\) times an
element of \(K\cap p^cP\). The reverse inclusion is immediate.

For the cyclic operator ring
\[
B=W_\sigma[\Phi,\Psi]/
(\Phi\Psi=\Psi\Phi=p^{n-m})
\]
\(B\) is left Noetherian and \(p\) is central. Since \(P_a^j\) and
\(K^j\) are finitely generated over \(B\), Artin--Rees gives
\(
p^{N+c}P_a^j\cap K^j\subset p^NK^j.
\)
Thus the \(p\)-adic topology on \(K^j\) agrees with the topology induced from \(P_a^j\). Equivalently,
\(
\widehat{K^j}\longrightarrow \widehat{P_a^j}
\)
is injective with image the kernel of
\(
\widehat{P_a^j}\longrightarrow \widehat{\operatorname{im}(d)^j}.
\)
This agreement of the induced and intrinsic \(p\)-adic topologies
on \(K^j\) proves exactness after completion in every gauge degree.

Finally, each \(M^j\) is already \(p\)-adically complete, and
completion commutes with finite direct sums:
\[
\widehat{P_q}\simeq
\bigoplus_{r\in\mathrm{I}}\widehat{G}_r^{\oplus a_{q,r}}.
\]
Hence \(\widehat P_\bullet\to M\) is the required resolution.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{flatness of central completion}
Let \(H\) be a left and right Noetherian ring and let \(p\in Z(H)\).
Then \(\widehat H^{\,p}:=\varprojlim_{a\geq1}H/p^aH\) is left and
right Noetherian, and is flat as a left and as a right \(H\)-module.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
The Artin--Rees estimate above applies to finite modules on both sides.
For a short exact sequence \(0\to K\to P\to Q\to0\) of finite
modules, it shows that \(p^aK\) and \(K\cap p^aP\) are cofinal
filtrations. For each \(a\), the sequence
\[
0\to K/(K\cap p^aP)\to P/p^aP\to Q/p^aQ\to0
\]
is exact, and the transition maps on its left terms are surjective.
Taking inverse limits therefore shows that completion is exact.

Applying this exactness to
\(0\to p^aH\to H\to H/p^aH\to0\) and
\(H\twoheadrightarrow p^aH\) identifies
\(\widehat{p^aH}^{\,p}=p^a\widehat H^{\,p}\), hence
\(\widehat H^{\,p}/p^a\widehat H^{\,p}\cong H/p^aH\).
The Rees ring \(\bigoplus_{a\geq0}p^aHt^a\) is a quotient of
\(H[T]\), hence left and right Noetherian. Thus
\(\operatorname{gr}_p\widehat H^{\,p}\cong\operatorname{gr}_pH\)
is left and right Noetherian. Lifting generators of graded ideals
through the complete \(p\)-adic filtration shows that
\(\widehat H^{\,p}\) is left and right Noetherian.

For a finite right \(H\)-module \(L\), a finite presentation and this
exactness give \(L\otimes_H\widehat H^{\,p}\cong\widehat L^{\,p}\).
If \(J\subseteq H\) is a right ideal, the map
\(J\otimes_H\widehat H^{\,p}\to\widehat H^{\,p}\) is consequently the
injection \(\widehat J^{\,p}\to\widehat H^{\,p}\). The right-ideal
criterion for flatness proves that \(\widehat H^{\,p}\) is flat as a
left \(H\)-module. Applying the same argument to left ideals proves
right flatness.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- definition-31: body_md -->
\label{completed R-modules of level I}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\). An \(\widehat R\)-module of level \(\mathrm{I}\) is a graded \(\widehat R\)-module of the form
\[M^m\xrightarrow{d}M^{m+1}\xrightarrow{d}\cdots
\xrightarrow{d}M^n\]
such that \(M^i\) is an algebraic left \(\widehat R^{\,0}\)-module for
\(i<n\), whereas \(M^n\) is an algebraic left
\(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\)-module. The \(\widehat R^{\,0}\)-action on the
top term is induced by \(\iota\). 
Morphisms are componentwise homomorphisms over these coefficient rings that commute with the differential.
We denote this abelian category by
\(\widehat R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end definition-31 -->
<!-- definition-32: body_md -->
\label{definition of rho}
For \(i,j,s\in\mathrm{I}\), define the coordinate map
\[
\rho_i^{j,s}:e_sAe_j\longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
R^0,&i<n,\\
R^{\mathrm{top}},&i=n,
\end{cases}
\]
characterized as follows. Write \([x]^{j,i}\) for the element of
\(F\mathsf{G}(N)^{j,i}\) corresponding to \(x\in N^i\) 
under the identification with \(N^i\) or \(\sigma_*(N^i)\) in \Cref{definition of FG}(1). Then
\begin{equation}\label{coordinate characterization of rho}
a\cdot [x]^{j,i} 
=[\rho_i^{j,s}(a)\cdot x]^{s,i}
\in F\mathsf{G}(N)^{s,i}
\end{equation}
for every \(R\)-module \(N\) of level \(\mathrm{I}\). Here \(j\) and \(s\)
are the source and target gauge degrees, whereas \(i\) is the complex
degree.
<!-- end definition-32 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{relations satisfied by rho}
The coordinate maps \(\rho_i^{j,s}\) are additive and satisfy, for
\(a\in e_sAe_j\), \(b\in e_tAe_s\),
\[
\rho_i^{j,t}(ba)
=\rho_i^{s,t}(b)\rho_i^{j,s}(a).
\]
Moreover, if \(M\) is an \(F\)-gauge and \(m\in M^j\), then in \(\mathrm{t}(M)\)
one has
\begin{equation}\label{rho relation in rmt}
\beta_i\otimes(am)
=\rho_i^{j,s}(a)(\beta_i\otimes m).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Clear from \Cref{definition of FG} and \Cref{rmt}.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- definition-33: body_md -->
\label{definition of widehat rmt}
Let \(M\) be a left \(\widehat A\)-module. Define
\[
\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)\in\mathrm{Ch}(\widehat R\text{-}\mathrm{I})
\]
by the same generators as in \Cref{rmt}. Thus it is generated by symbols
\[
\beta_i\otimes m,
\qquad i\in\mathrm{I},\quad m\in M^j=e_jM,
\]
where \(\beta_i\otimes m\) has Raynaud-module degree \(i\) and complex
degree \(-i\), with the same truncation in degree \(-n\) as in \Cref{rmt}.
The coefficient ring in Raynaud-module degree \(i\) is \(\widehat R^{\,0}\)
for \(i<n\) and \(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\) for \(i=n\).
Impose relations \Cref{rmt}(1), \Cref{rmt}(2), and \Cref{rmt}(4),
interpreted in the completed level ringoid, and replace relation
\Cref{rmt}(3) by the following completed relation: for every
\(a\in e_s\widehat A e_j\) and \(m\in M^j\),
\[
\beta_i\otimes(am)
=\widehat\rho_i^{j,s}(a)(\beta_i\otimes m).
\]
Equivalently, if \(a\) is represented by a \(p\)-adically convergent series
of finite paths, take its image under
\(\widehat\rho_i^{j,s}\) in the corresponding coefficient ring, and let
that element act on \(\beta_i\otimes m\). The series is thus evaluated in
the coefficient ring, with no infinite sum taken inside the algebraically
free module.
<!-- end definition-33 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{widehat-rmt-tensor-product}
The argument of \Cref{rmt-tensor-product} also applies to
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}\), using the adjunction proved below. Put
\[
\mathcal T_{\widehat A}:=\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat A)
\cong\bigoplus_{j\in\mathrm{I}}\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat G_j),
\]
where the left regular module \(\widehat A\) corresponds to the
\(F\)-gauge \(\bigoplus_{j\in\mathrm{I}}\widehat G_j\). Right multiplication
on \(\widehat A\) induces a right \(\widehat A\)-action on
\(\mathcal T_{\widehat A}\), commuting with its left coefficient
actions and differential. Since \(\widehat\mathrm{t}\) preserves direct
sums and cokernels, there is a natural isomorphism
\[
\mathcal T_{\widehat A}\otimes_{\widehat A}M
\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)
\]
for every algebraic left \(\widehat A\)-module \(M\). This is the
ordinary algebraic tensor product, not a completed tensor product;
no completeness assumption on \(M\) is imposed.

Writing \(\widehat b_{i,j}:=\beta_i\otimes\alpha_j
\in\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat G_j)\cong\mathcal T_{\widehat A}e_j\),
the generator correspondence is
\[
\widehat b_{i,j}\otimes_{\widehat A}x
\longmapsto\beta_i\otimes x,
\qquad x\in M^j.
\]
For \(a\in e_\ell\widehat A e_j\), the completed relation reads
\[
\widehat b_{i,\ell}a
=\widehat\rho_i^{j,\ell}(a)\widehat b_{i,j}.
\]
The balancing relation for the tensor product is therefore
\(\beta_i\otimes(ax)=\widehat\rho_i^{j,\ell}(a)
(\beta_i\otimes x)\) in the preceding definition. The bidegrees
and the vanishing when the projective index differs from the gauge
degree are as in \Cref{rmt-tensor-generators} and its explanation.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-28: body_md -->
\label{adjunction between completed FG and t}
The functor \(\widehat\mathrm{t}\) is left adjoint to
\(Z^0\circF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\). More precisely, there is a natural isomorphism
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ch}(\widehat R\text{-}\mathrm{I})}(\widehat\mathrm{t}(M),N)
\cong
\mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat A}
\left(M,Z^0F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\right).
\]
<!-- end proposition-28 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Given a morphism \(f:\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)\to N\), send \(m\in M^j\) to the
cycle whose \(i\)-th coordinate is \(f(\beta_i\otimes m)\). Relations
\Cref{rmt}(1), \Cref{rmt}(2), and \Cref{rmt}(4) show, exactly as in
\Cref{adjunction between FG and t}, that this is a well-defined morphism of
\(F\)-gauges. The completed relation gives
\[
f(\beta_i\otimes am)
=\widehat\rho_i^{j,s}(a)f(\beta_i\otimes m),
\]
so the resulting morphism is \(\widehat A\)-linear.

Conversely, let
\(g:M\to Z^0F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\) be \(\widehat A\)-linear. Sending
\(\beta_i\otimes m\) to the \(i\)-th coordinate of \(g(m)\) extends uniquely
over the corresponding coefficient ring. The usual relations are
preserved by the same argument as for \(\mathrm{t}\), and
the completed relation is preserved because
\[
g(am)_i=(a\cdot g(m))_i
=\widehat\rho_i^{j,s}(a)g(m)_i.
\]
The two constructions are inverse and natural in \(M\) and \(N\), proving
the adjunction.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{coherent gauges embed into completed algebra}
The adjunction unit \(i(M)\to\operatorname{Res}(j(M))\) is an
isomorphism for every \(M\in D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\).
Consequently, \(j\) is fully faithful.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
First let \(M\) be a coherent gauge in degree zero, and choose a
projective resolution \(P^\bullet\to M\) by finite sums of the
\(G_r\). Since \(\widehat A\otimes_A G_r\cong\widehat G_r\),
the unit is represented by the natural map
\(P^\bullet\to\widehat P^\bullet\).
By \Cref{Exactness after completion}, the completed augmentation
\(\widehat P^\bullet\to M\) is again a quasi-isomorphism.
Its composite with \(P^\bullet\to\widehat P^\bullet\) is the
original augmentation, so the unit is a quasi-isomorphism as well.

For a bounded coherent complex \(M\), apply this conclusion to each
\(\mathrm{H}^q(M)\). The unit is a natural transformation between the exact
functors \(i\) and \(\operatorname{Res}\circ j\); induction along
the finitely many cohomological truncation triangles therefore proves
that it is an isomorphism on \(M\). This does not require termwise
completion to commute with the cohomology of an arbitrary complex.

Derived extension of scalars is left adjoint to
\(\operatorname{Res}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Hom}_{D(\widehat A)}(j(M),j(N))
&\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{D(A)}(i(M),\operatorname{Res}(j(N)))\\
&\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{D(A)}(i(M),i(N)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Morita equivalence identifies the last group with
\(\mathrm{Hom}_{D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})}(M,N)\), proving full faithfulness.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proposition-29: body_md -->
\label{derived widehat t equals widehat derived t}    
There is a commutative square: 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})} & {D(A)} & {D(R\text{-}\mathrm{I})} \\
	&{D(\widehat{A})} & {D(\widehat{R}\text{-} \mathrm{I})}
    \arrow["{i}",from=1-1, to=1-2]
    \arrow["{j}",from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}}", from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\mathrm{L}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}^{\mathrm{Tot}}}", from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
<!-- end proposition-29 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Choose a bounded projective resolution \(P^\bullet\to M\) by
finite sums of the \(G_r\), using \Cref{resolution of coherent complexes}.
Its termwise completion \(\widehat P^\bullet\) represents \(j(M)\)
and consists of projective \(\widehat A\)-modules. Hence the lower
route in the diagram is represented by
\[
 \mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(\widehat P^\bullet)\bigr).
\]
For every generator,
\(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(\widehat G_r)\cong\widehat{\mathrm{t}(G_r)}\),
naturally with respect to maps of generators. Completion commutes with
this bounded-above totalization: as in the uniform-width model in
\Cref{embedding-row-completeness}, the \(R_a\)-resolution direction
has degrees \([-2,0]\), the inverse-limit direction has degrees
\([0,1]\), and the inner direction lies in the finite interval
\(-\mathrm{I}\). Thus all the relevant totalizations have finite width in
these auxiliary directions. It follows that
\[
 \widehat{\mathrm{Tot}(\mathrm{t}(P^\bullet))}
 \simeq
 \mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(\widehat P^\bullet)\bigr).
\]
The left-hand side represents the upper route, and the generator
comparison is natural. The resulting identification is therefore
functorial in \(M\), as required.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{widehat t of FG(Hodge--Witt) }
    Let \(N\in  
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
_{\mathrm{HW}}\) be a Hodge--Witt diagonal complex               
                                                                           
                                                                     
                                                         
                               
    . Then the counit of the adjunction defining \(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}\) is an
    isomorphism of \(R\)-complexes:
    \[
    \widehat\epsilon_N:\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N))\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\widehat N.
    \]
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
By the diagonal decomposition for Hodge--Witt objects and the additivity
    of both functors, it is enough to treat a single \(V\)-topologically nilpotent Dieudonn\'e module \(D\)
    placed in bidegree \((r,-r)\), where \(r\in\mathrm{I}\). Put
    \(G=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(D[r])\). After identifying the underlying abelian groups,
    its gauge components and structure maps are
    \[
    G^j=\begin{cases}
        D,&j\leqslant r,\\
        \sigma_*D,&j>r,
    \end{cases}
    \qquad
    \widetilde F|_{G^j}=\begin{cases}
        p,&j<r,\\
        F_D,&j=r,\\
        1,&j>r,
    \end{cases}
    \qquad
    \widetilde V|_{G^j}=\begin{cases}
        1,&j\leqslant r,\\
        V_D,&j=r+1,\\
        p,&j>r+1.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    Here and below the identifications between the two tails are made using
    \(\tau\). For \(x\in D\), recall that \([x]^j\in G^j\) denotes
    the element corresponding to \(x\) under the above identification;
    the tail identification \(\tau\) preserves this underlying element.
    Then \(\beta_i\otimes[x]^j\) has module degree \(i\) and complex
    degree \(-i\). By the
    construction of the adjunction in \Cref{definition of widehat rmt}, the
    counit takes a generator to its \(i\)-th coordinate. Consequently,
    \begin{equation}\label{counit on a Hodge--Witt block}
        \widehat\epsilon_{D[r]}\bigl(\beta_i\otimes[x]^j\bigr)=
        \begin{cases}
            x,&i=r,\\
            0,&i\neq r,
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    where in the first line we use the preceding tail identifications. In
    particular the counit is surjective.

    To identify the kernel, we calculate the relations among the generators.
    First fix \(i<r\).
    The first five identities below follow from \Cref{rmt}(3), and the
    last from \Cref{rmt}(4):
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \beta_i\otimes[x]^j&=\beta_i\otimes[x]^i &&(j\leqslant i),\\
        \beta_i\otimes[x]^i&=V\beta_i\otimes[x]^{i+1},& &\\
        \beta_i\otimes[x]^j&=p^{r-j}\beta_i\otimes[x]^r
            &&(i<j\leqslant r),\\
        \beta_i\otimes[y]^j&=\beta_i\otimes[y]^{r+1} &&(j\geqslant r+1),\\
        \beta_i\otimes[F_Dx]^{r+1}&=\beta_i\otimes[x]^r,\\
        \beta_i\otimes[y]^{r+1}&=\beta_i\otimes[y]^i.
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    Combining these identities yields
    \begin{equation}\label{lower Hodge--Witt generators}
        \beta_i\otimes[x]^r
        =p^{r-i-1}V\beta_i\otimes[F_Dx]^r.
    \end{equation}
    Choose finitely many \(W\)-generators of \(D\), and let \(\mathbf b_i\)
    be the corresponding column of elements \(\beta_i\otimes[x]^r\). Equation
    \eqref{lower Hodge--Witt generators} has the form
    \(\mathbf b_i=B_i\mathbf b_i\), where the powers of \(B_i\) tend to
    zero in the defining topology of \(\widehat R^{\,0}\): every iteration
    contributes at least one further power of \(V\). Hence
    \(1-B_i\) is invertible, with inverse \(\sum_{q\geqslant0}B_i^q\), and
    \(\mathbf b_i=0\). Thus the diagonal term in module degree \(i<r\)
    vanishes.

    Next let \(i>r\). The same relations now give
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \beta_i\otimes[x]^j&=\beta_i\otimes[x]^r &&(j\leqslant r),\\
        \beta_i\otimes[y]^{r+1}&=\beta_i\otimes[V_Dy]^r,& &\\
        \beta_i\otimes[y]^j&=p^{j-r-1}\beta_i\otimes[y]^{r+1}
            &&(r+1\leqslant j\leqslant i),\\
        \beta_i\otimes[y]^{i+1}&=F\beta_i\otimes[y]^i,& &\\
        \beta_i\otimes[y]^j&=\beta_i\otimes[y]^{i+1} &&(j\geqslant i+1),\\
        \beta_i\otimes[y]^{i+1}&=\beta_i\otimes[y]^r.& &
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    Therefore
    \begin{equation}\label{upper Hodge--Witt generators}
        \beta_i\otimes[x]^r
        =p^{i-r-1}F \beta_i\otimes[V_Dx]^r.
    \end{equation}
    This again gives a finite matrix equation
    \(\mathbf b_i=B_i\mathbf b_i\). If \(i\geqslant r+2\), the positive
    power of \(p\) in \eqref{upper Hodge--Witt generators} makes the powers
    of \(B_i\) converge to zero. If \(i=r+1\), the same conclusion follows
    from the assumed topological nilpotence of \(V_D\). This also works when
    \(i=n\): in that case convergence is in the \(p\)-adic topology of
    \(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\). Thus \(1-B_i\) is invertible and all the
    diagonal terms with \(i>r\) vanish.

    We now identify the surviving term in module degree \(r\).
    All the generators reduce to \(\beta_r\otimes[x]^r\), and the two relations at the break are
    \[
        F\beta_r\otimes[x]^r=\beta_r\otimes[F_Dx]^r,
        \qquad
        V\beta_r\otimes[y]^r=\beta_r\otimes[V_Dy]^r.
    \]
    Since \(D\) is finitely generated over \(W\), complete, and \(V_D\) is
    topologically nilpotent, its \(R^0\)-action extends to
    \(\widehat R^{\,0}\). Hence
    \[
        D\longrightarrow
        \widehat{\mathrm{t}}(G)^{r,-r},
        \qquad x\longmapsto \beta_r\otimes[x]^r,
    \]
    is a well-defined inverse to the restriction of the counit. If \(r=n\),
    the level condition says that \(F_D\) is bijective. The same argument
    then uses the natural \(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\)-action on \(D\), with
    \(F^{-1}\) acting as \(F_D^{-1}\); restricted Laurent series converge
    because \(D\) is \(p\)-adically complete. This proves the assertion also
    at the top endpoint, including the case \(\mathrm{I}=[n,n]\).

    To finish, we must also check the off-diagonal term in bidegree \((k,-k+1)\).
    It is generated by \(\widehat R^{\,1}(\beta_{k-1}\otimes[x]^j)\) for \(x\in D\), so it vanishes
    whenever \(k-1\neq r\), by what we have just proved. If \(k=r+1\leqslant
    n\), relation \Cref{rmt}(2), applied with \(i=r+1\) and \([x]^r\in G^r\),
    gives
    \[
        (-1)^{r+1}\delta(\beta_{r+1}\otimes[x]^r)
        +d(\beta_r\otimes[x]^r)=0.
    \]
    The first term is zero because the diagonal term in module degree
    \(r+1\) is zero. Thus \(d(\beta_r\otimes[x]^r)=0\). The topological nilpotence of \(V_D\) now shows that the whole
    \(\widehat R^{\,1}(\beta_r\otimes[x]^r)\) is zero. Hence every
    off-diagonal term vanishes as well. Relation \Cref{rmt}(2) also shows
    that \(\delta\) is zero on the surviving copy of \(D\).

    We have proved that \(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(G)\) is \(D\) in bidegree
    \((r,-r)\) and is zero elsewhere, and by
    \eqref{counit on a Hodge--Witt block} the counit is the identity on this
    copy. Taking the finite direct sum over \(r\) proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{completed rmt on diagonal heart}
Let \(N\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) have level \(\mathrm{I}\). Then
\[
\mathrm{L}^i\widehat\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{I}(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N))=0
\qquad(i\ne0)
\]
in \(\mathrm{Ch}(\widehat R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\). Moreover,
\(\mathrm{L}^0\widehat\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{I}(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N))\in
\mathrm{Ch}(\widehat R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) represents \(N\) in \(D(R)\).
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Choose a bounded projective
resolution \(P^\bullet\toF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\) by finite sums of \(G_r\),
using \Cref{resolution of coherent complexes}. Its termwise
completion \(\widehat P^\bullet\) remains a resolution by
\Cref{Exactness after completion}. Take cohomology first in the
resolution degree. If \(p\) denotes the complex degree of
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}\) and \(q\) the resolution degree, this gives
\[
E_1^{p,q}
 =\mathrm{H}^q\bigl(\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat P^\bullet)^p\bigr)
 =\bigl(\mathrm{L}^q\widehat\mathrm{t}(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N))\bigr)^p,
\qquad
E_2^{p,q}=\mathrm{H}^p(E_1^{\bullet,q})
  \Longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^{p+q}(N).
\]
The abutment follows from
\Cref{derived widehat t equals widehat derived t,completed adjunction unit and counit are isomorphisms}.
By
\Cref{widehat-rmt-tensor-product,description of t(G_r)},
\(E_1^{-u,q}\) has nonzero components only in \(R\)-module degrees
\(u,u+1\). Thus, for \(r\geqslant2\), the source and target of
\(d_r:E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}\) have disjoint \(R\)-module
degrees. The spectral sequence therefore degenerates at \(E_2\).

We record the flatness step that will eliminate the unwanted rows.
Fix \(q\) and suppose \((E_2^{-u,q})^u=0\) for every \(u\in\mathrm{I}\).
The term \(E_1^{-u-1,q}\) has no \(R\)-module component of degree
\(u\), so
\((E_1^{-u,q})^u\to(E_1^{-u+1,q})^u\) is injective.
Its target is zero for \(u=m\). For \(m<u\leqslant n\), the terms of
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat P^\bullet)^{-u+1}\) are finite sums of
\(\widehat R(-(u-1))\). Taking resolution cohomology after tensoring
is valid because \(\widehat R^{\,1}\) is right flat over
\(\widehat R^{\,0}\), as established after
\Cref{flatness of central completion}. Hence
\[
(E_1^{-u+1,q})^u
 \cong\widehat R^{\,1}\otimes_{\widehat R^{\,0}}
       (E_1^{-u+1,q})^{u-1}.
\]
Starting at \(u=m\), induction makes both sides of each injection
zero. The remaining components are the same degree-\(u+1\)
components at the next step, and degree \(n+1\) is zero by the
level condition. Thus \(E_1^{\bullet,q}=0\) as an actual
\(R\)-complex.

Since \(N\) is diagonal, \(\mathrm{H}^{q-u}(N)^u=0\) unless \(q=0\) or
\(1\). Each \((E_2^{-u,q})^u\) is a subquotient of this group.
The induction therefore eliminates every row except \(q=0,1\).
For \(q=1\), \((E_2^{-u+1,1})^u\) is a subquotient of
\(\mathrm{H}^{2-u}(N)^u=0\). Thus \(E_2^{t,1}\) is concentrated in
\(R\)-module degree \(-t\).

The remaining spectral-sequence filtration gives an exact sequence
of graded \(R\)-modules
\[
 0\longrightarrow E_2^{t,0}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^t(N)
 \longrightarrow E_2^{t-1,1}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The quotient is concentrated in degree \(1-t\), so the
\(R\)-submodule \(E_2^{t,0}\) contains \(\mathrm{H}^t(N)^{-t}\).
It also contains its \(F\)-saturated boundaries, which equal
\(\mathrm{H}^t(N)^{1-t}\) by the diagonal-heart condition. Hence
\(E_2^{t-1,1}=0\) for every \(t\), and the same flatness
induction eliminates the \(q=1\) row. This proves strict vanishing.
The completed adjunction also gives
\begin{equation}\label{embedding-total-represents-N}
\mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{I}(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N))\bigr)
\simeq N\qquad\text{in }D(R).
\end{equation}
Since only outer degree zero remains, its cohomology object represents
\(N\).
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{completed rmt and diagonal cohomology}
Let \(M\in D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\). Then
\(\mathrm{L}^i\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)\in\mathrm{Ch}(\widehat R\text{-}\mathrm{I})\) represents the
diagonal cohomology object
\[
\mathrm{L}^i\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)\cong
\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^i\bigl((\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\bigr).
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Put \(N=\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}(M)\). The completed equivalence
identifies \(M\) with \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\). By
\Cref{completed rmt on diagonal heart}, the functor
\(\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t}\circF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) takes the diagonal heart to
the standard outer heart. Since the diagonal \(t\)-structure is
bounded, this functor is \(t\)-exact. Consequently
\[
\mathrm{L}^i\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)
 \cong
\mathrm{L}^0\widehat\mathrm{t}\bigl(
  F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^i(N))\bigr).
\]
By \Cref{completed rmt on diagonal heart}, the complex on the right
represents \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^i(N)\).
This proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-59 -->

\) gives a distinguished triangle
