<!-- example-3: body_md -->
We can see the effect of completion in \Cref{The first example}.
After Ekedahl completion, the free
\(R\)-modules in its resolution are replaced by their \(V\)-adic
completions:
\[\mathrm{L}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(M)\simeq \mathrm{Tot}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{t}(G_0)}\xrightarrow{\widehat{\mathrm{t}(\Phi-\Psi)}}\widehat{\mathrm{t}(G_0)}\right]. \]
In degree \(0\), the completed cokernel is
\[\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{L}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(M))^0\simeq \widehat{R^0}/\widehat{R^0}(F-pV)\simeq k[[V]].\]
Indeed, after imposing \(F=pV\), the relation \(FV=p\) gives \(p(V^2-1)=0\), and \(V^2-1\) is a unit in \(W[[V]]\), so \(p=0\).

Similarly, in module degree \(1\),
\[
\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t}(M))^1\simeq k[[dV]]_{>0},
\qquad
\mathrm{H}^{-1}(\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t}(M))^1\simeq W^2.
\]
All other graded cohomology groups vanish.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{interval-flat-completion}
 Let \(H\) be either \(\widehat A_{\mathrm J}\) or
 \(\widehat B_{\mathrm J}\), as defined above, and let
 $z$ be a central indeterminate. Define
 \[
 H\langle z\rangle:=\varprojlim_{\nu}(H/p^{\nu}H)[z].
 \]
 Then \(H\langle z\rangle\) is flat as a left and as a right
 \(H\)-module. In particular, for a vertex \(s\) of \(\mathrm J\), define
 \[
 \widehat G_{\mathrm J,s}\langle z\rangle
 \coloneqq\varprojlim_\nu(\widehat G_{\mathrm J,s}/p^\nu\widehat G_{\mathrm J,s})[z],
 \]
 with gauge operators acting coefficientwise. Then
 \(H\langle z\rangle e_s\cong\widehat G_{\mathrm J,s}\langle z\rangle\)
 under the Morita equivalence, so this is a flat left \(H\)-module.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Apply \Cref{flatness of central completion} to \(H[z]\), which is left
 and right Noetherian since \(H\) is and \(z\) is central. Its \(p\)-adic
 completion is \(H\langle z\rangle\), which is therefore flat on both
 sides over \(H[z]\). Since \(H[z]\) is free on both sides over \(H\),
 \(H\langle z\rangle\) is flat on both sides over \(H\). Finally,
 \(H\langle z\rangle e_s\) is a direct summand of \(H\langle z\rangle\).
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{interval-series-injection}
 With \(H\langle z\rangle\) as in \Cref{interval-flat-completion}, every right
 \(H\)-module \(T\) has a natural injective coefficient map
 \[
 T\otimes_H H\langle z\rangle\longrightarrow T[[z]].
 \]
 Here $T[[z]]=\prod_{j\geq0}Tz^j$ denotes the group of formal
 coefficient sequences.  This assertion does not identify the ordinary
 tensor product with a completed tensor product or with all of $T[[z]]$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
An element of \(H\langle z\rangle\) is a series $\sum_{j\geq0}a_jz^j$ with
 $a_j\to0$ $p$-adically in $H$.  Taking coefficients defines the stated
 map. To prove injectivity, consider an element of its kernel and choose
 a finitely generated right $H$-submodule $T_0\subseteq T$ containing the finitely many
 $T$-coordinates in a tensor expression for this element.  Flatness of
 \(H\langle z\rangle\) gives an injection
 \[
 T_0\otimes_H H\langle z\rangle\longrightarrow T\otimes_H H\langle z\rangle.
 \]
 The finite right $H$-module $T_0$ is $p$-adically complete and separated,
 since $H$ is Noetherian and $p$-adically complete.  Applied to the finite
 right $H[z]$-module $T_0[z]$, the finite-module completion formula gives
 \[
 T_0\otimes_H H\langle z\rangle
  \cong\varprojlim_{\nu}T_0[z]/p^{\nu}T_0[z].
 \]
 The latter module is the group of series in $T_0[[z]]$ whose
 coefficients tend to zero $p$-adically.  In particular, it injects into
 $T_0[[z]]$, and hence into $T[[z]]$.  The chosen element is therefore
 zero already in \(T_0\otimes_H H\langle z\rangle\).
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- proposition-30: body_md -->
\label{interval-right-flat-resolution}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\) and \(\mathrm J=[m,n+1]\), and use the reduced
presentation with vertices \(m,\ldots,n\). View the completed generators
as \(\widehat B_{\mathrm J}\)-modules via the Morita equivalence above.
For every \(r\in\mathrm{I}\), there
is an exact sequence of left \(\widehat B_{\mathrm J}\)-modules
\begin{equation}\label{interval-right-resolution-sequence}
0\longrightarrow
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,m}\oplus
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,m}\langle z\rangle
\xrightarrow{\ d_r\ }
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,r}\oplus
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,n}\langle z\rangle
\xrightarrow{\ \epsilon_r\ }
\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
The maps are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\epsilon_r\left(a,\sum_{j\geq0}a_jz^j\right)
&=a\alpha_r+
\sum_{j\geq0}a_j
(\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{n-m})^j
\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{r-m}\alpha_r,\\
d_r(u,q(z))
&=\bigl(-u\widetilde{V}^{r-m},\,
u\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}+
q(z)(\widetilde{V}^{n-m}-\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F} z)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\widetilde{F}:n\to n+1\) is the added boundary arrow. We take
\(u\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,m}\),
\(q(z)\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,m}\langle z\rangle\),
\(a\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,r}\), and
\(a_j\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,n}\) with \(a_j\to0\) \(p\)-adically.
The inverse \(\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\) acts on \(\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\), and an empty
power of \(\widetilde{V}\) is an identity arrow. Both modules to the left of
\(\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\) are flat over \(\widehat B_{\mathrm J}\).
<!-- end proposition-30 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
We first prove the uncompleted sequence of \(B_{\mathrm J}\)-modules
 \[
 0\longrightarrow
 G_{\mathrm J,m}\oplus G_{\mathrm J,m}[z]
 \xrightarrow{\ d_r\ }
 G_{\mathrm J,r}\oplus G_{\mathrm J,n}[z]
 \xrightarrow{\ \epsilon_r\ }
 G_{\mathrm{I},r}\longrightarrow0
 \]
 is exact. Here \(G_{\mathrm{I},r}\) is viewed at level \(\mathrm J\), and
 the maps use the formulas above with polynomials in \(z\).
 On a gauge of level \(\mathrm{I}\), the added arrow \(\widetilde{F}\) is invertible and
 \(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}=\tau_\mathrm{I}\).

 Write \(\beta_r\) for the generator of the \(G_{\mathrm J,r}\)
 summand and \(\beta_n\) for that of the \(G_{\mathrm J,n}[z]\)
 summand, whose \(B_{\mathrm J}\)-generators are \(z^j\beta_n\)
 for \(j\geq0\). When \(r=n\), the two occurrences of \(\beta_n\)
 belong to different summands.
 The augmentation to \(G_{\mathrm{I},r}\) sends
 \[
 \beta_r\longmapsto\alpha_r,\qquad
 z^j\beta_n\longmapsto
 (\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{n-m})^j\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\widetilde{V}^{r-m}\alpha_r.
 \]
 The image of \(d_r\) imposes exactly the relations
 \begin{equation}\label{interval-right-resolution-relations}
 (\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F})\beta_n=\widetilde{V}^{r-m}\beta_r,\qquad
 (\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F})z^{j+1}\beta_n
 =\widetilde{V}^{n-m}z^j\beta_n\quad(j\geq0).
 \end{equation}
 Here \(z\) is an auxiliary central variable, not a gauge operator.
 The relations show that this is a \(B_{\mathrm J}\)-linear augmentation
 and that \(\epsilon_r d_r=0\).

 To identify the cokernel, we reduce paths using the defining relations.
 For \(m\leq i\leq n\), the cokernel at vertex \(i\) is spanned by:
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item all pure forward paths from $r$ to $i$, applied to \(\beta_r\);
 \item the short internal backward path from $r$ to $i$, applied to
 \(\beta_r\), if $i<r$;
 \item \(\widetilde{V}^{n-i}z^j\beta_n\) for \(j\geq0\).
 \end{enumerate}
 The trivial forward path is included when $i=r$.  To verify that this
 collection spans, first cancel opposite arrows in an arbitrary path.
 A backward path on \(\beta_r\) that crosses the new boundary arrow
 \(\widetilde{V}\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\) can be
 reduced using
 \[
 (\widetilde{V}\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1})\widetilde{V}^{r-m}\beta_r=p\beta_n.
 \]
 A full backward cycle on \(z^j\beta_n\) can be reduced using
 \[
 (\widetilde{V}\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1})\widetilde{V}^{n-m}z^j\beta_n
 =pz^{j+1}\beta_n.
 \]
 Finally, every nonempty forward path on \(z^j\beta_n\) starts with
 \(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}\);
 \eqref{interval-right-resolution-relations} reduces it either to a
 path on \(\beta_r\), or, when \(j>0\), to a path on
 \(z^{j-1}\beta_n\), after cancellation of opposite internal arrows.
 This proves the spanning assertion.

 After the boundary arrow \(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}\) has been made
 invertible, the three
 collections above are exactly the distinct reduced forward and
 backward paths that give the standard $W$-basis of $G_{{\mathrm{I}},r}^i$.
 Indeed, the second collection is the backward path that has not yet
 crossed the old endpoint identification, and the third comprises those
 that have crossed it at least once.  Thus their images under the
 augmentation are linearly independent.  The augmentation identifies
 the cokernel with $G_{{\mathrm{I}},r}$, and in particular this cokernel is
 $p$-torsion-free.  Moving coefficients through the paths applies powers
 of $\sigma$ or $\sigma^{-1}$ and leaves this basis calculation unchanged.

 The map on the left is also injective. If \(d_r(u,q(z))=0\), then
 \(u\widetilde{V}^{r-m}=0\). Composing \(\widetilde{V}^{r-m}\) with the opposite forward
 path gives \(p^{r-m}e_m\), so \(p\)-torsion-freeness gives \(u=0\). Write
 \(q(z)=\sum_{j\geq0}q_jz^j\), with finite support. Comparing the constant
 term in \(q(z)(\widetilde{V}^{n-m}-\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F} z)=0\) gives
 \(q_0\widetilde{V}^{n-m}=0\). The opposite forward path shows that right
 multiplication by \(\widetilde{V}^{n-m}\) is injective on \(G_{\mathrm J,m}\). Hence
 $q_0=0$.  The coefficient equations
 \[
 q_j\widetilde{V}^{n-m}=q_{j-1}\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}\quad(j\geq1)
 \]
 give $q_j=0$ successively.

 We may now complete this short exact sequence.  Since its cokernel
 $G_{{\mathrm{I}},r}$ is $p$-torsion-free, reduction modulo $p^{\nu}$ remains
 short exact for every $\nu$.  The transition maps on the reduced left
 terms are surjective.  Taking inverse limits therefore preserves
 exactness.  Moreover
 \[
 \varprojlim_{\nu}(G_{\mathrm J,s}/p^{\nu}G_{\mathrm J,s})[z]
  =\widehat G_{\mathrm J,s}\langle z\rangle
  \qquad(s=m,n).
 \]
 This gives \eqref{interval-right-resolution-sequence}. Exactness here
 follows from the reduction and inverse-limit argument; it requires
 neither projectivity of a completed infinite direct sum nor an
 Artin--Rees statement for an infinite module.
 Flatness of its terms follows from
 \Cref{interval-flat-completion}.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- proposition-31: body_md -->
\label{interval-left-flat-resolution}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\) and \(\mathrm J=[m-1,n]\), and use the reduced
presentation with vertices \(m,\ldots,n\). View the completed generators
as \(\widehat B_{\mathrm J}\)-modules via the Morita equivalence above.
For every \(r\in\mathrm{I}\), there is an exact sequence of left
\(\widehat B_{\mathrm J}\)-modules
\begin{equation}\label{interval-left-resolution-sequence}
0\longrightarrow
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,n}\oplus
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,n}\langle z\rangle
\xrightarrow{\ d_r\ }
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,r}\oplus
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,m}\langle z\rangle
\xrightarrow{\ \epsilon_r\ }
\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
The maps are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\epsilon_r\left(a,\sum_{j\geq0}a_jz^j\right)
&=a\alpha_r+
\sum_{j\geq0}a_j
(\tau_\mathrm{I}\widetilde{F}^{n-m})^j
\tau_\mathrm{I}\widetilde{F}^{n-r}\alpha_r,\\
d_r(u,q(z))
&=\bigl(-u\widetilde{F}^{n-r},\,
u\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}+
q(z)(\widetilde{F}^{n-m}-\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V} z)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\widetilde{V}:m\to m-1\) is the added boundary arrow. We take
\(u\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,n}\),
\(q(z)\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,n}\langle z\rangle\),
\(a\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,r}\), and
\(a_j\in\widehat G_{\mathrm J,m}\) with \(a_j\to0\) \(p\)-adically.
The map \(\tau_\mathrm{I}\) acts on \(\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\), and an empty power
of \(\widetilde{F}\) is an identity arrow. Both modules to the left of
\(\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\) are flat over \(\widehat B_{\mathrm J}\).
<!-- end proposition-31 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
We first prove the uncompleted sequence of \(B_{\mathrm J}\)-modules
\[
0\longrightarrow
G_{\mathrm J,n}\oplus G_{\mathrm J,n}[z]
\xrightarrow{\ d_r\ }
G_{\mathrm J,r}\oplus G_{\mathrm J,m}[z]
\xrightarrow{\ \epsilon_r\ }
G_{\mathrm{I},r}\longrightarrow0
\]
is exact. Here \(G_{\mathrm{I},r}\) is viewed at level \(\mathrm J\), and
the maps use the formulas above with polynomials in \(z\).
On a gauge of level \(\mathrm{I}\), the added arrow \(\widetilde{V}\) is invertible and
\(\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}=\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\).
Write \(\beta_r\) for the generator of the \(G_{\mathrm J,r}\)
summand and \(\beta_m\) for that of the \(G_{\mathrm J,m}[z]\)
summand, whose \(B_{\mathrm J}\)-generators are \(z^j\beta_m\)
for \(j\geq0\). When \(r=m\), the two occurrences of \(\beta_m\)
belong to different summands.
The augmentation sends \(\beta_r\) to \(\alpha_r\) and \(z^j\beta_m\) to
\((\tau_\mathrm{I}\widetilde{F}^{n-m})^j\tau_\mathrm{I}\widetilde{F}^{n-r}\alpha_r\).
The image of \(d_r\) imposes exactly the relations
\begin{equation}\label{interval-left-resolution-relations}
(\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V})\beta_m=\widetilde{F}^{n-r}\beta_r,\qquad
(\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V})z^{j+1}\beta_m
=\widetilde{F}^{n-m}z^j\beta_m\quad(j\geq0).
\end{equation}
These relations make it \(B_{\mathrm J}\)-linear and give
\(\epsilon_r d_r=0\).

At vertex \(i\), the cokernel has the reduced-path basis consisting
of pure backward paths on \(\beta_r\), the short internal forward path on
\(\beta_r\) when \(i>r\), and \(\widetilde{F}^{i-m}z^j\beta_m\) for \(j\geq0\).
Indeed, forward paths crossing the new boundary reduce by
\((\widetilde{F}\tau_{\mathrm J})\widetilde{F}^{n-r}\beta_r=p\beta_m\) or
\((\widetilde{F}\tau_{\mathrm J})\widetilde{F}^{n-m}z^j\beta_m=pz^{j+1}\beta_m\);
backward paths on \(z^j\beta_m\) reduce by
\eqref{interval-left-resolution-relations}. Their images are the
distinct reduced paths of \(G_{\mathrm{I},r}\). Thus the cokernel is
\(G_{\mathrm{I},r}\) and is \(p\)-torsion-free.

If \(d_r(u,q(z))=0\), then \(u\widetilde{F}^{n-r}=0\). Composing with the opposite
backward path gives \(p^{n-r}u=0\), hence \(u=0\). Writing
\(q(z)=\sum q_jz^j\), the remaining equations are
\(q_0\widetilde{F}^{n-m}=0\) and
\(q_j\widetilde{F}^{n-m}=q_{j-1}\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}\) for \(j\geq1\).
The opposite backward path makes right multiplication by
\(\widetilde{F}^{n-m}\) injective, so all \(q_j\) vanish.
Since the cokernel is \(p\)-torsion-free, reduction modulo \(p^\nu\)
and passage to inverse limits preserve exactness, as in
\Cref{interval-right-flat-resolution}. Flatness follows from
\Cref{interval-flat-completion}.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{interval-old-generators-acyclic}
 In either elementary enlargement, let $T$ be any $p$-torsion-free
 right $\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{J}}$-module.  Then
 \[
 \operatorname{Tor}^{\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{J}}}_a(T,\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},r})=0
 \qquad(a>0).
 \]
 In particular, every $\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},r}$ is
 $\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{{\mathrm{J}}}$-acyclic:
 \[
 \mathrm{L}^q\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{{\mathrm{J}}}(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},r})=0
 \qquad(q<0).
 \]
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
The two-term flat resolutions give vanishing of Tor in degrees at
least two. For degree one, let \(s=m\) for the right enlargement and
\(s=n\) for the left. Since
\(\widehat G_{\mathrm J,s}\cong\widehat B_{\mathrm J}e_s\),
tensoring with \(T\) gives
\(T\otimes_{\widehat B_{\mathrm J}}\widehat G_{\mathrm J,s}
\cong Te_s\) and
\[
Te_s\oplus
\bigl(T\otimes_{\widehat B_{\mathrm J}}
\widehat G_{\mathrm J,s}\langle z\rangle\bigr)
\hookrightarrow Te_s\oplus(Te_s)[[z]],
\]
where the second summand embeds by
\Cref{interval-series-injection}. Thus we may write a kernel element
as \((u,q(z))\), where \(u\in Te_s\) and
\(q(z)=\sum_{j\geq0}q_jz^j\) lies in the image of this injection,
with each \(q_j\in Te_s\). The first component gives
\(u\widetilde{V}^{r-m}=0\) in the right enlargement or
\(u\widetilde{F}^{n-r}=0\) in the left. Each path has an opposite whose
composite is a power of \(p\), so \(u=0\).
By \Cref{interval-series-injection}, we may compare the coefficients
\(q_j\) of \(q(z)\). The constant coefficient is
\(q_0\widetilde{V}^{n-m}\) or \(q_0\widetilde{F}^{n-m}\), respectively.
The same opposite-path argument gives \(q_0=0\); comparing
successive coefficients then gives \(q_j=0\) for all \(j\).
Thus the differential remains injective, proving the Tor assertion.

 By \Cref{widehat-rmt-tensor-product} and the reduced Morita
 equivalence above,
 \[
 \widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm J}(X)
 \cong
 \widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm J}(\widehat B_{\mathrm J})
 \otimes_{\widehat B_{\mathrm J}}X.
 \]
 Each bidegree of \(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm J}(\widehat B_{\mathrm J})\)
 is a finite direct sum of the
 completed coefficient modules $\widehat R^0$, $\widehat R^1$, or the
 completed top module, by \Cref{description of t(G_r)} and the completed
 generator computation.  These modules are $p$-torsion-free.  Applying
 the first assertion to each such right $\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{J}}$-module shows that every
 bidegree of every higher left derived functor vanishes. The vanishing
 is in the resolution direction, with values in
 $\mathrm{Ch}(\widehat R\text{-}{\mathrm{J}})$, and therefore holds before totalizing
 the inner $R$-complex.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{interval-two-vertex-example}
 Let \(\mathrm{I}=[0,1]\) and \(\mathrm J=[0,2]\), and identify \(2\) with \(0\)
 through \(\tau_{\mathrm J}\). The opposite-arrow pairs are
 \((\widetilde{F}:0\to1,\ \widetilde{V}:1\to0)\) and
 \((\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}:1\to0,\ \widetilde{V}\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}:0\to1)\);
 their composites are multiplication by \(p\).
 For \(r=0\), the first component of \(d_r\) in
 \eqref{interval-right-resolution-sequence} is \(-u\). Cancelling it gives
 \begin{equation}\label{interval-two-vertex-flat-resolution}
 0\longrightarrow\widehat G_{[0,2],0}\langle z\rangle
 \xrightarrow{\ \cdot(\widetilde{V}-\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F} z)\ }
 \widehat G_{[0,2],1}\langle z\rangle
 \longrightarrow\widehat G_{[0,1],0}\longrightarrow0.
 \end{equation}
 Writing \(\beta_1\) for the generator of the polynomial term, its
 relations are
 \(\widetilde{V} z^j\beta_1=(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F})z^{j+1}\beta_1\), and
 \(z^j\beta_1\) maps to
 \((\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\widetilde{V})^j\tau_\mathrm{I}^{-1}\alpha_0\) for \(j\geq0\).
 Under endpoint identifications the two
 components of the old generator are copies, with the appropriate
 scalar twists, of
 \[
 \widehat{W_{\sigma}[\Phi,\Psi]/(\Phi\Psi=\Psi\Phi=p)},
 \]
 and these elements correspond to $1,\Psi,\Psi^2,\ldots$ in its
 vertex-$1$ component.  The old endpoint arrow $\tau_{{\mathrm{I}}}$ is
 invertible in the preadditive gauge category, so its two representable
 modules $\widehat{G}_{[0,1],0}$ and $\widehat{G}_{[0,1],1}$ are isomorphic.  The
 semilinearity of $\tau_{{\mathrm{I}}}$ changes scalar identifications, but does
 not obstruct this isomorphism of modules over the gauge algebra.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{interval-uncompleted-tensor-example}
Acyclicity alone does not make the comparison on old completed
generators an isomorphism. To see the remaining obstruction, we
calculate the actual complex in the smallest nontrivial right
enlargement, before applying derived reduction. In this example
only, assume \(k=\mathbb{F}_p\), so that \(W=\mathbb{Z}_p\) and the scalar
twists disappear. Take \(\mathrm{I}=[0,1]\) and \(\mathrm J=[0,2]\).
All tensor products and quotients below are algebraic; in particular, we
do not complete a tensor product or take the closure of a relation
submodule.

Identify the endpoint \(2\) with \(0\) by \(\tau_{\mathrm{J}}\).  The resulting
two-vertex operator algebra has arrows
\[
 \widetilde{F}_0:0\longrightarrow1,\quad
 \widetilde{V}_1:1\longrightarrow0,\quad
 \tau_{\mathrm{J}}\widetilde{F}_1:1\longrightarrow0,\quad
 \widetilde{V}_2\tau_{\mathrm{J}}^{-1}:0\longrightarrow1,
\]
 with both composites of each opposite pair equal to multiplication
 by \(p\).
Its corner at \(0\) and the old one-vertex operator algebra are
\[
 C=\varprojlim_s\bigl(\mathbb{Z}_p[X,Y]/(XY-p^2)\bigr)/p^s,
 \qquad
 D=\varprojlim_s\bigl(\mathbb{Z}_p[\Phi,\Psi]/(\Phi\Psi-p)\bigr)/p^s.
\]
Here \(X=\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_1\widetilde{F}_0\) and
\(Y=\widetilde{V}_1\widetilde{V}_2\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\).
Both components of \(\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},0}\) identify with \(D\);
the four displayed arrows act as \(\Phi,\Psi,1,p\), respectively.
Consequently the corner action on \(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},0}^0=D\) is
\[
 C\longrightarrow D,\qquad X\longmapsto\Phi,\quad
 Y\longmapsto p\Psi.
\]

The right \(C\)-actions on the coefficient modules are obtained by
right multiplication by the entries in the following table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &X&Y\\\hline
 \rho_0&F&pV\\
 \rho_1&pF&V\\
 \rho_2&p^2F&F^{-1}
\end{array}
\]
The first two rows apply to both \(\widehat R^0\) and
\(\widehat R^1\); the last applies to
\(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\). These actions include the entire completed
corner ring \(C\), not merely its polynomial subring.

For \(\epsilon=0,1\), define
\[
\begin{split}
 K_0^\epsilon
 &=\frac{(\widehat R^{\,\epsilon})_{\rho_0}\otimes_C D}
 {\langle qV\otimes x-q\otimes\Psi x:
             q\in\widehat R^{\,\epsilon},\ x\in D\rangle},\\
 K_1^\epsilon
 &=\frac{(\widehat R^{\,\epsilon})_{\rho_1}\otimes_C D}
 {\langle q\otimes x-qF\otimes\Psi x:
             q\in\widehat R^{\,\epsilon},\ x\in D\rangle},\\
 K_2&=(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}})_{\rho_2}\otimes_C D.
\end{split}
\]
The angle brackets denote the relation submodules in the displayed
algebraic tensor products.  Then the possibly nonzero components of
\(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm{J}}(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},0})\), indexed by (Raynaud-module degree, complex
degree), are exactly
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 (u,s)&(0,0)&(1,0)&(1,-1)&(2,-1)&(2,-2)\\\hline
 \widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm{J}}(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},0})^{u,s}
 &K_0^0&K_0^1&K_1^0&K_1^1&K_2.
\end{array}
\]
The Raynaud action of \(d\) is induced by left multiplication:
\[
 K_i^0\longrightarrow K_i^1,\qquad
 [q\otimes x]\longmapsto[dq\otimes x]\quad(i=0,1).
\]
The differential of the complex, with the signs of \Cref{rmt}, is
\[
 K_2\xrightarrow{\delta_2}K_1^1,
 \quad[q\otimes x]\longmapsto-[qd\otimes x],
 \qquad
 K_1^0\xrightarrow{\delta_1}K_0^1,
 \quad[q\otimes x]\longmapsto[qd\otimes x].
\]
In the first formula, \(qd\) is defined using the action of
\(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\) on \(\widehat R^{\,1}\): left multiplication
by \(F\) is invertible there, and its inverse sends \(d\) to \(dV\).
The identities \(dF=pFd\), \(Vd=pdV\), and \(FdV=d\) show that these
formulas respect the displayed relations.

To verify this presentation, read it directly from the relations in
\Cref{rmt}. At \(\beta_0\), the coefficient of
\(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_1\) is \(1\); eliminate the vertex-\(1\) symbols
using this path, and the remaining relation for \(\widetilde{V}_1\) is
\(qV\otimes x=q\otimes\Psi x\). At \(\beta_1\),
the coefficient of \(\widetilde{V}_1\) is \(1\), so a vertex-\(1\) symbol with argument
\(x\) becomes the vertex-\(0\) symbol with argument \(\Psi x\).  The
relation for \(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_1\) then becomes
\(q\otimes x=qF\otimes\Psi x\).
At \(\beta_2\), the same elimination gives
\(q\otimes x=qpF\otimes\Psi x\), which is already the corner-balancing
relation for \(Y\), since \(\rho_2(Y)=F^{-1}\).
The other arrows give the displayed corner relations or their
consequences.

The new top component \(K_2\) accounts for the failure of the
comparison: it is nonzero, even though multiplication by \(p\) on it
is bijective.  Indeed, \(C,D,\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\) are domains,
and the two homomorphisms from \(C\) to \(D\) and
\(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\) are injective.  The injections can be checked in
the Laurent expansions: the coefficients of positive powers and of
negative powers remain distinct, and are only multiplied by nonzero
powers of \(p\).  The domain assertion for \(C,D\) follows, for example,
by assigning an irrational weight strictly between \(0\) and \(2\) to
\(X\), respectively strictly between \(0\) and \(1\) to \(\Phi\);
the complementary weights of \(Y,\Psi\) are then positive, and every
nonzero restricted series has a unique term of least weight.  The
domain assertion for \(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\) follows from its
\(p\)-adic separation and its domain reduction
\(\mathbb{F}_p[F,F^{-1}]\).
Thus, writing \(K=\operatorname{Frac}(C)\), the localization
\[
 K\otimes_C K_2
 \simeq
 (K\otimes_C \widehat R^{\mathrm{top}})
 \otimes_K(K\otimes_C D)
\]
is a tensor product of two nonzero \(K\)-vector spaces, and is nonzero.
On the other hand, corner balancing for \(Y\) gives
\[
 F^{-1}\otimes1=1\otimes p\Psi,
 \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 1\otimes1=p(F\otimes\Psi)
 \quad\text{in }K_2.
\]
The tensor product \(K_2\) is a commutative algebra, so \(p\) is a unit
in it.  In particular, its derived reduction modulo \(p\) vanishes,
although \(K_2\) itself does not.

The old complex \(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},0})\) has three components
\(\widehat R^0,\widehat R^1,\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\)
at \((0,0),(1,0),(1,-1)\), respectively,
and has no component at \((2,-2)\).  Thus the natural comparison on
this old completed generator is not an isomorphism of \(R\)-complexes.
The coherence hypothesis explains why this example falls outside the
interval-independence statement: \(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},0}\) is not coherent over \(W\).
For coherent inputs, a further completeness argument recovers the
comparison from its derived reduction.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{interval-r1-completed-coefficients}
The canonical maps induce isomorphisms
\[
 R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widehat R\simeq R_1,
 \qquad
 R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}
 \simeq k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}].
\]
Both right-hand sides are concentrated in auxiliary cohomological
degree zero. In particular, neither derived tensor product has higher
\(\operatorname{Tor}\).
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
This is clear from the definitions and the free resolution of \(R_1\)
in the proof of \Cref{Basic Vanishing}.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{interval-r1-polynomial-operators}
There is an exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow R_1[z]
 \xrightarrow{\,\cdot(1-Fz)\,}R_1[z]
 \longrightarrow k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}]\longrightarrow0.
\]
Here the last map is right \(F\)-localization in degree zero and zero
in degree one: it sends \(\sum_jx_jz^j\) to
\(\sum_jx_j^0F^{-j}\), where \(x_j^0\in R_1^0\) is the degree-zero
component of \(x_j\).
Moreover, \(\cdot(1-Vz)\) is an automorphism of \(R_1[z]\).
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
If \((\sum_jx_jz^j)\cdot(1-Fz)=0\), its constant coefficient is
\(x_0=0\), and its successive coefficients give
\(x_j=x_{j-1}\cdot F=0\). The cokernel is the direct limit under
right multiplication by \(F\).
On \(R_1^0\) this is \(k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}]\), and on
\(R_1^1\) it is zero because right multiplication by \(F\)
is zero. This also proves the assertion about the displayed last map.
For the second assertion, the inverse is
\(\sum_{a\geq0}(\cdot(Vz))^a\). This expression is a finite sum on every
input polynomial, since there are only finitely many coefficients and
right multiplication by \(V\) is locally nilpotent on each of them.
Thus the inverse is defined on the polynomial module itself; no
formal power-series enlargement is needed.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{interval-r1-polynomial-elimination}
Let \(S\) be an abelian group, and let \(b,b_r\) be commuting
additive endomorphisms of \(S\), written as right operators
\(x\mapsto xb\) and \(x\mapsto xb_r\). Write
\(S[z]=\bigoplus_{j\geq0}Sz^j\). For
\(y(z)=\sum_j y_jz^j\), set \(y(b)=\sum_j y_jb^j\), and extend
\(b\) coefficientwise to \(S[z]\).
Then the following sequence of abelian groups is exact:
\begin{equation}\label{interval-r1-monic-matrix}
0\longrightarrow S\oplus S[z]
\xrightarrow{\ d\ }S\oplus S[z]
\xrightarrow{\ \epsilon\ }S\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Here \(d(u,q)=(-ub_r,u+q(b-z))\) and
\(\epsilon(x,y(z))=x+y(b)b_r\). Under the induced isomorphism
\(\operatorname{coker}(d)\cong S\), the first summand of the middle
term maps identically to \(S\).
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
Suppose \(d(u,q)=0\). If \(q\neq0\) has degree \(d_0\) and
leading coefficient \(q_{d_0}\), then the coefficient of
\(z^{d_0+1}\) in \(u+q(b-z)\) is \(-q_{d_0}\neq0\), a
contradiction. Thus \(q=0\), and then \(u=0\), proving injectivity.

Evaluation at \(b\) sends \(q(b-z)\) to zero, so
\(\epsilon\circ d=0\). Moreover, every polynomial \(y\in S[z]\)
admits a unique expression
\[
 y(z)=y(b)+q(z)(b-z).
\]
Indeed, successively eliminating the highest-degree term gives a
constant remainder, which must be \(y(b)\) upon evaluation at \(b\);
uniqueness follows from the same leading-coefficient argument.
If \(\epsilon(x,y)=0\), then \(x=-y(b)b_r\), and this expression
gives
\[
 (x,y)=d\bigl(y(b),q\bigr).
\]
Hence \(\ker(\epsilon)=\operatorname{im}(d)\). Finally,
\(\epsilon(x,0)=x\), proving surjectivity and the assertion about
the first summand.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- proposition-32: body_md -->
\label{interval-r1-generator-comparison}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\), let \(r\in \mathrm{I}\), and let
\(\mathrm{J}=[m,n+1]\) or \(\mathrm{J}=[m-1,n]\). Regard
\(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},r}\) as a gauge of level \(\mathrm{J}\). The natural
comparison from the larger interval to the smaller interval induces,
for every inner \(R\)-complex degree \(s\), an isomorphism
\[
 R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}
       \bigl(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm{J}}(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},r})\bigr)^s
 \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
 R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}
       \bigl(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},r})\bigr)^s.
\]
These isomorphisms commute with the inner differential \(\delta\)
and are natural for morphisms between finite sums of the
\(\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{I},r}\). Both sides have no higher \(R_1\)-Tor. In inner
degree \(s\), their common degree-zero value is
\[
\begin{cases}
R_1(-i),&s=-i,\quad m\leq i<n,\\
k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}](-n),&s=-n,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end proposition-32 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
The comparison sends \(\beta_i\otimes x\) to the same symbol for
\(i\in \mathrm{I}\), and sends the symbols at the added endpoint to zero.
At the old top endpoint it uses the coefficient homomorphism
\(\widehat R^0\to\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\). These formulas respect the defining
relations of \Cref{definition of widehat rmt}, including those for
\(\delta\), and hence define a natural morphism of actual
\(R\)-complexes.

Let
\[
 0\longrightarrow P^{-1}\xrightarrow{d_r}P^0
 \longrightarrow\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\longrightarrow0
\]
be the flat resolution of
\Cref{interval-right-flat-resolution,interval-left-flat-resolution}.
By \Cref{interval-old-generators-acyclic}, applying
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm J}\) gives a short exact sequence of actual
\(R\)-complexes. In each fixed inner degree \(s\), the derived
\(R_1\)-reduction of the cokernel is computed by reducing the two-term
complex \([\widehat\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm J}(P^{-1})^s
\to\widehat\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm J}(P^0)^s]\).

Write \(s=-i\), and put \(S_i=R_1\) below the top of \(\mathrm J\),
\(S_i=k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}]\) at the top, and \(S_i=0\) outside
\(\mathrm J\). By \Cref{description of t(G_r),interval-r1-completed-coefficients},
each generator and polynomial summand, for \(j\in\mathrm J\), reduces as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}
 \bigl(\widehat\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm J}(\widehat G_{\mathrm J,j})\bigr)^{-i}
 &\simeq S_i(-i),\\
 R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}
 \bigl(\widehat\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm J}(\widehat G_{\mathrm J,j}\langle z\rangle)\bigr)^{-i}
 &\simeq S_i[z](-i).
\end{aligned}
\]
Both reductions have no higher \(R_1\)-Tor. For the second formula,
use the coefficient tensor description \eqref{interval-coefficient-tensor}:
\(\widehat G_{\mathrm J,j}\langle z\rangle\) is flat over
\(\widehat A_{\mathrm J}\) by \Cref{interval-flat-completion}, so the
free right \(R\)-resolution of \(R_1\) may first be applied to the
coefficient bimodule. By the first formula at every vertex, its
reduction is concentrated in degree zero and killed by \(p\); moreover,
\(\widehat G_{\mathrm J,j}\langle z\rangle/p
 =(\widehat G_{\mathrm J,j}/p)[z]\).
This gives the polynomial term, with its prescribed scalar action.
The identifications respect the path actions and \(z\), so
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}_{\mathrm J}(d_r)\) reduces coefficientwise. After
suppressing the module shift \((-i)\), its source and target are both
\(S_i\oplus S_i[z]\), in auxiliary degrees \(-1,0\). In the formulas
below, each path denotes its coefficient operator \(\rho_i\), acting on
the right of \(S_i\) and coefficientwise on \(S_i[z]\), where \(z\) is
central. Integral coefficients are reduced modulo \(p\).

First suppose that \(\mathrm{J}=[m,n+1]\). By
\Cref{interval-right-flat-resolution}, the reduced differential is
\begin{equation}\label{interval-r1-right-reduced-matrix}
 (u,q)\longmapsto
 \bigl(-u\widetilde{V}^{r-m},\,
 u\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_n+q(\widetilde{V}^{n-m}-\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_n z)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Here \(\widetilde{V}^{r-m}:r\to m\), \(\widetilde{V}^{n-m}:n\to m\), and
\(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_n:n\to m\). The table lists their images under
\(\rho_i\), acting on \(S_i\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 i&\widetilde{V}^{r-m}&\widetilde{V}^{n-m}&\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_n\\\hline
 m\leq i<n&
 \begin{cases}1,&r\leq i,\\p^{r-i-1}V,&r>i\end{cases}
 &p^{n-i-1}V&1\\
 i=n&1&1&F\\
 i=n+1&1&1&pF.
\end{array}
\]
For \(i<n\), use \eqref{interval-r1-monic-matrix}; it gives zero
kernel and cokernel \(R_1\), with the first generator unchanged.
For \(i=n\), the first component of
\eqref{interval-r1-right-reduced-matrix} is \(-u\). Eliminating it gives
\[
 \operatorname{coker}\bigl(\cdot(1-Fz):R_1[z]\longrightarrow R_1[z]\bigr)
 \simeq k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}],
\]
and zero kernel, by \Cref{interval-r1-polynomial-operators}.
To identify this isomorphism with the natural comparison, we must
keep track of the first summand. Elimination represents
\(x\) in the polynomial summand by \(xF\), so the localization
isomorphism must be followed by right multiplication by \(F^{-1}\).
Equivalently, the comparison on the quotient is
\[
 (x,\sum_jy_jz^j)\longmapsto
 x+\sum_j y_jF^{-(j+1)}\quad\text{in }k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}].
\]
It consequently sends the original generator to that same generator,
as required for the natural comparison. For \(i=n+1\), reduction
kills \(\tau_{\mathrm J}\widetilde{F}_n=pF\), and the matrix is simply
\((u,q)\mapsto(-u,q)\). Both its kernel and its cokernel are zero.

Now suppose that \(\mathrm{J}=[m-1,n]\). By
\Cref{interval-left-flat-resolution}, the reduced differential is
\begin{equation}\label{interval-r1-left-reduced-matrix}
 (u,q)\longmapsto
 \bigl(-u\widetilde{F}^{n-r},\,
 u\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}_m
 +q(\widetilde{F}^{n-m}-\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}_m z)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Here \(\widetilde{F}^{n-r}:r\to n\), \(\widetilde{F}^{n-m}:m\to n\), and
\(\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}_m:m\to n\). The table lists their images
under \(\rho_i\), acting on \(S_i\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 i&\widetilde{F}^{n-r}&\widetilde{F}^{n-m}&\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}_m\\\hline
 i=m-1&1&1&V\\
 m\leq i<n&
 \begin{cases}1,&i<r,\\p^{i-r}F,&i\geq r\end{cases}
 &p^{i-m}F&1\\
 i=n&p^{n-r}&p^{n-m}&F^{-1}.
\end{array}
\]
At the added bottom endpoint, elimination of the first component
reduces the matrix to \(\cdot(1-Vz)\) on \(R_1[z]\). It is an
isomorphism by \Cref{interval-r1-polynomial-operators}, so nothing
survives there. For \(m\leq i<n\),
\eqref{interval-r1-monic-matrix} again gives zero kernel and cokernel
\(R_1\), with the first generator unchanged.

At \(i=n\), the coefficient module is \(k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}]\), and
\(\tau_{\mathrm J}^{-1}\widetilde{V}_m=F^{-1}\) is a unit. Right multiplication
of the second output component by \(F\) changes
\eqref{interval-r1-left-reduced-matrix} into
\[
 (u,q)\longmapsto
       (-u p^{n-r},u+q(p^{n-m}F-z)).
\]
This is \eqref{interval-r1-monic-matrix}, so its kernel is zero and
its cokernel is \(k_\sigma[F,F^{-1}]\), again with the first summand mapping
identically. This calculation includes \(m=n=r\): in that case the
powers \(p^{n-r}\) and \(p^{n-m}\) are both \(1\), not \(0\).
The right-enlargement calculation likewise includes width zero.

In every old inner \(R\)-complex degree, the calculation identifies the isomorphism
induced by the natural comparison. That comparison was defined on
actual complexes, so it is compatible with \(\delta\) and natural in
all gauge morphisms. The result therefore holds separately in every
inner \(R\)-complex degree, before inner totalization, as asserted.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{interval-independence-derived}
Let \(\mathrm{I}\subseteq \mathrm{J}\) be finite intervals and let
\(M\in D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-} \mathrm{I})\). The natural comparison induces an
isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{interval-derived-comparison}
 \mathrm{L}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm{J}}(E_{\mathrm{J}\mathrm{I}}M)
       \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
 \mathrm{L}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}(M)
 \qquad\text{in }D(\mathrm{Ch}(R)).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every \(a\in\mathbb{Z}\), there is a natural isomorphism of
actual \(R\)-complexes
\[
 \mathrm{L}^a\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm{J}}(E_{\mathrm{J}\mathrm{I}}M)
       \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }
 \mathrm{L}^a\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}(M).
\]
In particular, for a coherent \(F\)-gauge structure, both
\(\mathrm{L}^{-1}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}\) and
\(\mathrm{L}^0\widehat{\mathrm{t}}=\widehat{\mathrm{t}}\) are independent of the chosen
finite interval. The comparisons are compatible with successive
enlargements.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
First suppose that \(\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{I}^+\) or \(\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{I}^-\). By
\Cref{resolution of coherent complexes,Exactness after completion},
choose a bounded-above resolution \(P^\bullet\to M\), each of whose terms
is a finite direct sum of \(\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r}\)'s.
Change of level is exact, and
\Cref{interval-old-generators-acyclic} shows that the same resolution
computes the functor at the larger level. Hence, putting
\[
 X_\mathrm{I}=\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}(P^\bullet),\qquad
 X_{\mathrm{J}}=\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm{J}}(E_{\mathrm{J}\mathrm{I}}P^\bullet),
\]
we obtain representatives of the two objects in
\eqref{interval-derived-comparison}, together with the comparison
\(X_{\mathrm{J}}\to X_\mathrm{I}\).
Fix the inner \(R\)-complex degree \(s\), and take the cone in the outer direction:
\[
 C^s=\operatorname{Cone}
       \bigl(X_{\mathrm{J}}^{\bullet,s}\longrightarrow X_\mathrm{I}^{\bullet,s}\bigr)
       \in D(R).
\]
The generator comparison in \Cref{interval-r1-generator-comparison} applies to every term \(P^a\).
The right-free resolution of \(R_1\) in the proof of
\Cref{Basic Vanishing} has uniformly finite length.
Hence totalizing in the resolution and \(R_1\)-resolution directions
involves only finitely many terms in each total degree and gives
\begin{equation}\label{interval-cone-r1-vanishing}
 R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}} C^s=0
 \qquad\text{for every }s.
\end{equation}
No totalization in the inner direction is taken here.

To deduce vanishing from this reduction, we verify that \(C^s\) is
Ekedahl-complete.
For \(X_\mathrm{I}^{\bullet,s}\), use the chosen bounded-above
\(\mathrm{I}\)-projective resolution: its terms are finite sums of grading
shifts of \(\widehat R\), or of the top module
\(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\). These modules are complete.
For the top module, this can also be checked directly: its differential
\(d\) is zero, \(F\) is invertible, and \(V=pF^{-1}\), so its
Ekedahl completion is its \(p\)-adic completion.
\Cref{embedding-row-completeness} shows that a bounded-above complex
of these complete modules is complete.

For \(X_{\mathrm{J}}^{\bullet,s}\), use a bounded-above resolution of
\(E_{\mathrm{J}\mathrm{I}}M\) by the completed projective generators
\(\widehat G_{\mathrm{J},t}\). The same argument proves that the resulting
outer complex in inner \(R\)-complex degree \(s\) is complete. Since it represents
\(X_{\mathrm{J}}^{\bullet,s}\), both \(X_{\mathrm{J}}^{\bullet,s}\) and \(C^s\) are
complete. This uses a resolution at the larger level; completeness of
\(\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_{\mathrm{J}}(\widehat G_{\mathrm{I},r})^s\) is not required.

Since \(C^s\) is bounded above and complete,
\Cref{R1 detects vanishing of complete complexes} and
\eqref{interval-cone-r1-vanishing} give \(C^s=0\) for every \(s\).
Evaluation in each inner \(R\)-complex degree is exact,
and these evaluations jointly detect outer quasi-isomorphisms.
We therefore obtain \eqref{interval-derived-comparison} in
\(D(\mathrm{Ch}(R))\), not merely after totalization in \(D(R)\).
Taking outer cohomology proves the asserted isomorphisms in \(\mathrm{Ch}(R)\).

An arbitrary finite enlargement is a succession of elementary left
and right enlargements. The cocycle identity
\eqref{interval-comparison-cocycle}, and its derived version, show
that the resulting comparison is independent of the succession chosen
and is natural in \(M\).
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{interval-independence-scope}
The proof uses the bounded-above resolutions with finite direct sums
in each degree supplied by
\Cref{resolution of coherent complexes,Exactness after completion}.
By \Cref{embedding-row-completeness}, these suffice for the completeness
argument, even when the projective resolutions have infinite length.
The intermediate syzygies need not be coherent as \(W\)-modules, and
coherence of \(\mathrm{L}^{-1}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}(M)\) as a diagonal complex is
not assumed in advance. Likewise, \(p\)-torsion-freeness of a resolution
does not imply \(p\)-torsion-freeness of its cohomology: the derived
functor retains nonzero \(p\)-torsion, including domino contributions.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{embedding-row-completeness}
Let $P^\bullet$ be a bounded-above complex of graded $R$-modules whose
terms, regarded as objects of $D(R)$, are Ekedahl-complete. Then
$P^\bullet$ is Ekedahl-complete. In particular, a graded $R$-module
represented by a bounded-above complex of finite direct sums of shifts
of $\widehat R$ is Ekedahl-complete.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
For every $a\geq1$, the following sequence for the right $R$-module
$R_a$ of \Cref{reduction by R_n} is exact:
\begin{equation}\label{embedding-rn-resolution}
0\longrightarrow R(-1)
 \xrightarrow{\binom{F^a}{-F^ad}\,\bullet}
 R(-1)\oplus R
 \xrightarrow{(dV^a,V^a)\,\bullet}
 R\longrightarrow R_a\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
The entries act by left multiplication on free right modules.

Denote the three-term free complex in
\eqref{embedding-rn-resolution} by $K_a$, placed in degrees $[-2,0]$.
The quotient maps $R_{a+1}\to R_a$ lift to maps $K_{a+1}\to K_a$
given, in degrees $-2,-1,0$, respectively, by
\[
 p,\qquad \operatorname{diag}(V,V),\qquad\mathrm{id}.
\]
Compatibility follows from $VF^{a+1}=pF^a$ and
$dV^aV=dV^{a+1}$.

Compute derived completion with $K_a$ and the usual product-cone
model for $R\varprojlim_a$. The $K_a$-direction has degrees $[-2,0]$,
and the derived inverse-limit direction has degrees $[0,1]$.
The combined auxiliary direction therefore has the uniform finite range
$[-2,1]$. These computations may be checked on the underlying graded
complexes; the completion map retains its natural $R$-linear structure.

Apply this model to $P^\bullet$. For each fixed complex degree $s$,
the corresponding column computes the completion of $P^s$, and the
natural map from $P^s$ to that column is a quasi-isomorphism by
hypothesis. These columnwise quasi-isomorphisms induce a
quasi-isomorphism on total complexes. Indeed, the auxiliary direction
has uniform finite width, so the associated spectral sequence has a
finite filtration in every total degree. Interchanging the
inverse-limit model with totalization uses only products and finite
direct sums in each degree. The resulting total complex is precisely
the model for the derived completion of $P^\bullet$.
Hence $P^\bullet\to\widehat{P^\bullet}$ is a quasi-isomorphism.

The final assertion follows because $\widehat R$ and its grading
shifts are complete and completeness is invariant under
quasi-isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{embedding-hom-comparison}
Let $C,D\in\mathrm{Ch}(R)$ be bounded complexes such that $C^s$ and $D^s$
are supported in Raynaud-module degrees $-s$ and $-s+1$.
Assume the following:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item For every $s$, the graded module $C^s$ has a bounded-above
 representative in $D(R)$ whose terms are finite direct sums of
 $\widehat R(s)$.
 \item Every graded module $D^s$ is Ekedahl-complete.
\end{enumerate}
Then localization induces a natural bijection
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ch}(R)}(C,D)
       \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }
 \operatorname{Hom}_{D(R)}(C,D).
\]
Moreover every chain homotopy between maps $C\to D$ is zero.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
All Hom and Ext groups in this proof preserve the Raynaud-module
grading. We first prove
\begin{equation}\label{embedding-backward-ext-vanishing}
 R\operatorname{Hom}_R(C^s,D^v)=0\qquad(v<s).
\end{equation}
For a complete target $Y$, the adjunction defining derived completion
gives
\[
 R\operatorname{Hom}_R(\widehat R(s),Y)
   \simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_R(R(s),Y)
   \simeq Y^{-s}.
\]
Here $Y^{-s}$ denotes evaluation in Raynaud-module degree $-s$.
Taking $Y=D^v$ and $v<s$ makes this zero, since $D^v$ is supported
in degrees $-v,-v+1$, both strictly larger than $-s$.

To pass from the free coefficient modules to the row module, use the
representative $P_s^\bullet$ in (1). Every finite stupid
truncation of $P_s^\bullet$ is obtained by finite cones from finite
sums of $\widehat R(s)$, and consequently has zero derived Hom into
$D^v$ when $v<s$. The bounded-above complex $P_s^\bullet$ is the
homotopy colimit of these finite stupid truncations. Derived Hom in
the first variable converts this homotopy colimit into a homotopy
limit, proving \eqref{embedding-backward-ext-vanishing}.
No finite-length row resolution is required.

We now use this vanishing in the bounded-complex hyper-Ext spectral sequence
\[
 E_1^{p,q}=\bigoplus_s
     \operatorname{Ext}_R^q(C^s,D^{s+p})
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     \operatorname{Hom}_{D(R)}(C,D[p+q]).
\]
The terms with $q<0$ vanish because $C^s,D^{s+p}$ are modules.
Those with $p<0$ vanish by
\eqref{embedding-backward-ext-vanishing}. In total degree zero,
there is therefore only the term $(p,q)=(0,0)$, and
\[
 E_2^{0,0}
  =\ker\left(
    \bigoplus_s\operatorname{Hom}_R(C^s,D^s)
     \longrightarrow
    \bigoplus_s\operatorname{Hom}_R(C^s,D^{s+1})
   \right)
  =\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ch}(R)}(C,D).
\]
There is no quotient by degree-minus-one Hom, since that group is
already zero. No higher differential enters this term, because its
source would have $p<0$, and none leaves it, because its target would
have $q<0$. The edge isomorphism is the map induced by localization,
which proves the asserted bijection.

Finally, a chain homotopy would have components
$C^s\to D^{s-1}$, and each such Hom group is zero by
\eqref{embedding-backward-ext-vanishing}.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Interval independence allows us to meet the hypotheses of
\Cref{embedding-hom-comparison} by enlarging the upper endpoint beyond
the Raynaud-module support of the representatives. Every nonzero row
then has the form of an ordinary row of
the completed generator complex, with coefficient $\widehat R(s)$;
the exceptional top module does not occur in that row. If outer
cohomology is concentrated in degree zero, taking the corresponding
row of the projective gauge resolution supplies the representative
in (1), and \Cref{embedding-row-completeness} supplies (2).
<!-- end remark-8 -->

\(q:\mathrm{Ch}(R)\to D(R)\) is localization. Its values are supported in

For an object \(N\) of finite level \(\mathrm{I}\), this functor is naturally

<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
For a fixed interval, \Cref{embedding-natural-representative} gives
the representative property and exactness. To prove full faithfulness,
put \(C=\mathcal S_\mathrm{I}(N)\) and \(D=\mathcal S_\mathrm{I}(N')\).
By \Cref{interval-independence-derived}, we may enlarge \(\mathrm{I}\) to a
common interval \(\mathrm{J}\) whose upper endpoint lies strictly above the
\(R\)-degree supports of both \(C\) and \(D\).

Choose bounded-above resolutions of
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\) and \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N')\) by finite direct sums of the
completed \(\mathrm{J}\)-projective generators. By
\Cref{completed rmt on diagonal heart}, the outer complex in each
inner \(R\)-complex degree \(s\) represents \(C^s\), respectively \(D^s\), as an
object of \(D(R)\). For every \(s\) with \(C^s\ne0\) or \(D^s\ne0\),
the corresponding row terms are finite direct sums of \(\widehat R(s)\).
By \Cref{embedding-row-completeness},
each \(D^s\) is complete. Thus \Cref{embedding-hom-comparison} gives
the natural bijection
\[

 \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
 \operatorname{Hom}_{D(R)}(qC,qD)
 \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{

}}              
    {\,

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);

}}

To assemble the functor across levels, use the comparison isomorphisms

<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{embedding-diagonal-cohomology}
Let \(M\in D_c^b({F\text{-}\mathsf{Gauge}}\text{-} \mathrm{I})\), and put
\[
 N=\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}(M).
\]
For every \(a\in\mathbb{Z}\), there is a natural isomorphism of actual
\(R\)-complexes
\[
 \mathrm{L}^a\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}(M)
 \cong \mathcal S_\mathrm{I}\bigl(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{\,a}(N)\bigr).
\]
In particular, \(\mathrm{L}^a\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}(M)\) represents
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{\,a}(N)\), and is a coherent diagonal complex
after passage to \(D(R)\).
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
The completed coherent equivalence gives \(N\in D_c^b(R\text{-} \mathrm{I})\).
Since diagonal truncations preserve level \(\mathrm{I}\), the bounded diagonal
\(t\)-structure is available on this fixed-level category.
Consider the triangulated functor
\[
 \mathcal X_\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{L}\widehat{\mathrm{t}}_\mathrm{I}\circF\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}
 :D_c^b(R\text{-} \mathrm{I})\longrightarrow D(\mathrm{Ch}(R)).
\]
By \Cref{completed rmt on diagonal heart}, it takes the diagonal
heart to the standard outer heart. The diagonal \(t\)-structure
on the source is bounded; induction on its truncation triangles
therefore shows that \(\mathcal X_\mathrm{I}\) is \(t\)-exact for these two
\(t\)-structures. Consequently it commutes with their cohomology
functors:
\[
 H^a_{\mathrm{out}}\mathcal X_\mathrm{I}(N)
 \cong
 \mathcal S_\mathrm{I}\bigl(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{\,a}(N)\bigr).
\]
The completed equivalence identifies \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\) with \(M\).
Substitution gives the claimed isomorphism, and the representative
property follows from \Cref{embedding-diagonal-complexes}.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- proposition-33: body_md -->
\label{acyclic diagonal complexes and boundary 0 F-gauge structures}
The functor \(N\mapsto\mathrm{H}^1(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N))\) induces an equivalence between
the category of \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic diagonal complexes and the category of
coherent \(F\)-gauges \(M\) satisfying \(M^\infty=0\).

_g\). By

<!-- definition-34: body_md -->
\label{M(I J)}
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\) be a finite interval and \(J\subseteq[m,n-1]\).
Define \(M(\mathrm{I},J)\) by
\[
M(\mathrm{I},J)^i=\begin{cases}k,&i\in\mathrm{I},\\0,&i\notin\mathrm{I},\end{cases}
\]
with \(\widetilde{F}:M(\mathrm{I},J)^i\to M(\mathrm{I},J)^{i+1}\) equal to the identity for
\(i\in J\) and zero otherwise, and \(\widetilde{V}\) equal to the identity on
the remaining edges of \(\mathrm{I}\) and zero otherwise. We use the same notation for
the associated \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic diagonal complex.
<!-- end definition-34 -->
<!-- proposition-34: body_md -->
\label{indecomposable Tot acyclic objects are M(I J)}
The \(M(\mathrm{I},J)\) are precisely the indecomposable
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic diagonal complexes killed by \(p\).
<!-- end proposition-34 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
By the preceding proposition, we classify indecomposable coherent
gauges \(N\) with \(N^\infty=0\) and \(pN=0\). Such a gauge has finite
support: it has finite level and zero boundary, and coherence makes
each component finite-dimensional over \(k\). Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\) be the
smallest interval containing its support, and induct on \(n-m\). If
\(m=n\), indecomposability gives \(N^m\cong k\). Now assume \(m<n\), and set
\(N'^m=0\) and \(N'^i=N^i\) for \(i>m\), with the
adjacent maps zero. Since \(pN=0\), this remains a coherent gauge with
zero boundary value. Decompose \(N'\) into indecomposables; by
induction, each is an interval gauge. Any summand missing degree
\(m+1\) has no link to \(N^m\) and splits off \(N\).
Thus every summand meets degree \(m+1\).

Between any two interval summands meeting degree \(m+1\), there is a
morphism in one direction whose component there is the identity. To
see this, compare their directed graphs from \(m+1\). If one is an
initial segment of the other, the first extra arrow gives an inclusion
or projection. If their first differing arrows have opposite
orientations, the graph with a right-pointing arrow projects onto the
common initial segment, which embeds into the graph with a left-pointing
arrow. For equal graphs, use the identity.

Suppose \(\widetilde{F}:N^m\to N^{m+1}\) is nonzero. Choose a one-dimensional
subspace \(k\subseteq N^m\) on which \(\widetilde{F}\) is nonzero, and write
\(N'=\bigoplus_iN_i\). If \(\widetilde{F}(k)\) has nonzero components in two
summands, the morphism just constructed gives a shear
\(\mathrm{id}+\varphi\) that eliminates one component. Repeating this,
we may assume
\(\widetilde{F}(k)\subseteq N_{i_0}^{m+1}\) for one \(i_0\). Let
\(\pi:N^{m+1}\to N_{i_0}^{m+1}\) be the projection and put
\(T=\ker(\pi\widetilde{F})\). Since \(\widetilde{F}(k)\) spans
\(N_{i_0}^{m+1}\cong k\), we have \(N^m=k\oplus T\). The map \(\widetilde{F}\)
takes \(k\) into \(N_{i_0}^{m+1}\) and \(T\) into the other summands.
The relations \(\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=p=0\) give
\(\widetilde{V}(N_{i_0}^{m+1})=0\) and
\(\widetilde{V}(\bigoplus_{i\ne i_0}N_i^{m+1})\subseteq T\).
All other maps respect the decomposition of \(N'\). Hence
\[
N''=(\cdots0\leftrightarrows k\leftrightarrows
N_{i_0}^{m+1}\leftrightarrows N_{i_0}^{m+2}
\leftrightarrows\cdots)
\]
is a nonzero direct summand of \(N\). By indecomposability,
\(N=N''\), an interval gauge. If \(\widetilde{F}=0\) but \(\widetilde{V}\ne0\) at the
boundary, apply the same argument to the finite-dimensional graded
\(k\)-dual, which exchanges \(\widetilde{F}\) and \(\widetilde{V}\). If both maps vanish,
\(N=N^m\oplus N'\), reducing to the one-vertex case.

Conversely, each \(M(\mathrm{I},J)\) is killed by \(p\) and has zero boundary
value. Thus it gives a \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic object by
\Cref{acyclic diagonal complexes and boundary 0 F-gauge structures}.
Every endomorphism acts by a scalar on each one-dimensional component,
and every identity edge forces adjacent scalars to agree. Hence
\(\operatorname{End}(M(\mathrm{I},J))=k\), so \(M(\mathrm{I},J)\) is indecomposable.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- definition-35: body_md -->
\label{definition of diagonal domino}
A diagonal domino is a \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-torsion diagonal complex without finite
torsion.
<!-- end definition-35 -->

<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
For (1), \(U_0[k](-k)\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. By
\Cref{sub and quotient object of Tot-torsion objects}(2), the image of
any map \(U_0[k](-k)\to M\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion. This proves one
direction. Conversely, suppose the Hom groups vanish for all \(k\).
Since \(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\) is torsion, the universal coefficient theorem
reduces its vanishing to
\[
\mathrm{H}^{-1}\bigl(k\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}\mathrm{Tot}(M)\bigr)=0.
\]
By \Cref{Hodge numbers in degree plus minus 1}, the terms with
\(i+j=-1\) vanish in the spectral sequence
\[
\mathrm{H}^{i}\!\left(R_1\otimes_R^\mathrm{L} M\right)^j
\Longrightarrow
\mathrm{H}^{i+j}\!\bigl(k\otimes_W^\mathrm{L} \mathrm{Tot}(M)\bigr)
\]
Thus \(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))=0\). If \(N\hookrightarrow M\) is a
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion subobject, then
\(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(N))\hookrightarrow\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))=0\), while
\(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(N))=0\). Hence \(N\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. If nonzero,
it contains some \(U_0[i](-i)\) by
\Cref{simple Tot acyclic objects are U_0^i}, contradicting the
Hom vanishing. The quotient statement is dual.

For (2), \Cref{without finite torsion implies artinian}(1) identifies
\(D(M)\) with \(\widetilde D^{\,0}(M)\), shows that it has no finite
torsion, and gives biduality. The formula
\[
\mathrm{Tot}(D(M))=R\!\operatorname{Hom}_W(\mathrm{Tot}(M),W)
\]
shows that \(\widetilde D^{\,0}(M)\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-torsion, and that it is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion precisely when \(M\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion.

For (3), duality and
\(D(M(\varphi))=D(M)(\text{-}\varphi\text{-})\), where
\(\text{-}\varphi\text{-}(a)=-\varphi(-a)\), reduce the claims to the
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion case under negative modification. Since twists
add, it suffices to consider \(-\delta_i\). A \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion domino \(N\)
has \(G^2(N)=0\), hence \(N[1]\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
_g\). Choose a level interval
containing \(i\) and the support of \(N\). By
\Cref{Ekedahl equivalence and the G t-structure},
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\) is concentrated in cohomological degree \(1\), and
\Cref{definition of FG}(3) gives
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)^i\simeq\mathrm{Tot}(N(-\delta_i)).
\]
Thus \(N(-\delta_i)\) has no degree-zero total cohomology. Nygaard
modification preserves diagonality and the absence of finite torsion;
its degree-one total cohomology is torsion by \Cref{Basic Vanishing}(1).
It is therefore a \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion domino. Duality gives the
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion assertion.
<!-- end proof-77 -->

<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{type filtration on diagonal domino}
Every diagonal domino \(M\) carries a canonical type filtration with the
following properties.

    {\rm (1)} It is a finite, exhaustive, and separated decreasing filtration:
    \[M \supseteq ...\supseteq W^{s-\frac{1}{2}}(M)\supseteq W^s(M)\supseteq W^{s+\frac{1}{2}}(M)\supseteq ...,\quad s\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}. \]
    Its graded pieces satisfy the following conditions.

    {\rm (i)} If \(s\in \mathbb{Z}\), then \(m_s(W^s(M)/W^{s+\frac{1}{2}}(M))\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. 

    {\rm (ii)} If \(s\in \frac{1}{2}+\mathbb{Z}\), then \[\begin{aligned}
        \mathrm{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(U_0[k](-k), m_{s+\frac{1}{2}}(W^s(M)/W^{s+\frac{1}{2}}(M)))=0\\
        \mathrm{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(m_{s+\frac{1}{2}}(W^s(M)/W^{s+\frac{1}{2}}(M)),U_{-1}[k](-k))=0
    \end{aligned}\]

    {\rm (2)} Conditions (i) and (ii) characterize the filtration. Each
    \(W^s\) is an idempotent radical, and
    \[m_r(W^s(M))=W^{s-r}(m_r(M)).\]

    {\rm (3)} There is a natural isomorphism
    \[\widetilde{D}^0(W^s(M))\cong
    (\mathrm{Id}/W^{-s+\frac{1}{2}})\widetilde{D}^0(M).\]

<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
Let \(F^1,F^2,G^1,G^2\) be the two fundamental filtrations of \(M\).
Their common quotient \(F^2/F^1=G^2/G^1\) is Mazur--Ogus. Its first
total cohomology vanishes by \Cref{Mazur-Ogus vanishing}, and its
zeroth vanishes because \(M\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-torsion. A Mazur--Ogus object
that is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic is zero, leaving
\[
0\subseteq G^1\subseteq F^1\subseteq M,
\]
where \(F^1\) is the largest \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion subobject,
\(M/G^1\) is the largest \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient, and
\(F^1/G^1\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. Thus \(F^1\) and \(G^1\) are
admissible idempotent radicals.

We next need the inclusions
\[
m_r(F^1(M))\subseteq G^1(m_rM)\quad(r<0),
\qquad
F^1(m_rM)\subseteq m_r(G^1(M))\quad(r>0).
\]
The second is dual to the first. By
\Cref{Tot 0 or Tot 1 of diagonal domino}(3), \(m_r(F^1(M))\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion. Its image in
\(F^1(m_rM)/G^1(m_rM)\) is also \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. If this image were
nonzero, it would have a quotient \(U_0[i](-i)\); after applying \(m_{-r}\),
the \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion object \(F^1(M)\) would have a quotient
\(U_r[i](-i)\) with nonzero \(\mathrm{H}^1\), a contradiction. The image is
therefore zero.

For \(s\in\mathbb{Z}\), define
\[
W^sM:=m_{-s}F^1(m_sM),
\qquad
W^{s+\frac12}M:=m_{-s}G^1(m_sM).
\]
These admissible subobjects form a decreasing filtration by the
inclusions above. Property (i) follows from the \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclicity of
\(F^1(m_sM)/G^1(m_sM)\). To prove (ii), put
\[
H:=m_1G^1(m_{-1}N)/F^1N
\]
for a diagonal domino \(N\). By construction, \(H\) has no nonzero
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion subobject, while \(m_{-1}H\) has no nonzero
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient. The required Hom vanishings follow
from \Cref{Tot 0 or Tot 1 of diagonal domino}(1).

For uniqueness, modifications translate the indices, so we need only
recover \(W^0\) and \(W^{1/2}\). Conditions
(i) and (ii), together with
\Cref{Tot 0 or Tot 1 of diagonal domino}, give
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]

    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(W^{1/2},U_0[k](-k))=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice

    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);

  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(U_0[k](-k),M/W^0)=0.
\]
Hence \(W^{1/2}\subseteq G^1\), while \(M/W^0\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion. Since \(W^0/W^{1/2}\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion, the quotient \(M/W^{1/2}\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion, and therefore \(G^1\subseteq W^{1/2}\).
Thus \(W^{1/2}=G^1\); the equality \(W^0=F^1\) is dual.

Compatibility with \(m_r\) follows directly from the definition. Each
\(W^s\) is an idempotent radical because \(F^1\) and \(G^1\) are.
Part (3) follows from \Cref{Tot 0 or Tot 1 of diagonal domino}(2) and
the identities
\[
\widetilde D^0(F^1(-))=\widetilde D^0(-)/G^1\widetilde D^0(-),
\qquad
\widetilde D^0(G^1(-))=\widetilde D^0(-)/F^1\widetilde D^0(-).
\]

Finally, \Cref{without finite torsion implies artinian} yields
\(s_0\) such that \(W^s=W^{s_0}\) for all \(s\geqslant s_0\). For
this stable term, every sufficiently positive modification is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion. By
\Cref{Tot 0 or Tot 1 of diagonal domino}(3), the same holds after every
modification \(\varphi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\). The finite-torsion criterion
\Cref{description of finite torsion object} then makes \(W^{s_0}\)
finite torsion, hence zero. This proves separation and finiteness in
one direction. Duality and (3) give exhaustiveness and finiteness in
the other.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- definition-36: body_md -->
\label{type function}
For a diagonal domino \(M\), define its type to be the function
\(\sigma:\frac12\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{Z}}\) given by
\[\sigma(s)(i)= T^{-i,i}\!\left( W_M^s/W_M^{s+1/2}
\right).\]
We say that \(M\) is of type \(s\) if
\(\sigma(t)\) is the zero function whenever \(t\neq s\).
<!-- end definition-36 -->
<!-- proposition-35: body_md -->
\label{when is a torsion object in G a type 1/2 diagonal domino}
A diagonal domino of type \(\frac12\) lies in \(G\). Conversely, a
torsion object \(M\in G\) is a diagonal domino of type \(\frac12\) if
and only if
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_G(U_1[k](-k),M)=0
\]
for every \(k\).
<!-- end proposition-35 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->

\begin{proof}
Applying \(m_i\), we may assume \(i=0\). By

\[\mathrm{H}^i(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}} N)^j \Longrightarrow

<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{type 1/2 F-gauge structures}
The category of type \(1/2\) diagonal complexes is equivalent to the
category of torsion coherent \(F\)-gauges \(M\) satisfying the following
condition:

\[
(*)\qquad
\left\{
\begin{array}{l}
\text{For any } i,\ \text{if }
x\in M^{i+1},\ y\in M^{i-1},
\\[2mm]
\widetilde{V} x=0,\quad \widetilde{F} y=0,\quad
\tau \text{ applied to the image of }x
\text{ in }M^\infty
\text{ equals the image of }y
\text{ in }M^{-\infty},
\\[2mm]
\text{then } x=y=0.
\end{array}
\right.
\]
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-82: body_md -->
The preceding proposition reduces the claim to computing maps from
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(U_1[k](-k))\), as \(k\) varies. This gauge complex has
cohomology only in degree zero, and its cohomology gauge has components
\[
\mathrm{H}^0\!\bigl(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(U_1[k](-k))\bigr)^i
=
\begin{cases}
k,& i\neq k+1,\\
0,& i=k+1.
\end{cases}
\]
On this gauge, \(\widetilde{F}\) is the identity above degree \(k+1\) and zero
otherwise, while \(\widetilde{V}\) is the identity below degree \(k+1\) and
zero otherwise; \(\tau\) is the \(p\)-power map. Thus, for any
\(F\)-gauge \(M\),
\[
\mathrm{Hom}\!\bigl(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(U_1[k](-k)),M\bigr)
=
\Bigl\{
(x,y)\in M^{k+2}\times M^k
:\widetilde{V} x=0,\ \widetilde{F} y=0,\ \tau(x_{\infty})=y_{-\infty}
\Bigr\}.
\]
Replacing \(k+1\) by \(i\) gives exactly condition \((*)\).
<!-- end proof-82 -->
