<!-- proposition-36: body_md -->
\label{swap direction isomorphic}
There is an isomorphism of diagonal dominos
\[
(\cdots i^*\!\longrightarrow i+1\cdots)
\cong
(\cdots i\longleftarrow(i+1)^*\cdots),
\]
with every other vertex and arrow fixed.
<!-- end proposition-36 -->
<!-- proof-84: body_md -->
Apply the inverse Nygaard modification at every distinguished vertex
common to both graphs. We may thus assume that \(i\) and \(i+1\) are,
respectively, the only distinguished vertices on the two sides. Let
\(M(\mathrm{I},J)\) be the acyclic interval object underlying the left graph,
with \(i\in J\), and put
\(\theta=\varphi_{\{i\}}-\varphi_{\{i+1\}}\). The claim becomes
\(M(\mathrm{I},J)(\theta)\cong M(\mathrm{I},J\setminus\{i\})\).

The object \(M(\mathrm{I},J)\) is characterized by
\[
\dim_k M(\mathrm{I},J)^j=
\begin{cases}
1,&j\in\mathrm{I},\\
0,&j\notin\mathrm{I},
\end{cases}
\]
and by the requirement that
\(M([j,j+1],\{j\}\cap J)\) occur as a subquotient for each
\(j\in[m,n-1]\). Assuming the two-vertex case, this characterization
settles the general case directly. Regard \([m,i-1]\) and
\([i+2,n]\) as two tails. An arrow pointing into a tail makes it a
subobject, and an arrow pointing out makes it a quotient. This gives a filtration with
\(M([i,i+1],\{i\})\) as its middle subquotient. The tails are fixed
by \(\theta\), since their \(R\)-degrees avoid \(i\); the two-vertex
calculation replaces the middle factor by the opposite acyclic
interval. Exactness of Nygaard modification in \(D(R)\) and extension
closure therefore show that \(M(\mathrm{I},J)(\theta)\) is acyclic. It remains
indecomposable and killed by \(p\), so it is an interval object by
\Cref{indecomposable Tot acyclic objects are M(I J)}. By
\Cref{domino numbers of Tot acyclic diagonal dominos}(2)--(3), its
cohomology gauge has the same vertex dimensions as \(M(\mathrm{I},J)\).
The tails retain their subobject or quotient positions, and their
boundary extensions remain nonsplit. Thus their arrows are unchanged,
while the central arrow reverses. These are exactly the required
two-vertex subquotients, so the characterization gives
\(M(\mathrm{I},J)(\theta)\cong M(\mathrm{I},J\setminus\{i\})\).

It remains to prove the two-vertex case. After shifting, assume
\(i=0\) and put
\(Q=(0^*\!\rightarrow1)(-\varphi_{\{1\}})\).
The exact sequence \(0\to(1)\to(0\to1)\to(0)\to0\) gives
\[
0\longrightarrow U_{-1}\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow
U_1[-1](1)\longrightarrow0,
\]
and hence
\(0\to\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot} Q)\to k\to k\to\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot} Q)\to0\).
If \(Q\) were not \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic, both end groups would be \(k\).
Then \(0\neq W^0Q\neq Q\), and
\Cref{two fundamental filtrations} shows that
\(W^0Q\to U_1[-1](1)\) is an isomorphism after totalization.
By \Cref{Totsubquo}, its kernel and cokernel are \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic.
The target has no nonzero acyclic quotient, and the kernel lies in
\(U_{-1}\), which has no nonzero acyclic subobject. Thus the map is an
isomorphism and the sequence splits. Twisting back would decompose
\((0\to1)\), contrary to
\Cref{indecomposable Tot acyclic objects are M(I J)}.
Therefore \(Q\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic.

By \Cref{domino numbers of Tot acyclic diagonal dominos}(2)--(3),
\(\mathrm{H}^1(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(Q))\) has one copy of \(k\) in gauge degrees
\(0,1\) and is zero elsewhere. Modification also preserves
indecomposability, so \(Q\) is either \((0\to1)\)
or \((0\leftarrow1)\). The first is impossible: twisting it by
\(\varphi_{\{1\}}\) would give an undistinguished source and a
distinguished sink, whereas
\(Q(\varphi_{\{1\}})=(0^*\!\rightarrow1)\) has type \(1/2\).
Hence \(Q\cong(0\leftarrow1)\). The preceding reduction proves the
general case; applying \(\varphi_{\{i+1\}}\) and restoring the common
distinguished vertices gives the stated isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-84 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{type 1/2 pullback stability}
Pulling back or pushing out a short exact sequence of diagonal dominos
of type \(1/2\) in \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) along a morphism between such objects again
produces a sequence of the same type.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-85: body_md -->
Let \(0\to N_1\to N_2\xrightarrow{j}N_3\to0\) be exact and let
\(p:M_3\to N_3\) be a morphism of diagonal dominos of type \(1/2\). Put
\(M_2=N_2\times_{N_3}M_3\). This is again a diagonal domino, since it
fits into \(0\to N_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0\). Functoriality gives
\(W^1(M_2)\subseteq W^1(N_2\oplus M_3)=0\). It also places
\(N_1\) and the quotient \(M_3\) inside the type \(1/2\) part of
\(M_2\), so \(W^{1/2}(M_2)=M_2\). Thus \(M_2\) has type
\(1/2\). The pushout argument is dual.
<!-- end proof-85 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{kernel reduction for weakly simple dominos}
Let \(M\) be a weakly simple type \(1/2\) diagonal domino and suppose
that in \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) there is an exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow U_1[i](-i)
\longrightarrow0.
\]
If \(W^{1/2}N=0\), then \(N\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic.
Otherwise \(N\) itself is a weakly simple type \(1/2\) diagonal domino.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-86: body_md -->
Since \(N\subseteq M\), we have \(W^1N=0\), so
\(W^{1/2}N\) is of type \(1/2\).
Suppose \(W^{1/2}N\neq0\), and set
\(B=N/W^{1/2}N\), \(Q=M/W^{1/2}N\).
The radical property gives \(W^{1/2}B=0\), while
\[
0\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow U_1[i](-i)
\longrightarrow0
\]
is exact. The type filtration makes \(B\) a diagonal domino; hence
\(Q\) is one as well.
As a quotient of \(M\), it has no nonzero \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion
quotient, so it lies in \(G\).
Since \(0\neq W^{1/2}N\neq M\), weak simplicity implies that \(Q\) is not
of type \(1/2\). By
\Cref{when is a torsion object in G a type 1/2 diagonal domino},
there is a nonzero map \(U_1[j](-j)\to Q\).
This map cannot factor through \(B\), since
\(W^{1/2}U_1[j](-j)=U_1[j](-j)\) and \(W^{1/2}B=0\).
Its composite with \(Q\to U_1[i](-i)\) is nonzero. Under
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\), the gauge of \(U_1[a](-a)\) vanishes exactly in degree
\(a+1\); compatibility with \(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{V},\tau\) at this gap shows that
maps between gauges with different gaps vanish, while every nonzero
endomorphism is an isomorphism. Thus \(j=i\), and the composite is an
isomorphism.
Thus \(Q\simeq B\oplus U_1[i](-i)\). But \(B\) is a quotient of \(M\), so
functoriality and
\(W^{1/2}M=M\) give \(W^{1/2}B=B\).
Hence \(B=0\), proving \(N=W^{1/2}N\).

Now suppose that \(0\to A\to N\to B\to0\) is admissible in the type
\(1/2\) category, with \(A,B\neq0\).
Again \(Q=M/A\) lies in \(G\) but is not of type \(1/2\).
The same argument, using \(\mathrm{Hom}(U_1[j](-j),B)=0\), splits
\(0\to B\to Q\to U_1[i](-i)\to0\).
Let \(E\subseteq M\) be the preimage of the \(U_1[i](-i)\)-factor.
Then \(0\to A\to E\to U_1[i](-i)\to0\) and \(M/E=B\).
The class \(W^{1/2}X=X\) is extension-closed, so \(W^{1/2}E=E\);
also \(W^1E=0\), since \(E\subseteq M\).
Thus \(E\) and \(B\) have type \(1/2\), contradicting the weak
simplicity of \(M\). Hence \(N\) is weakly simple.

If \(W^{1/2}N=0\), then \(N\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion and
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot} M)\longrightarrow k
 \longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot} N)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The first term is nonzero because \(M\) is a nonzero object of pure
type \(1/2\). Its injection into \(k\) is therefore an isomorphism.
Hence \(N\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic.
<!-- end proof-86 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{weakly simple type 1/2 diagonal dominos}
The additive category of type \(1/2\) diagonal dominos, with the
exact sequences induced from \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\), is exact, weakly noetherian
and weakly artinian. Its weakly simple objects are precisely
\[
N_{m,n}\quad\text{and}\quad N'_{m,n},\qquad m<n.
\]
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-87: body_md -->
Extension closure and \Cref{type 1/2 pullback stability} give the exact
structure. Ascending admissible chains stabilize because \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) is
Noetherian; descending chains stabilize by
\Cref{without finite torsion implies artinian}.

On the type \(1/2\) category the functors
\[
E_0(X)=\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot} X),\qquad E_1(X)=\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(m_1X))
\]
are exact and detect zero objects. Indeed, \(X\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion, whereas \(m_1X\) is pure type \(-1/2\) and
therefore \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion. If either indicated cohomology
vanishes, the corresponding object is acyclic and thus zero by purity.
The vertex filtration computes
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &\operatorname{length}_W E_0&\operatorname{length}_W E_1\\ \hline
N_{m,n}&1&n-m\\
N'_{m,n}&n-m&1 .
\end{array}
\]
A distinguished vertex contributes \(k\) to \(E_0\) and becomes
acyclic after \(m_1\); an undistinguished vertex is initially
acyclic and contributes \(k\) to \(E_1\) after \(m_1\).
If an exact functor detects zero objects, an object whose image has
length one admits no nontrivial admissible short exact sequence.
Hence both families are weakly simple.

For exhaustiveness, let \(M\) be weakly simple.
Kernels and images of multiplication by \(p\), taken in \(G\),
are torsion subobjects of \(M\) with no maps from any \(U_1[j](-j)\),
hence are of type \(1/2\).
The resulting sequence is exact in \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) as well, since all its
objects belong to both hearts.
Multiplication by \(p\) cannot be injective on the nonzero finite
torsion module \(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot} M)\); its kernel is therefore nonzero.
Weak simplicity gives \(pM=0\).

The type filtration supplies a nonzero map \(M\to U_1[i](-i)\) for
some \(i\). It is surjective: a nonzero proper image would be a
\(U_j[i](-i)\) with \(j\leqslant0\), excluded as a quotient of a pure
type \(1/2\) object by the type filtration.
Write the kernel as \(N\).
We induct on the total domino number \(\sum_a T^{a,-a}(M)\). It is
finite and additive, and decreases on passing to \(N\).

If \(N\) is acyclic, the cohomology sequence in gauge degree \(i+1\)
gives \(\mathrm{H}^0(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{i+1})=0\): the corresponding groups for
\(N\) and \(U_1[i](-i)\) vanish, and \(M\in G\).
Consequently \(M(-\varphi_{\{i+1\}})\) is acyclic.
It is still indecomposable and killed by \(p\).
By \Cref{indecomposable Tot acyclic objects are M(I J)} and the
source-and-sink criterion, its decorated graph has a single
distinguished source and arrows pointing away from that source.
By \Cref{swap direction isomorphic}, we may move the distinguished
vertex to the right endpoint, giving \(M\simeq N_{m,n}\).

Otherwise \Cref{kernel reduction for weakly simple dominos} makes
\(N\) weakly simple of type \(1/2\); by induction it belongs to one of
the two families.
Put \(t=i+1\), the new vertex contributed by \(U_1[i](-i)\).

First suppose that \(N=N_{m,n}\).
If \(t\in[m,n]\), move the unique distinguished vertex to \(t\).
Modification by \(-\varphi_{\{t\}}\) then makes the kernel and
quotient acyclic, hence also \(M\).
The resulting indecomposable acyclic object has domino number two
at \(t\), contradicting the classification of indecomposable
acyclic objects killed by \(p\).
Thus \(t\notin[m,n]\).
Modification by \(-\varphi_{\{n,t\}}\) gives an indecomposable acyclic
object with vertex set \([m,n]\cup\{t\}\).
Its support must be an interval, so \(t=m-1\) or \(t=n+1\).

The source-and-sink criterion and local swaps put the decorated
graph in the form
\[
(a^*\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow c
 \longleftarrow\cdots\longleftarrow b^*),\qquad a<c<b.
\]
For a right-end extension, move the old distinguished vertex
leftwards to obtain this form; a left-end extension already has
this form.
If \(c-a\geqslant2\), move the left distinguished vertex to \(c-1\)
and the right one to \(c\). Cut the arrow \((c-1)^*\to c^*\).
The two interval pieces both have a unique distinguished source
and undistinguished sinks, and each has at least two vertices.
They are members of the first family up to local swaps.
Cutting this arrow gives a nontrivial admissible short exact sequence,
contradicting weak simplicity.
If \(b-c\geqslant2\), use the symmetric construction, moving the
stars to \(c,c+1\) and cutting \((c+1)^*\to c^*\).
Thus \(c-a=b-c=1\), and
\[
M\simeq(a^*\to a+1\leftarrow(a+2)^*)\simeq N'_{a,a+2}.
\]

Now suppose that \(N=N'_{m,n}\).
Local swaps move the unique undistinguished vertex to any
\(q\in[m,n]\).
If \(t\in[m,n]\), choose \(q\neq t\) and set
\(K=[m,n]\setminus\{q\}\).
Modification by \(-\varphi_K\) makes both \(N\) and \(U_1[i](-i)\)
acyclic. Again the resulting indecomposable acyclic object has
domino number two at \(t\), a contradiction.

For \(t\notin[m,n]\), take
\(K=\{m+1,\ldots,n\}\cup\{t\}\).
The same acyclic classification forces \(t=m-1\) or \(t=n+1\).
The new distinguished vertex cannot be a sink, so the two
possibilities are
\[
\begin{aligned}
M&=(m\leftarrow(m+1)^*\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow n^*
 \leftarrow(n+1)^*)=N'_{m,n+1},\\
M&=((m-1)^*\to m\leftarrow(m+1)^*\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow n^*)
 \simeq N'_{m-1,n}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last isomorphism is one local swap.
This completes the induction.
<!-- end proof-87 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
Zhang constructs a Harder--Narasimhan filtration on torsion diagonal
complexes whose restriction to diagonal dominos refines Ekedahl's
type filtration \cite[Theorems~3.9 and~3.12]{ZhangHN}.
For his diagonal slope \(\mu_\Delta\), the objects \(N_{m,n}\) and
\(N'_{m,n}\) are stable of slopes \(\frac{1}{n-m+1}\) and
\(\frac{n-m}{n-m+1}\), respectively
\cite[Theorem~4.22]{ZhangHN}. Equivalently, they are simple in their
respective abelian categories of semistable objects of fixed slope
\cite[Theorem~3.13]{ZhangHN}.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{virtual F crystal}
A virtual \(F\)-crystal is a triple \((U,F,N)\), where
\(K=\operatorname{Frac}(W)\), \(U\) is a finite-dimensional
\(K\)-vector space, \(F\) is a \(\sigma\)-linear automorphism of \(U\),
and \(N\subseteq U\) is a \(W\)-submodule satisfying \(KN=U\).
It is of finite type if \(N\) is finitely generated over
\(W\).

Let \(M\) be a torsion-free \(F\)-gauge such that
\(M^{-\infty}\otimes_WK\) is finite-dimensional. The relation
\(\widetilde{F}\widetilde{V}=p\) identifies every component after inverting \(p\); in
particular,
\[M^0\otimes_W K
\xrightarrow{\cong}
M^{\infty}\otimes_W K\]
and likewise at the negative end. Thus \(M\) determines a virtual
\(F\)-crystal with \(U=M^{-\infty}\otimes_WK\),
\(N=M^{-\infty}\), and Frobenius the composite
\[
M^{-\infty}\otimes_W K
\leftarrow 
M^{0}\otimes_W K
\rightarrow
M^{\infty}\otimes_W K\xrightarrow{\tau}M^{-\infty}\otimes_W K.
\]
Taking the colimit along \(\widetilde{V}\) gives canonical maps
\(M^i\to M^{-\infty}=\varinjlim_{j\to-\infty}M^j\hookrightarrow U\).
The first two arrows above identify \(M^{-\infty}\otimes_W K\) and
\(M^\infty\otimes_W K\) through \(M^0\otimes_W K\). Under this
identification, the image of \(M^i\) in \(M^\infty\otimes_W K\)
corresponds to \(p^{-i}M^i\subseteq U\).
The submodules \(M^i\subseteq U\) form a decreasing filtration satisfying:

{\rm (1)}
\(
pM^i\subseteq M^{i+1}.
\)

{\rm (2)}
\(
N=\bigcup_i M^i .
\)

{\rm (3)}
$F$ maps \(\bigcup_i p^{-i}M^i\)
bijectively to 
\(\bigcup_i M^i .\)

Conversely, a virtual \(F\)-crystal with a decreasing filtration
\(\{M^i\}\) satisfying (1)--(3) defines an \(F\)-gauge: \(\widetilde{V}\) is
inclusion, \(\widetilde{F}\) is multiplication by \(p\), and (3) supplies
\(\tau\). The virtual crystal is of finite type exactly when
\(M^{-\infty}=\bigcup_iM^i\) is finitely generated. Then
\(\bigcup_ip^{-i}M^i\) is also finitely generated, and the filtration
has finite level. Conversely, finite level and finite generation of one
component imply finite generation of every component and of the
virtual crystal.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- definition-37: body_md -->

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);

}(M,N)=\mathrm{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\,

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(N,M)=0\]

\label{Mazur--Ogus criterion}
For \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\), the following conditions are equivalent:

{\rm (1)} $M$ is Mazur--Ogus.

{\rm (2)} The spectral sequence
\[
E_1^{i,j}=\mathrm{H}^i(R_1\otimes^{\mathrm{L}}_{R}M)^j
\Longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^{i+j}(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
\]
degenerates at the \(E_1\)-page, \(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(M))=0\), and
\(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\) is torsion-free.

{\rm (3)} \(b_0(M)=\sum_i h^{\,i,-i}(M)\).
<!-- end proposition-37 -->
<!-- proof-88: body_md -->
(1) implies (2) by \Cref{Mazur-Ogus vanishing}. To compare (2) and
(3), we have
\[
\sum_i h^{i,-i}(M)
\leqslant\dim_k\mathrm{H}^0(k\otimes_W^{\mathrm{L}}\mathrm{Tot}(M)),
\]
The first inequality is an equality precisely when
\[\mathrm{H}^j\!(R_1\otimes^{\mathrm{L}}_{R}M)^i=E^{i,j}_1=
E^{i,j}_{\infty}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
b_0(M)\leqslant \dim_{k}(\mathrm{H}^0(k\otimes _W^{\mathrm{L}}\mathrm{Tot}(M))),
\]
with equality precisely when \(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\) and
\(\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\) are torsion-free. By \Cref{Basic Vanishing}, these
comparisons give the equivalence of (2) and (3).

Now assume (2). By \Cref{Hodge numbers in degree plus minus 1},
\[
\mathrm{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(U_0[i](-i),M)=\mathrm{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
}(M,U_0[i](-i))=0
\]
for every \(i\). By \Cref{Tot 0 or Tot 1 of diagonal domino}(1),
\(M\) has no nonzero \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion subobject or
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion quotient. Let \(N\) be \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic.
By \Cref{sub and quotient object of Tot-torsion objects}(2),
every quotient of \(N\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(0\)-torsion, and every
subobject of \(N\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-\(1\)-torsion. Thus the image of
any map \(N\to M\) or \(M\to N\) is zero. Both Hom groups in
the definition therefore vanish, proving (1).

The torsion subobject \(W^{1/2}(F^1M)\) of \(M\) also vanishes. Therefore
\(F^1M\) is \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic, \(G_M^2=M\), and \(G_M^1=F^1M\).

For (2), take a finite-type virtual \(F\)-crystal \(N\) and set
\(M=\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t}(\mathrm{Nyg}(N))\). The Nygaard gauge is coherent and
torsion-free, so \(M\) is torsion-free in \(

    {\,

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);

    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);

_g\). By (1), \(G^1M\) is
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic, and
\[
F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{-\infty}
=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M/G^1M)^{-\infty}=N.
\]
By the adjunction of \Cref{virtual F crystal}, the identity on the
virtual crystal \(N\) gives a retraction
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M/G^1M)\to\mathrm{Nyg}(N)=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\). Hence
\(0\to G^1M\to M\to M/G^1M\to0\) splits. But a
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic object lying in \(

For (3), let \(M\) be Mazur--Ogus and put
\(N=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)^{-\infty}\). The adjunction gives
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\to\mathrm{Nyg}(N)\). After applying
\(\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t}\), we obtain a morphism
\[
M\longrightarrow\mathrm{L}\widehat\mathrm{t}(\mathrm{Nyg}(N))
\]
whose totalization is an isomorphism. Thus its kernel and cokernel are
\(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. Source and target are Mazur--Ogus, so orthogonality
forces both to vanish. Applying \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}\) proves (3).

If \(M\in

  \end{tikzpicture}}}

    {\,

    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) is Mazur--Ogus, then the Hodge filtration on
\(\mathrm{Tot}(M)/p\) is induced by the images of the \(\mathrm{H}^0(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M))^i\).
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-90: body_md -->
Put \(N=\mathrm{H}^0(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M))\). By
\Cref{Mazur-Ogus object and the Hodge F-gauge structure of virtual F-crystal},
\(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(M)\simeq N[0]\), where \(N\) is torsion-free and
\(N^{-\infty}\cong\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\).
By \Cref{distinguished triangle of M(F V)}(3),
\[
t_{\geqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(M)
\simeq \operatorname{Cone}(\widetilde{F}:N^{i-1}\to N^i).
\]
Since \(\widetilde{V}\widetilde{F}=p\), the map \(\widetilde{F}\) is injective, so the zeroth
cohomology of this cone is \(N^i/\widetilde{F} N^{i-1}\).

At sufficiently negative gauge degrees, \(N^i=N^{-\infty}\)
and \(\widetilde{F}=p\); hence the same comparison identifies
\(\mathrm{Hod}(M)\) with \(N^{-\infty}/p\).
Naturality with respect to \(\widetilde{V}\) identifies the Hodge filtration
map with the map of cones induced by
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
N^{i-1} \arrow[r,"\widetilde{F}"] \arrow[d] &
N^i \arrow[d] \\
N^{-\infty} \arrow[r,"p"] &
N^{-\infty},
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where the vertical arrows are the canonical maps to the colimit
along \(\widetilde{V}\). Thus the induced map
\(N^i/\widetilde{F} N^{i-1}\to N^{-\infty}/p\) sends the class of \(x\)
to its canonical image modulo \(p\).
Its image is exactly the image of \(N^i\), as claimed.
<!-- end proof-90 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{equivalence between Mazur-Ogus objects and virtual F-gauge structures.}
The functors \(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(-)^{-\infty}\) and
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}(\mathrm{Nyg}(-))\) are inverse equivalences between the
category of Mazur--Ogus diagonal complexes and the category of
finite-type virtual \(F\)-crystals.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-91: body_md -->
Combine \Cref{Mazur-Ogus object and the Hodge F-gauge structure of virtual F-crystal} with the degree-zero case of \Cref{completed rmt and diagonal cohomology}.
<!-- end proof-91 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{completeness for t'(M)^i}
Let \(M\) be a coherent \(F\)-gauge of level \(\mathrm{I}\). Then
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)^i\) is complete, and hence separated, for the standard
topology for every \(i\).
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-92: body_md -->
By \Cref{resolution of coherent complexes}, choose a presentation
\(P^1\xrightarrow{d_1}P^0\to M\to0\) by finite sums of the
\(G_r\). By \Cref{Exactness after completion} and right exactness of
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}\), for every \(i\) we obtain an exact sequence
\[
\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat P^{\,1})^i
\xrightarrow{\;\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat d_1)^i\;}
\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat P^{\,0})^i
\longrightarrow\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)^i\longrightarrow0.
\]
By \Cref{description of t(G_r)} and
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}(\widehat G_r)\cong\widehat{\mathrm{t}(G_r)}\), the first
two terms are complete. Since the standard topology on the quotient
is the quotient topology, it remains to
prove that the first map has closed image.

In \(R\)-module degree \(-i\), this follows from Artin--Rees for
finite free \(\widehat R^{\,0}\)-modules with their \(V\)-adic
topology, or for finite free \(\widehat R^{\mathrm{top}}\)-modules
with their \(p\)-adic topology at the top. The \(V\)-adic case uses
the same Rees-module argument as \Cref{Exactness after completion}:
since \(V\) is regular and normal, its Rees ring is a skew polynomial
ring over the Noetherian ring \(\widehat R^{\,0}\).

The remaining component, in \(R\)-module degree \(-i+1\), is a map
\((\widehat R^{\,1})^{\oplus a}\to(\widehat R^{\,1})^{\oplus b}\)
given by right multiplication by a matrix over \(R^0\), since it
comes from the uncompleted presentation. Recall the normal form
\[
\widehat R^{\,1}
=\Bigl(\prod_{q>0}WdV^q\Bigr)
 \oplus\Bigl(\bigoplus_{q\geqslant0}WF^qd\Bigr)^{\wedge}_p.
\]
Let \(M^+\) be the sum of the \(a\) copies of the second summand,
and choose \(j\geqslant0\) bounding the powers of \(V\) in the matrix.
Then \(M^+\) maps into
\(\bigl((\bigoplus_{q\geqslant-j}WF^qd)^{\wedge}_p\bigr)^{\oplus b}\),
where \(F^{-q}d=dV^q\) for \(q>0\).
Both are finite free modules over \(W_\sigma\{F\}\), which is
Noetherian by \Cref{flatness of central completion}; their induced
standard topologies agree with the \(p\)-adic topologies. The
restriction is linear over this ring, so Artin--Rees shows that its
image is closed. The displayed normal form also shows that
the target of this restriction is closed in
\((\widehat R^{\,1})^{\oplus b}\), so the restricted image is closed
there as well.

After quotienting the source by \(M^+\), we obtain
\(\bigl(\prod_{q>0}WdV^q\bigr)^{\oplus a}\) with the product
\(p\)-adic topology. This is linearly compact, being an inverse
limit of discrete finite-length \(W\)-modules. The target modulo
the restricted image is Hausdorff, so the induced map has closed
image. Pulling back shows that the original image is closed,
proving the claim.
<!-- end proof-92 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{F_iN=d_iN}
Let \(N\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
_g\) be Mazur--Ogus. Then \(F_iN=d_iB\) for every \(i\).
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-93: body_md -->
We already have \(F_iN\subseteq d_iB\). For the reverse inclusion, it
suffices to show that
\(d_iB\to N/F_iN\) is zero. Put \(M=F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(N)\); by
\Cref{completed rmt and diagonal cohomology}, identify \(N\) with
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)\). For \(m_{-\infty}\in d_iB\), we must show that
\(\beta_j\otimes m_{-\infty}=0\) for \(j<i\). Since the filtration
\(d_\bullet B\) is decreasing, it suffices to take \(j=i-1\).

Choose \(m_{i-1}\in M^{i-1}\) and \(m_i\in M^i\) mapping to
\(m_{-\infty}\). The defining relations give
\[
\beta_{i-1}\otimes m_{-\infty}
=\beta_{i-1}\otimes m_{i-1}
=V(\beta_{i-1}\otimes m_i).
\]
Divisibility gives \(m'_{-\infty}\in d_iB\) with
\(Fm_{-\infty}=p^im'_{-\infty}\). Unwinding the Frobenius on the
associated virtual crystal gives
\(\tau\gamma_i^+(m_i)=m'_{-\infty}\), and the relations of
\(\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)\) therefore identify
\(\beta_{i-1}\otimes m_i\) with
\(\beta_{i-1}\otimes m'_{-\infty}\). Repeating the argument gives
\[
\beta_{i-1}\otimes m_{-\infty}
\in\bigcap_{\ell\geqslant0}V^\ell
\widehat\mathrm{t}(M)^{i,-i}=0,
\]
where the last equality follows from
\Cref{completeness for t'(M)^i}. Hence \(d_iB\subseteq F_iN\).
<!-- end proof-93 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{Structure of Mazur-Ogus object}
The category of Mazur--Ogus diagonal complexes is equivalent to the
category of tuples
\[
(M_1,M_2,N_1,N_2,\psi,\varphi,\rho)
\]
where \(M_1,M_2\) are torsion-free Hodge--Witt diagonal complexes;
\(N_1,N_2\) are diagonal dominos satisfying \(W^0N_1=0\) and
\(W^{1/2}N_2=N_2\); the maps
\(\psi:M_1\hookrightarrow M_2\) and
\(\varphi:N_1\hookrightarrow N_2\) have finite-torsion cokernels; and
\(
\rho:\operatorname{Coker}\psi
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Coker}\varphi
\)
is an isomorphism between these cokernels.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-94: body_md -->
Let \(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
_{\mathrm{MO}}\). In the notation of \Cref{definition of HW}, set
\[
M_1:={}_{\mathrm{HW}}(M),\qquad
M_2:=D({}_{\mathrm{HW}}(D(M))),\qquad
N_1:=\ker(M\to M_2),\qquad N_2:=M/M_1.
\]
Here \(M_2\) is the largest torsion-free Hodge--Witt quotient of
\(M\).

Let \(\psi:M_1\to M_2\) and \(\varphi:N_1\to N_2\) be the composites
through \(M\). Their cokernels are canonically identified:
\[
\operatorname{Coker}\psi
=
(M/N_1)/\operatorname{Im}M_1
=
M/(N_1+M_1)
=
(M/M_1)/\operatorname{Im}N_1
=
\operatorname{Coker}\varphi.
\]
Take this identification as \(\rho\).

Both \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) are torsion without finite-torsion
subobjects, hence diagonal dominos. Their intersection \(N_1\cap M_1\)
is both a diagonal domino and Hodge--Witt, so it vanishes. Since
\[
N_1\cap M_1
=
\operatorname{Ker}\psi
=
\operatorname{Ker}\varphi,
\]
both maps are monomorphisms. Their common cokernel is torsion as a
quotient of \(N_2\) and Hodge--Witt as a quotient of \(M_2\), hence
finite torsion.

Finally,
\[
W^0N_1=F^1N_1\subseteq F^1M=0,
\]
and
\[
0=M/G^2M
\twoheadrightarrow N_2/G^2N_2=
N_2/W^{1/2}N_2.
\]

Conversely, take a tuple as in the statement. Identify the two
cokernels via
\(\operatorname{Coker}\psi
\xrightarrow{\rho}
\operatorname{Coker}\varphi,\)
call the common object \(N'\), and let \(M\) be the pullback
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& {N_2} \\
	{M_2} & {N'}
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
where the arrows are the quotient maps followed by the chosen
identifications
\(N_2\twoheadrightarrow
\operatorname{Coker}\varphi
\stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow}
N',\)
and
\(M_2\twoheadrightarrow
\operatorname{Coker}\psi
\stackrel{\sim}{\longrightarrow}
N'.\)

Let \(A\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\) be \(\mathrm{Tot}\)-acyclic. To show that \(M\) is
Mazur--Ogus, we check both Hom groups using the pullback sequences
\[
0\to M_1\to M\to N_2\to0,
\qquad
0\to N_1\to M\to M_2\to0.
\]
We have \(\mathrm{Hom}(M_1,A)=0\) because \(M_1\) is Hodge--Witt, and
\(\mathrm{Hom}(N_2,A)=0\) because
\(W^{1/2}N_2=N_2\) while \(W^{1/2}A=0\). Hence
\(\mathrm{Hom}(M,A)=0\). Similarly, \(W^0A=A\), \(W^0N_1=0\), and the
Mazur--Ogus property of \(M_2\) give \(\mathrm{Hom}(A,M)=0\). Thus \(M\) is
Mazur--Ogus. The constructions are functorial and inverse.
<!-- end proof-94 -->

}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
_{\mathrm{MO}}\),
and if
\[
M=(M_1,M_2,N_1,N_2,\psi,\varphi,\rho),
\]
then
\[
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M)
=
\bigl(
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M_2),
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M_1),
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(N_2),
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(N_1),
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(\psi),
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(\varphi),
\widetilde{D}^{\,1}(\rho)^{-1}
\bigr).
\]

In particular, if
\(M\xrightarrow{\sim}\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M)\) is a perfect pairing then
\[v_p\!\left(\operatorname{disc}(\mathrm{Tot}(M_1))\right)=2\cdot\operatorname{length}
\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(N_2)),\]
where \(v_p(-)\) is the \(p\)-adic valuation on \(W\) with
\(v_p(p)=1\).
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-95: body_md -->
Since \(M\) has no nonzero finite-torsion subobject,
\Cref{finite torsion} gives \(D(M)=\widetilde D^{\,0}(M)\). By duality,
a nonzero map between \(D(M)\) and an acyclic object would yield a
nonzero map between \(M\) and the dual acyclic object, contrary to the
Mazur--Ogus condition. Thus
\(\widetilde D^{\,0}(M)\) is again Mazur--Ogus.

Under duality, \(\widetilde D^{\,0}(M_2)\) is the maximal Hodge--Witt
subobject of \(\widetilde D^{\,0}(M)\), and \(\widetilde D^{\,0}(M_1)\)
is its maximal Hodge--Witt quotient. This gives the stated tuple.

For the discriminant formula,
\[
v_p\!\left(\operatorname{disc}(\mathrm{Tot}(M_1))\right)
=
\operatorname{length}\,
\mathrm{Tot}\!\left(
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M_1)/M_1
\right),
\]
as
\[
\mathrm{Tot}\!\left(\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M_1)\right)
=
\operatorname{Hom}(\mathrm{Tot}(M_1),W).
\]

Now
\[
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M_1)=M_2,
\]
and
\[
M_2/M_1
=
N_2/N_1
=
N_2/\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(N_2),
\]
and so
\[
\operatorname{length}\,
\mathrm{Tot}\!\left(
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(M_1)/M_1
\right)
=
\operatorname{length}\,
\mathrm{Tot}(N_2)
-
\operatorname{length}\,
\mathrm{Tot}\!\left(
\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(N_2)
\right)
\]
\[
=
\operatorname{length}
\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(N_2))
+
\operatorname{length}
\mathrm{H}^1\!\left(
\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde{D}^{\,0}(N_2))
\right)
=
2\cdot
\operatorname{length}
\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(N_2)),
\]
where the final equality follows by duality.
<!-- end proof-95 -->

To check the asserted type of \(\check R_n\), it suffices to show that
\(dV^{n-1}:\check{R}_n^0\longrightarrow\check{R}_n^1\)
is injective and \(\dim_k\operatorname{ker} dV^{n-2}=1\).
Equivalently, by duality, \(dV^{n-1}:R_n^0\longrightarrow R_n^1\)
is surjective and
\(\dim_k\operatorname{coker} dV^{n-2}=1\).
The normal form of \(R_n\) gives both claims. This proves (1), and (2)
follows from (1), the degeneration criterion above, and duality. In
fact, \(\check R_n\) has types
\(n-1,n-3,\ldots,-(n-3),-(n-1)\).

<!-- proof-97: body_md -->
The Hodge--Witt objects \({}_{\mathrm{HW}}(M)\) and \(M_{\mathrm{HW}}\) satisfy the
degeneration criterion at every level. Thus
\Cref{level n Hodge--de Rham degenerate: first criterion} reduces the
two Hom vanishings to those for \({}_pM\) and \(M_p\).
By \Cref{type filtration on diagonal domino}, for any diagonal domino
\(N\),
\[
W^{1-n}(N)=0
\Longleftrightarrow
\mathrm{Hom}_{ 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\,

By \Cref{Mazur-Ogus vanishing}, an object \(M\in D_c^b(R)\) lies in
\(

\bigr)=\bigl(R_1\otimes^{\mathrm{L}}_R(-)\bigr)
