<!-- definition-39: body_md -->
\label{Mazur--Ogus in degree n}
An object \(M\in D_c^b(R)\) is Mazur--Ogus in degree \(n\) if
\[
b_n(M)=\sum_{i+j=n}h^{i,j}(M).
\]
It is Mazur--Ogus if this holds for every \(n\), equivalently if
\[
\sum_n b_n(M)=\sum_{i,j}h^{i,j}(M).
\]
Recall that the corresponding inequality holds degreewise.
<!-- end definition-39 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{properties of Mazur--Ogus in degree n}
The Mazur--Ogus condition in degree \(n\) has the following properties.

{\rm (1)} An object \(M\in D_c^b(R)\) is Mazur--Ogus in degree \(n\)
if and only if
\(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{n}(M)\) is Mazur--Ogus,
\(G^2\!\left(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{\,n-1}(M)\right)
=\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{n-1}(M),\) and \(F^1\!\left(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{n+1}(M)\right)=0.\)

{\rm (2)} If \(M\) is Mazur--Ogus in degree \(n\), then the Hodge
filtration on \(\mathrm{H}^n(\mathrm{Tot}(M))/p\) is the reduction modulo \(p\) of the
Nygaard filtration on
\((\mathrm{H}^n(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\otimes_WK,F,\mathrm{H}^n(\mathrm{Tot}(M)))\).

{\rm (3)} Under the same hypothesis, the filtrations on the virtual
\(F\)-crystals \(\mathrm{H}^n(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\otimes_WK\) and
\(\mathrm{H}^{n+1}(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\otimes_WK\) induced by
\[
\mathrm{H}^i(M)^j\Longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^{i+j}(\mathrm{Tot}(M))
\]
are the filtrations by the maximal subcrystals divisible by successive
powers of \(p\).

{\rm (4)} If \(M\in D_c^b(R)\) is Mazur--Ogus in degree \(n\), then
\[M \simeq \widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant n-1}M \oplus \widetilde{\tau}_{>n-1}M.\]
In particular, if \(M\) is Mazur--Ogus, then
\[M\simeq \bigoplus_n\widehat{\mathrm{t}}\!\left(
\mathrm{Nyg}\bigl(\mathrm{H}^n(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\otimes K \bigr)\right)[-n].\]

{\rm (5)} Suppose \(M\in D_c^b(R)\) is Mazur--Ogus in degree \(m\) but
not Hodge--Witt in degree \(m\). Suppose also that
\[
nb_m(M)
=
\sum_{i+j=m}
\operatorname{length}
\mathrm{H}^j\!\left(
R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M
\right)^i
\]
for some \(n\). Then
\[
2n-1
\leqslant
\max_i
m^{m+i,-i}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-100: body_md -->
For (1), \Cref{Totsubquo} gives
\(b_n(M)=b_0(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M))\) and
\(h^{i,n-i}(M)\geqslant h^{i,-i}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M))\).
Together with the Hodge--Betti inequality, this yields
\[
b_n(M)
\leqslant\sum_i h^{i,-i}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M))
\leqslant\sum_i h^{i,n-i}(M).
\]
If \(M\) is Mazur--Ogus in degree \(n\), equality holds throughout.
Thus \(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M)\) is Mazur--Ogus by
\Cref{Mazur--Ogus criterion}, and the Hodge-number inequalities are
equalities term by term.

To determine the neighboring diagonal cohomology objects, consider
the spectral sequence
\begin{equation}\label{Hodge and widetilde H spectral sequence}
    E_2^{i,j}=\mathrm{H}^i\!\left(
    R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{j}(M)
    \right)
    \Longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^{i+j}\!\left(
    R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M
    \right).
\end{equation}
Fix an \(R\)-module degree \(a\). By \Cref{Basic Vanishing}(2),
the spectral sequence is supported in the three columns
\(i=-a-1,-a,1-a\). Its only possible differentials are therefore
\(d_2\)'s from the first column to the third. In total degree
\(n-a\), the middle term \((E_2^{-a,n})^a\) survives automatically.
The only differentials that could affect the other two terms are
\[
\begin{aligned}
(E_2^{-1-a,n})^a&\xrightarrow{\ d_2\ }(E_2^{1-a,n-1})^a,\\
(E_2^{-1-a,n+1})^a&\xrightarrow{\ d_2\ }(E_2^{1-a,n})^a.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M)\) is Mazur--Ogus,
the source of the first and the target of the second vanish by
\Cref{Mazur-Ogus vanishing}. Thus all three terms survive to
\(E_\infty\). Taking dimensions in the resulting filtration of
\(\mathrm{H}^{n-a}(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^a\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
h^{a,n-a}(M)
={}&h^{a,1-a}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^{n-1}(M))
  +h^{a,-a}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M))\\
 &+h^{a,-1-a}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^{n+1}(M)).
\end{aligned}
\]
By the termwise equality above, the middle summand equals the
left-hand side. The other two summands therefore vanish for every
\(a\); equivalently,
\[
h^{i,j}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^{n-1}(M))=0\quad(i+j=1),
\qquad
h^{i,j}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^{n+1}(M))=0\quad(i+j=-1).
\]
By \Cref{Tot 0 or Tot 1 of diagonal domino,Hodge numbers in degree plus minus 1},
these vanishings are equivalent to
\(G^2(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^{n-1}(M))=\widetilde\mathrm{H}^{n-1}(M)\) and
\(F^1(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^{n+1}(M))=0\), respectively.

Conversely, the stated conditions eliminate both neighboring
contributions. The spectral sequence therefore identifies
\(h^{i,n-i}(M)\) with \(h^{i,-i}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M))\) for every \(i\).
Since \(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M)\) is Mazur--Ogus,
\[
b_n(M)=b_0(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M))
=\sum_i h^{i,-i}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M))
=\sum_{i+j=n}h^{i,j}(M).
\]

For (2), \(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M)\) is Mazur--Ogus by (1). By
\Cref{equivalence between Mazur-Ogus objects and virtual F-gauge structures.,Hodge filtration from the Nygaard gauge},
its Hodge filtration is the reduction modulo \(p\) of its Nygaard
filtration. Part (1) identifies
\(\mathrm{H}^n(\mathrm{Tot}(M))\otimes_WK\) with
\(\mathrm{H}^0(\mathrm{Tot}(\widetilde\mathrm{H}^n(M)))\otimes_WK\) as filtered virtual
\(F\)-crystals. The canonical maps
\(\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant n}(M)\longrightarrow M\)
and \(\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant n}(M)
\longrightarrow \widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{n}(M)[-n]\)
also induce isomorphisms on
\(\mathrm{H}^i(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}(-))^j\) for \(i+j=n\).
These identifications give the same comparison of filtrations on
\(\mathrm{H}^n(\mathrm{Tot}(M))/p\), proving (2).

For (3), the argument of \Cref{Totsubquo} reduces us to \(n=0\) and
\(M\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\); by (1), \(F^1M=0\). The inclusion
\(F^2M\hookrightarrow M\) is an isomorphism on zeroth total
cohomology. Functoriality therefore reduces the claim to \(F^2M\),
which is Mazur--Ogus; now apply \Cref{F_iN=d_iN}.

For (4), the obstruction to the decomposition lies in
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{D(R)}
\bigl(\widetilde{\tau}_{>n-1}M,\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant n-1}M\bigr).\]
We show that this group vanishes. Indeed,
\[
R\!\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(-,-)^0
=
R\!\operatorname{Hom}_{R}
\bigl(
W,
R\!\operatorname{Hom}^{!}_{R}(-,-)
\bigr)^0
=
\bigl(
R\!\operatorname{Hom}^{!}_{R}(-,-)^F
\bigr)^0.
\]

By dévissage, the functor \(((-)^F)^0\) has \( 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
\)-amplitude \([0,1]\).
It therefore suffices to show that
\[
R\!\operatorname{Hom}^{!}_{R}
\bigl(\widetilde{\tau}_{>n-1}M,
\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant n-1}M
\bigr)\]
has \(\widetilde D_g\)-amplitude \((-\infty,-1]\). By (1) and
\Cref{Basic Vanishing}(2),
\((R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widetilde\tau_{>n-1}M)^j\) has amplitude
\([n+j,\infty)\), and its totalization has amplitude
\([n,\infty)\). Likewise,
\((R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widetilde\tau_{\leqslant n-1}M)^j\) has
amplitude \((-\infty,n-1+j]\), and its totalization has amplitude
\((-\infty,n-1]\). The criterion
\Cref{criteria for G-amplitude [m n]} now gives the required vanishing.

For (5), the same reduction to \(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{m}(M)\) gives
\[
nb_0(\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{m}(M))
=
\sum_i
\operatorname{length}\mathrm{H}^i\!\left(
R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{m}(M)
\right)^{-i},
\]
so the hypotheses of \Cref{Maximal n that Hodge--de Rham degenerate}
are satisfied. That corollary gives the desired bound.
<!-- end proof-100 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{three supergeneral examples}
    Let \(A\) be an abelian threefold over \(k\), and let \(D_{0,2}\) denote the domino
    \[\mathrm{H}^2(A,WO_A)/V^{-\infty}Z_2^{0,2}\longrightarrow F^{\infty}B_2^{1,2}(\mathrm{H}^2(A,W\Omega^1_{A/k}))\]

    Suppose \(\mathrm{H}^1_{\mathrm{cris}}(A/W)\simeq W_{\sigma}[F,V]/(P)\).
    In each case below, there is a short exact sequence
    \[
    0\longrightarrow U_3\oplus U_s\longrightarrow D_{0,2}
    \longrightarrow U_2\longrightarrow 0.
    \]
    The last column records the types of the elementary dominos in this extension:
    \[
    \begin{array}{c|l|c|c}
    \text{case} & P & s & \text{types in the extension}\\ \hline
    (1) & F^3+V^3 & 4 & \{2,3,4\}\\
    (2) & F^3+pF+V^3 & 7 & \{2,3,7\}\\
    (3) & F^3+pF+pV+V^3 & 6 & \{2,3,6\}.
    \end{array}
    \]
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- proof-101: body_md -->
In each case put \(M=\mathrm{H}^1_{\mathrm{cris}}(A/W)\), and let \(v\) be its cyclic generator.
We carry out the calculation in three stages: determine the maximal
stable lattice, identify the two layers killed by \(p\) in the quotient
gauge, and compare the resulting domino with the geometric one.

For the common Frobenius calculation, put
\[
 (\alpha,\beta)=(0,0),\ (1,0),\ (1,1),
 \qquad
 F^3v+p\alpha Fv+p\beta Vv+V^3v=0.
\]
Choose the basis
\[
 e_0=v,\quad e_1=Fv,\quad e_2=F^2v,\quad
 e_3=-V^3v,\quad e_4=-V^2v,\quad e_5=-Vv.
\]
The corresponding \(\sigma\)-linear Frobenius is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Fe_0&=e_1,& Fe_1&=e_2,&
 Fe_2&=e_3-p\alpha e_1+p\beta e_5,\\
 Fe_3&=pe_4,& Fe_4&=pe_5,& Fe_5&=-pe_0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The negative sign in the last formula follows from
\(e_5=-Vv\) and \(FV=p\).
Set \(E=\bigwedge^2M\), \(b_{ij}=e_i\wedge e_j\), and
\(T=F_E/p\), where \(F_E=\bigwedge^2F\). Its action on the fifteen
basis vectors is
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-uniform-T}
 \begin{aligned}
 Tb_{01}&=p^{-1}b_{12},&
 Tb_{02}&=p^{-1}b_{13}+\beta b_{15},\\
 Tb_{03}&=b_{14},& Tb_{04}&=b_{15},\\
 Tb_{05}&=b_{01},&
 Tb_{12}&=p^{-1}b_{23}+\alpha b_{12}+\beta b_{25},\\
 Tb_{13}&=b_{24},& Tb_{14}&=b_{25},\\
 Tb_{15}&=b_{02},&
 Tb_{23}&=b_{34}-p\alpha b_{14}-p\beta b_{45},\\
 Tb_{24}&=b_{35}-p\alpha b_{15},&
 Tb_{25}&=b_{03}-p\alpha b_{01}+p\beta b_{05},\\
 Tb_{34}&=pb_{45},& Tb_{35}&=pb_{04},\\
 Tb_{45}&=pb_{05}.&&
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The maximal \(T\)-stable lattice can be described by congruences on
the coefficients. These congruences arise by requiring successive
iterates to remain integral. For \(x=\sum_{i<j}x_{ij}b_{ij}\in E\),
define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \ell_4(x)&=x_{45}+\beta x_{25}-\alpha x_{14},&
 \ell_5(x)&=\beta x_{14}-\alpha x_{03},\\
 \ell_6(x)&=\beta x_{03}-\alpha x_{25},&
 \ell_7(x)&=\beta x_{25}-\alpha x_{14}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
We claim that the maximal \(W\)-submodule \(\Lambda\subseteq E\)
such that \(T\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda\) is given by
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-lattice-congruences}
 \begin{gathered}
 x_{01}\in p^2W,\qquad
 x_{02},x_{04},x_{12},x_{15}\in pW,\\
 x_{05}-p\alpha x_{25}\in p^2W,\qquad
 \ell_4(x),\ell_5(x),\ell_6(x),\ell_7(x)\in pW.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
These conditions contain \(p^2E\), so they define a full lattice.

For maximality, let \(K\subseteq E\) be \(T\)-stable and take
\(x\in K\). Integrality of \(Tx\) first gives
\(x_{01},x_{02},x_{12}\in pW\). Applying these conditions to \(Tx\)
gives \(x_{01}\in p^2W\) and \(x_{05},x_{15}\in pW\).
Applying the latter conditions once more gives
\(x_{04}\in pW\) and \(x_{05}-p\alpha x_{25}\in p^2W\).
Successively applying the resulting conditions to \(Tx\) gives
\(\ell_4(x)\in pW\), then \(\ell_5(x)\in pW\), then
\(\ell_6(x)\in pW\), and finally \(\ell_7(x)\in pW\).
Thus \(K\subseteq\Lambda\).

The following coordinate identities verify these implications and
also prove stability. Let \(y\) be the coefficient
vector defined by \((Tx)_{ij}=\sigma(y_{ij})\); thus \(y\) is obtained
by applying the matrix in \eqref{supergeneral-uniform-T} to the
coefficient vector of \(x\). The coordinates needed for the first
conditions are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 y_{01}&=x_{05}-p\alpha x_{25},&y_{02}&=x_{15},\\
 y_{12}&=p^{-1}x_{01}+\alpha x_{12},&y_{13}&=p^{-1}x_{02},\\
 y_{23}&=p^{-1}x_{12},&y_{04}&=px_{35},\\
 y_{15}&=\beta x_{02}+x_{04}-p\alpha x_{24}.&&
 \end{aligned}
\]
The remaining identities are
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-lattice-stability-identities}
 \begin{aligned}
 y_{05}-p\alpha y_{25}
   &=p\ell_4(x)-p\alpha\beta x_{12},\\
 \ell_4(y)
   &=\ell_5(x)+\beta^2x_{12}
       +p\bigl((\alpha^2-\beta)x_{23}+x_{34}\bigr),\\
 \ell_5(y)&=\ell_6(x)-p\alpha\beta x_{23},\\
 \ell_6(y)&=\ell_7(x)-\alpha\beta x_{12},\\
 \ell_7(y)&=\ell_5(x)+\beta^2x_{12}+p\alpha^2x_{23}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Since \(\sigma\) fixes \(p,\alpha,\beta\) and preserves every ideal
\(p^aW\), the displayed divisibility conditions hold for \(Tx\)
if and only if they hold for \(y\). The identities show that
\eqref{supergeneral-lattice-congruences} is preserved by \(T\).
Consequently \(T\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda\), proving the claim.
This argument uses no division by \(2\), and applies also when
\(p=2\).

Specializing the congruences gives a basis in each case. This makes
the differences between the three lattices explicit and prepares the
quotient calculation. Angle brackets denote the \(W\)-span of the
listed vectors; each list has fifteen elements. In the first case,
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-lattice-first}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Lambda_{(1)}=\langle{}
 &p^2b_{01},p^2b_{05},\\
 &pb_{02},pb_{04},pb_{12},pb_{15},pb_{45},\\
 &b_{03},b_{13},b_{14},b_{23},b_{24},b_{25},b_{34},b_{35}
 \rangle_W.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In the second case, the additional congruences require three more
basis vectors to be divisible by \(p\):
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-lattice-second}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Lambda_{(2)}=\langle{}
 &p^2b_{01},p^2b_{05},\\
 &pb_{02},pb_{03},pb_{04},pb_{12},pb_{14},pb_{15},pb_{25},pb_{45},\\
 &b_{13},b_{23},b_{24},b_{34},b_{35}
 \rangle_W.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In the third case, the congruences couple three coefficients rather
than forcing them separately to vanish modulo \(p\). To express the
resulting basis, put
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-fixed-gstar}
 g_*:=b_{25}+b_{03}+b_{14}+pb_{05}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-lattice-third}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Lambda_{(3)}=\langle{}
 &p^2b_{01},p^2b_{05},\\
 &pb_{02},pb_{03},pb_{04},pb_{12},pb_{14},pb_{15},pb_{45},\\
 &b_{13},b_{23},b_{24},b_{34},b_{35},g_*
 \rangle_W.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the last four congruences in this case reduce to
\(x_{03}\equiv x_{14}\equiv x_{25}\pmod p\) and
\(x_{45}\equiv0\pmod p\). Subtracting \(x_{25}g_*\) gives exactly
the remaining divisibilities in the displayed basis.
Moreover, \eqref{supergeneral-uniform-T} gives \(Tg_*=g_*\).

The matrix of \(F\) on \(M\) has determinant \(p^3\), and hence
the matrix of \(T\) on \(E\) has determinant
\((p^3)^5/p^{15}=1\). The integral matrix of \(T\) on each
\(\Lambda_{(i)}\) therefore has unit determinant. Thus \(T\) is
bijective on all three lattices. Over algebraically closed \(k\),
Frobenius descent for this slope-zero crystal gives
\[
 \Lambda_{(i)}=W\cdot\Lambda_{(i)}^{T=1}
             =W\cdot E^{F_E=p}.
\]
For the last equality, any element of \(E^{F_E=p}\) spans a
\(T\)-stable \(W\)-submodule of \(E\), and hence belongs to the
maximal lattice.

For the quotient gauge, we also need the first Nygaard step. Write
\(E^1=\mathrm{Fil}_N^1(E)=E\cap F_E^{-1}(pE)\). Its basis is
obtained from the \(b_{ij}\)'s by replacing
\(b_{01},b_{02},b_{12}\) with \(pb_{01},pb_{02},pb_{12}\).
The preceding bases give the following elementary divisors:
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c}
  i&E/\Lambda_{(i)}&E^1/\Lambda_{(i)}\\ \hline
  1&(W/p^2W)^2\oplus k^5&W/p^2W\oplus k^4\\
  2&(W/p^2W)^2\oplus k^8&W/p^2W\oplus k^7\\
  3&(W/p^2W)^2\oplus k^7&W/p^2W\oplus k^6
 \end{array}
\]

The elementary divisors determine the sizes of the quotient modules,
but the gauge arrows are needed to identify their domino factors.
We therefore describe the quotient \(F\)-gauge before separating its
two \(p\)-layers. Write $E^q=\mathrm{Fil}_N^qE$. The Frobenius formulas above give
\[
\begin{aligned}
E^0&=E,\\
E^1&=\langle pb_{01},pb_{02},pb_{12},\ b_{ij}\ (0\leq i<j\leq5,\ j\geq3)\rangle_W,\\
E^2&=\langle p^2b_{01},p^2b_{02},p^2b_{12},\
pb_{ij}\ (0\leq i\leq2<j\leq5),\ b_{34},b_{35},b_{45}\rangle_W.
\end{aligned}
\]
Let $\mathcal G$ be the gauge of level $[0,2]$ with pieces $E^q$,
with $\widetilde{F}$ given by multiplication by $p$, $\widetilde{V}$ by inclusion, and
$\tau=F_E/p^2:E^2\xrightarrow{\sim}E^0$.
For the corresponding maximal lattice $\Lambda$, the subgauge
\[
\mathcal H=(\Lambda,\Lambda,p\Lambda)\subset\mathcal G
\]
is the extension to level $[0,2]$ of a gauge of level $[1,2]$.
Indeed, it is the gauge of the Dieudonn\'e module
$D_\Lambda=(\Lambda,F_D=T,V_D=pT^{-1})$ placed in bidegree $(1,-1)$.
In particular, $V_D$ is topologically nilpotent.
Put $Q=\mathcal G/\mathcal H$, so that
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-quotient-gauge}
Q^0=E/\Lambda,\qquad Q^1=E^1/\Lambda,\qquad Q^2=E^2/p\Lambda.
\end{equation}
The map $\tau$ identifies the last piece with the first semilinearly.
Recording degree $2$ through this identification, the four arrows are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde{F}_0:Q^0\longrightarrow Q^1,&\qquad x\longmapsto px,\\
\widetilde{V}_1:Q^1\longrightarrow Q^0,&\qquad x\longmapsto x,\\
\tau\circ\widetilde{F}_1:Q^1\longrightarrow Q^0,&\qquad x\longmapsto Tx,\\
\widetilde{V}_2\circ\tau^{-1}:Q^0\longrightarrow Q^1,&\qquad x\longmapsto pT^{-1}x.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, $Q^1$ is a submodule of $Q^0$. In this description,
$T$ is a partial operator on $Q^0$ with domain $Q^1$. Keeping track
of this domain will determine where the chains in the calculation
below terminate.

The displayed lattice bases show that $p^2Q=0$. Define
$K=Q[p]=\ker(p:Q\to Q)$ and $P=pQ$. There is a short exact sequence
of \(F\)-gauges
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-p-layers}
0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow Q\xrightarrow{p}P\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
On both $K$ and $P$, the arrows $x\mapsto px$ and
$x\mapsto pT^{-1}x$ from degree $0$ to degree $1$ vanish.
For the second assertion, if $px\in\Lambda$, then
$pT^{-1}x=T^{-1}(px)\in\Lambda$, since $T^{-1}\Lambda=\Lambda$.
This applies to $K$, and also to $P$ because $p^2Q=0$.
Thus each layer is described by two $k$-vector spaces $C\subset B$
and the two maps
\[
\iota:C\hookrightarrow B,\qquad T:C\longrightarrow B,
\]
where $\iota$ is linear and $T$ is $\sigma$-linear. Degree $2$ is
recovered from $B$ using $\tau$.

For $s\geq1$, a direct application of \Cref{definition of FG} to $U_s$
shows that $F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(U_s)$ is quasi-isomorphic to the gauge
$U_s:=\mathrm{H}^0(F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(U_s))$ placed in complex degree $0$.
This gauge has the following model:
\[
B_s=\langle u_0,\ldots,u_{s-1}\rangle_k,\qquad
C_s=\langle u_1,\ldots,u_{s-1}\rangle_k\subset B_s,\qquad
Tu_\ell=u_{\ell-1}\quad(1\leq\ell<s).
\]
Thus a chain of $s$ vertices gives the gauge of $U_s$ when its
nonterminal vertices form a basis of the middle space. The terminal
vertex lies outside the domain of the partial operator. In particular,
the index of the domino counts all vertices, including the terminal
one.

For the calculations below, introduce the following classes in $Q^0$:
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-quotient-basis-notation}
\begin{aligned}
a&=\overline{pb_{01}},&b&=\overline{b_{02}},&c&=\overline{b_{03}},&
d&=\overline{b_{04}},&e&=\overline{pb_{05}},\\
f&=\overline{b_{12}},&g&=\overline{b_{14}},&h&=\overline{b_{15}},&
i&=\overline{b_{25}},&j&=\overline{b_{45}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The letter $g$ here denotes a quotient class, not the lattice
generator $g_*$ used in the third case above.
In every case,
\[
P^0=\langle a,e\rangle_k,\qquad
P^1=\langle e\rangle_k\subset P^0,\qquad Te=a.
\]
Consequently the quotient in \eqref{supergeneral-p-layers} is
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-p-image-U2}
P\cong U_2.
\end{equation}

The image of multiplication by \(p\) is therefore the same in all
three cases. The differences lie in the \(p\)-kernels, which we
describe by choosing bases adapted to the partial operator.
In each case put $B=K^0$ and regard $C=K^1$ as a subspace of $B$.
All spans in the remainder of this step are over $k$.

In case (1), \(c=g=i=0\), and
\[
B=\langle a,b,d,e,f,h,j\rangle_k,\qquad
C=\langle a,d,e,h,j\rangle_k.
\]
The complete table on $C$ is
\[
Ta=f,\qquad Td=h,\qquad Te=a,\qquad Th=b,\qquad Tj=e.
\]
It gives the two chains
\[
j\xrightarrow{T}e\xrightarrow{T}a\xrightarrow{T}f,
\qquad
d\xrightarrow{T}h\xrightarrow{T}b.
\]
The two chains already supply the required bases: their vertices
form a basis of $B$, and their nonterminal vertices form a basis of
$C$. Hence
\[
K\cong U_4\oplus U_3.
\]

In case (2), all ten classes in
\eqref{supergeneral-quotient-basis-notation} form
a basis of $B$, and
\[
C=\langle a,c,d,e,g,h,i,j\rangle_k.
\]
The complete table is
\[
\begin{aligned}
Ta&=f,&Tc&=g,&Td&=h,&Te&=a,\\
Tg&=i,&Th&=b,&Ti&=c-a,&Tj&=e.
\end{aligned}
\]
The chain $d\mapsto h\mapsto b$ again gives a summand $U_3$.
On the complementary seven-dimensional space, the displayed table
does not yet have chain form. The following change of basis puts it
in that form:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
\ell&6&5&4&3&2&1&0\\ \hline
x_\ell&g+j&i+e&c&g&i&c-a&g-f.
\end{array}
\]
These satisfy $Tx_\ell=x_{\ell-1}$ for $1\leq\ell\leq6$;
in particular, $T(i+e)=(c-a)+a=c$.
The change of basis is invertible, with inverse
\[
\begin{aligned}
g&=x_3,&i&=x_2,&c&=x_4,\\
a&=x_4-x_1,&e&=x_5-x_2,&j&=x_6-x_3,&f&=x_3-x_0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $x_1,\ldots,x_6,d,h$ form a basis of $C$, while adjoining
$x_0,b$ gives a basis of $B$. The two terminal classes modulo $C$
are $-f,b$. Therefore
\[
K\cong U_7\oplus U_3.
\]

In case (3), the lattice generator \(g_*\) gives the relation
\(i=-c-g-e\).
Consequently
\[
B=\langle a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h,j\rangle_k,\qquad
C=\langle a,c,d,e,g,h,j\rangle_k.
\]
The table on $C$ is
\[
\begin{aligned}
Ta&=f,&Tc&=g,&Td&=h,&Te&=a,\\
Tg&=-c-g-e,&Th&=b,&Tj&=e.
\end{aligned}
\]
The chain $d\mapsto h\mapsto b$ still gives $U_3$. The relation
from the lattice leaves a six-dimensional complement, for which we
choose the basis
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
\ell&5&4&3&2&1&0\\ \hline
y_\ell&c+g+j&-c&-g&c+g+e&-c-e+a&-g-a+f.
\end{array}
\]
Then $Ty_\ell=y_{\ell-1}$ for $1\leq\ell\leq5$.
For example, $T(c+g+j)=g+(-c-g-e)+e=-c$.
The inverse change of basis is
\[
\begin{aligned}
c&=-y_4,&g&=-y_3,&e&=y_2+y_4+y_3,\\
a&=y_1+y_2+y_3,&j&=y_5+y_4+y_3,&f&=y_0+y_1+y_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, $y_1,\ldots,y_5,d,h$ form a basis of $C$, and the
two terminal classes modulo $C$ are $f,b$. Hence
\[
K\cong U_6\oplus U_3.
\]
Each change of basis, as well as its inverse, has integral
coefficients fixed by $\sigma$. The chain descriptions therefore
respect the semilinear maps and remain valid in every characteristic,
including $p=2$.

The two layers are now identified, so we can pass from the gauge
calculation to an extension of dominos.
Write \(s=4,7,6\) in cases (1), (2), (3), respectively. By
\Cref{Ekedahl's equivalence theorem}, the preceding calculations give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}(K)&\simeq U_3\oplus U_s,\\
\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}(P)&\simeq U_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Set \(D=\widehat{(\mathrm{L}\mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{Tot}}}(Q)\). Applying the same functor
to \eqref{supergeneral-p-layers} gives a distinguished triangle
\[
U_3\oplus U_s\longrightarrow D\longrightarrow U_2
\longrightarrow (U_3\oplus U_s)[1].
\]
Both end terms are graded $R$-modules concentrated in complex
degree $0$. Taking cohomology for the usual $t$-structure on $D(R)$
therefore shows that \(D\) is represented by a graded
$R$-module, with an exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{supergeneral-domino-extension}
0\longrightarrow U_3\oplus U_s\longrightarrow D
\longrightarrow U_2\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Dominos are closed under extensions, so $D$ is a domino. The passage
to this exact sequence uses the distinguished triangle and the
concentration of its two computed end terms in degree zero. No
general preservation of $p$-kernels by the completed inverse functor
is required.

It remains to identify $D$ with the geometric domino $D_{0,2}$.
This comparison is where the Mazur--Ogus results connect the lattice
calculation to the de Rham--Witt complex.
Let $C_A=R\Gamma(A,W\Omega^\bullet_{A/k})$ and
$X=\widetilde{\mathrm{H}}^{2}(C_A)\in 
  \mathrel{\mathchoice
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}              
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.16, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}           
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.11, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}             
    {\, 
  \mathrel{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\hbox{ 
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.08, line width=0.6pt]
    \draw (0,0) -- (2,0) -- (1.2,1.75) -- (0.8,1.75) -- cycle;
    \draw (1.6,0)-- (0.8,1.75);
  \end{tikzpicture}}} 
}}                   
  } 
$; this notation places the diagonal
cohomology object in the diagonal heart, with no additional shift.
The usual cohomology formulas for an abelian variety give torsion-free
crystalline cohomology and equality of the Betti number with the sum
of Hodge numbers in each total degree. In degree $2$, this is
\[
\operatorname{rank}_W\mathrm{H}^2_{\mathrm{cris}}(A/W)=15
=h^{0,2}+h^{1,1}+h^{2,0}=3+9+3,
\qquad \mathrm{H}^2_{\mathrm{cris}}(A/W)\cong\wedge^2M=E.
\]
Thus $C_A$ is Mazur--Ogus in every degree. By
\Cref{properties of Mazur--Ogus in degree n,Totsubquo,Mazur-Ogus object and the Hodge F-gauge structure of virtual F-crystal},
$X$ is Mazur--Ogus and its \(F\)-gauge is the Nygaard gauge
$F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(X)\cong\mathcal G$ of $E$.
Let $H$ be $D_\Lambda$ placed in bidegree $(1,-1)$, so that
$F\mathsf{G}^{\mathrm{Tot}}(H)\cong\mathcal H$. Applying the completed inverse functor to
$0\to\mathcal H\to\mathcal G\to Q\to0$ gives
\[
H\longrightarrow X\longrightarrow D\longrightarrow H[1].
\]
Since $H$ has usual cohomology only in degree $-1$, this triangle
identifies $\mathrm{H}^0(X)$ with $D$.

On the other hand, the commuting $t$-structures of
\Cref{diagonal t-structure} identify
\[
\mathrm{H}^0(X)\cong
\frac{\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant0}\mathrm{H}^2(C_A)}{\widetilde{\tau}_{\leqslant-1}\mathrm{H}^2(C_A)}.
\]
The denominator is zero because $\mathrm{H}^2(C_A)$ is concentrated in
nonnegative $R$-degrees. The numerator is the graded $R$-module
\[
\mathrm{H}^2(A,WO_A)\longrightarrow
F^\infty B_2^{1,2}\bigl(\mathrm{H}^2(A,W\Omega^1_{A/k})\bigr).
\]
The identification with $D$ shows that this graded module is a
domino. Its degree-zero term therefore has zero
$V^{-\infty}Z_2^{0,2}$ part, so forming its associated domino leaves it
unchanged. It is consequently $D_{0,2}$ as defined in the example.
Substituting $s=4,7,6$ in \eqref{supergeneral-domino-extension}
proves the three asserted exact sequences.
<!-- end proof-101 -->
<!-- proposition-40: body_md -->
\label{Ek2I.1.1}
    Let \(A\) be a thick subcategory of ungraded \(W\)-modules,
    stable under \(\sigma_*\), and let \(M\in D(R)\).

    {\rm (1)} Suppose that \(M\) is bounded to the left or bounded above.
    If, for some \(r,s\in\mathbb{Z}\), one has
    \(\mathrm{H}^j(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^i\in A\) for every
    \[\begin{aligned}
        (i,j)\in \;\;&\bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\big| i+j=r,\;\text{and}\;j\geqslant s\bigr\}\\
        \cup &\bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\big|i+j=r+1,\;\text{and}\;j\geqslant s+1\bigr\}\\
        \cup &\bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\big|i+j=r-1,\;\text{and}\;j\geqslant s\bigr\},
    \end{aligned}\]
    then \(\mathrm{H}^j(R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^i\in A\) for every
    \(n\geqslant1\) whenever \(i+j=r\) and \(j\geqslant s\).

    {\rm (2)} Suppose that \(M\) is bounded to the right or bounded below.
    If, for some \(r,s\in\mathbb{Z}\), one has
    \(\mathrm{H}^j(R_1\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^i\in A\) for every
    \[\begin{aligned}
        (i,j)\in\;\; &\bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\big| i+j=r,\;\text{and}\; j\leqslant s\bigr\}\\
        \cup&\bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\big|i+j=r+1,\;\text{and}\;j\leqslant s\bigr\}\\
        \cup&\bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\big|i+j=r-1,\;\text{and}\;j\leqslant s-1\bigr\},
    \end{aligned}\]
    then \(\mathrm{H}^j(R_n\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^i\in A\) for every
    \(n\geqslant1\) whenever \(i+j=r\) and \(j\leqslant s\).
<!-- end proposition-40 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{Ek2I.1.1.1}
    Let \(M\in D(R)\). If \(R_1^{i,j}=0\), then
    \[B_1^{i+1,j}\leqq Z_1^{i,j+1}, \quad B_1^{i,j+1}\leqq Z_1^{i,j+1},\quad Z_1^{i,j}\leqq B_1^{i,j},\quad Z_1^{i,j} \leqq B_1^{i+1,j-1}.\]
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-102: body_md -->
The exact sequences of graded right \(R\)-modules
    \[\begin{aligned}
        &0\rightarrow Z_1\rightarrow R_1\rightarrow B_1(1)\rightarrow 0,\\
        0&\rightarrow \sigma_*(B_1)\rightarrow \sigma_*(Z_1)\rightarrow R_1\rightarrow 0,
    \end{aligned}\]
    induce the long exact sequences \[\begin{aligned}...\rightarrow B_1^{i+1,j-1}\rightarrow Z_1^{i,j}\rightarrow &R_1^{i,j}\rightarrow B_1^{i+1,j}\rightarrow Z_1^{i,j+1}\rightarrow...\\
    ...\rightarrow \sigma_*(B_1^{i,j})\rightarrow \sigma_*(Z_1^{i,j})\rightarrow &R_1^{i,j} \rightarrow \sigma_*(B_1^{i,j+1})\rightarrow \sigma_*(Z_1^{i,j+1}) \rightarrow  ...\end{aligned}\]
    The assertions follow by setting \(R_1^{i,j}=0\) and removing
    the Frobenius twists in the second sequence.
<!-- end proof-102 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{Ek2I.1.1.2}
    Let \(M\in D(R)\). 

    {\rm (1)} If \(M\) is bounded to the left or bounded above and \(R_1^{i,j}=0\) for all \[(i,j)\in \Bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\Big|i+j=r\; \text{or}\;\; r-1, \;\text{and}\; j\geqslant  s\Bigr\},\] then \(Z_1^{i,j}=B_1^{i,j}=0\) for all \((i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\) such that \(i+j=r\) and \(j\geqslant s\). 

    {\rm (2)}  If \(M\) is bounded to the right or bounded below and \(R_1^{i,j}=0\) for all \[(i,j)\in \Bigl\{(i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\Big|i+j=r\; \text{or}\;\; r-1, \;\text{and}\; i\geqslant  r-s\Bigr\},\] then \(Z_1^{i,j}=B_1^{i,j}=0\) for all \((i,j)\in \mathbb{Z}^2\) such that \(i+j=r\) and \(j\leqslant s\).
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-103: body_md -->
We prove (1); the proof of (2) is analogous. The finite free
    resolutions \[\begin{aligned}
        &0 \rightarrow R\xrightarrow{(V,-F)} R\oplus R\xrightarrow{F+V} R\rightarrow B_1(1)\rightarrow 0\\
        0\rightarrow& R(-1)\xrightarrow{(F,-d)} R(-1)\oplus R\xrightarrow{dV^2+V} R\rightarrow Z_1\rightarrow 0, 
    \end{aligned}\]
    and the boundedness hypothesis give
    \(Z_1^{i,r-i}=B_1^{i,r-i}=0\) for \(i\ll0\).
    When \(r-i\geqslant s\), repeated application of
    \Cref{Ek2I.1.1.1} yields
    \[Z_1^{i,r-i}\leqq B_1^{i,r-i}\leqq Z_1^{i-1,r-i+1}
    \leqq B_1^{i-1,r-i+1}\leqq\cdots\leqq0.\]
    Hence \(Z_1^{i,r-i}=B_1^{i,r-i}=0\), as required.
<!-- end proof-103 -->
<!-- proof-104: body_md -->
We prove (1); the proof of (2) is analogous. We reduce to the case
\(A=0\) and argue by induction on \(n\), using the exact sequences
of graded right \(R\)-modules
\[\begin{aligned}
    0\rightarrow R_n\xrightarrow{\rho} R_{n+1} \rightarrow \mathrm{gr}^n_1\rightarrow 0\\
    0\rightarrow B_n(1)\rightarrow \mathrm{gr}^n_1\rightarrow Z_n\rightarrow 0\\
    0\rightarrow B_1\rightarrow B_{n+1}\rightarrow B_n\rightarrow 0\\
    0\rightarrow B_1\rightarrow Z_{n+1} \rightarrow Z_n\rightarrow  0. 
\end{aligned}\]
It suffices to prove \(\mathrm{H}^j(D\otimes_R^{\mathrm{L}}M)^i=0\) for
\(D=B_1,Z_1,B_1(1)\) whenever \(i+j=r\) and \(j\geqslant s\).
For \(D=B_1,Z_1\), this follows from \Cref{Ek2I.1.1.2}.
For \(D=B_1(1)\), the required vanishing is \(B_1^{i+1,j}=0\).
At the endpoint \(j=s\), \Cref{Ek2I.1.1.1} gives
\(B_1^{r+1-s,s}\leqq Z_1^{r-s,s+1}\), and
\Cref{Ek2I.1.1.2} gives
\(Z_1^{r-s,s+1}\leqq B_1^{r-s,s+1}\leqq\cdots\leqq0\).
For \(j\geqslant s+1\), apply \Cref{Ek2I.1.1.2} on the diagonal
of total degree \(r+1\).
<!-- end proof-104 -->
<!-- definition-40: body_md -->
\label{Hodge complex and its filtrations}
For \(M\in D(R)\), choose a semi-free resolution \(P\to M\). Here
semi-free means that \(P\) has an exhaustive increasing filtration by
subcomplexes, split on the underlying graded modules, whose successive
quotients are direct sums of the shifts \(R(i)[j]\). Set
\[
A=R_1\otimes_R P,\qquad Z=Z_1\otimes_R P.
\]
These represent the corresponding derived tensor products. Write
\(A^a,Z^a\) for their horizontal-degree-\(a\) columns. Left
multiplication by \(d\) factors through \(Z_1\), giving
\[
\partial:A^a\longrightarrow Z^{a+1},\qquad
j:Z^a\longrightarrow A^a,\qquad
j\partial=d,\quad \partial j=0.
\]
Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Hod}(M)&:=\mathrm{Tot}(A),\\
t_{\geqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(M)&:=
 \mathrm{Tot}\bigl(0\longrightarrow A^i\xrightarrow{d}A^{i+1}
                   \xrightarrow{d}\cdots\bigr),\\
\tau_{\leqslant i}\mathrm{Hod}(M)&:=
 \mathrm{Tot}\bigl(\cdots\xrightarrow{d}A^{i-2}
     \xrightarrow{d}A^{i-1}\xrightarrow{\partial}Z^i
     \longrightarrow0\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The columns retain their horizontal degrees, and \(\mathrm{Tot}\) uses direct
sums with differential
\(d+(-1)^a\delta\) on horizontal degree \(a\), where \(\delta\)
is the vertical differential. Thus a single column \(A^i\) contributes
\(A^i[-i]\) to the total complex.
<!-- end definition-40 -->
<!-- definition-41: body_md -->
\label{definition of ringoid}
A ringoid is a small preadditive category \(\mathcal C\): its objects
form a set, each \(\mathcal C(s,t)\) is an abelian group, and
composition is bilinear. Thus one can add arrows with the same source
and target, and multiply composable arrows. Each object has an
identity, but direct sums of objects are not required.
<!-- end definition-41 -->
<!-- definition-42: body_md -->
\label{modules over a ringoid}
A left \(\mathcal C\)-module is an additive covariant functor
\(M:\mathcal C\to\mathrm{Ab}\). Explicitly, it consists of abelian
groups \(M(s)\) and bilinear actions
\[
\mathcal C(s,t)\times M(s)\longrightarrow M(t),\qquad
(u,x)\longmapsto ux,
\]
with \(1_sx=x\) and \((vu)x=v(ux)\). A morphism \(M\to N\) is a
family of group homomorphisms \(f_s:M(s)\to N(s)\) commuting with
all these actions. We denote this category by
\(\mathcal C\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\).
A right \(\mathcal C\)-module is an additive functor
\(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Ab}\); an arrow \(u:s\to t\)
then acts from \(N(t)\) to \(N(s)\).
<!-- end definition-42 -->
<!-- proposition-41: body_md -->
\label{basic properties of ringoid modules}
Let \(\mathcal C\) be a ringoid.

{\rm (1)} The category \(\mathcal C\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\) is abelian,
and a sequence is exact if and only if it is exact at every object
of \(\mathcal C\). All small limits and colimits exist and are
computed objectwise. In particular,
\[
\left(\bigoplus_\lambda M_\lambda\right)(s)
 =\bigoplus_\lambda M_\lambda(s),\qquad
\left(\prod_\lambda M_\lambda\right)(s)
 =\prod_\lambda M_\lambda(s).
\]
Direct sums, products, and filtered colimits are exact.

{\rm (2)} The representable modules
\(P_s=\mathcal C(s,-)\) form a set of projective generators, and
\(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(P_s,M)\cong M(s)\).
In particular, every module has a resolution by direct sums of the
\(P_s\).

{\rm (3)} The category \(\mathcal C\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\) is a
Grothendieck abelian category and has enough injectives.
<!-- end proposition-41 -->
<!-- proof-105: body_md -->
Kernels, cokernels, limits, and colimits of abelian groups inherit
the operator actions objectwise. The abelian category axioms and the
exactness assertions therefore follow from those for abelian groups.
An additive natural transformation \(P_s\to M\) is determined by
the image of \(1_s\), giving the stated Hom formula. Since evaluation
at \(s\) is exact, \(P_s\) is projective. The maps corresponding to
all elements \(x\in M(s)\) give an epimorphism
\[
\bigoplus_{s\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)}
\ \bigoplus_{x\in M(s)}P_s\longrightarrow M.
\]
Repeating this construction on kernels gives a projective resolution.
Finally, \(\bigoplus_sP_s\) is a generator and filtered colimits are
exact, so the category is Grothendieck and hence has enough
injectives; see the Stacks Project,
\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/079H}{Tag 079H}.
<!-- end proof-105 -->
<!-- definition-43: body_md -->
\label{tensor products over a ringoid}
Let \(N\) be a right \(\mathcal C\)-module and \(M\) a left
\(\mathcal C\)-module. Define
\[
N\otimes_{\mathcal C}M
:=\left(\bigoplus_{c\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)}
N(c)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}M(c)\right)
\Big/\left\langle (nu)\otimes m-n\otimes(um)\right\rangle,
\]
where \(u:c\to d\), \(n\in N(d)\), and \(m\in M(c)\).
The two tensors in this relation belong to the summands indexed by
\(c\) and \(d\), respectively.
<!-- end definition-43 -->
<!-- definition-44: body_md -->
Let \(\mathrm{I}=[m,n]\). An \(R\)-module of level \(\mathrm{I}\) is a graded
left \(R\)-module of the form
\[
M^m\xrightarrow{d}M^{m+1}\xrightarrow{d}\cdots\xrightarrow{d}M^n
\]
with \(F\) bijective on \(M^n\). Equivalently, the top term carries
an action of \(R^{\mathrm{top}}=W_{\sigma}[F,F^{-1}]\) extending its
\(R^0\)-action. Morphisms are grading-preserving \(R\)-linear maps.
We denote this abelian category by \(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I}\).
<!-- end definition-44 -->
<!-- proposition-42: body_md -->
\label{derived category of R-modules of level I}
The exact inclusion of \(R\)-modules of level \(\mathrm{I}\) into graded
\(R\)-modules induces a fully faithful functor
\[
    D(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}\mathrm{I})\longrightarrow D(R).
\]
Its essential image consists precisely of those \(K\in D(R)\) for
which \(\mathrm{H}^q(K)\) is an \(R\)-module of level \(\mathrm{I}\) for every
\(q\in\mathbb{Z}\).
<!-- end proposition-42 -->
<!-- proof-106: body_md -->
Let \(\mathcal R\) be the coefficient ringoid of graded \(R\)-modules:
its objects are the integers and
\(\mathcal R(i,j)=R^{j-i}\). Let \(\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}\) be the
quotient--localization ringoid whose modules are the \(R\)-modules of
level \(\mathrm{I}\). It is obtained by retaining the consecutive vertices
\(m,\ldots,n\) and, at the terminal vertex, replacing
\(R^0\) by
\[
    R^0[F^{-1}]\cong W_\sigma[F,F^{-1}].
\]
The interval is convex: a composable string of homogeneous operators
whose endpoints lie in \(\mathrm{I}\) cannot leave \(\mathrm{I}\) and then return.
Moreover, \(R^0\to R^0[F^{-1}]\) is a flat Ore localization. Hence the
canonical multiplication map is a quasi-isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{level-I-homological-epimorphism}
    \mathcal R_\mathrm{I}\otimes_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{L}}\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}
       \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}.
\end{equation}
Thus \(\mathcal R\to\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}\) is a homological epimorphism.

Let \(\iota_*:D(\mathcal R_\mathrm{I})\to D(\mathcal R)\) denote restriction
of scalars. Its left adjoint is
\(\iota^*=\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}\otimes_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{L}}-\). For
\(X\in D(\mathcal R_\mathrm{I})\), \eqref{level-I-homological-epimorphism}
gives
\[
\iota^*\iota_*X
 \simeq
 \bigl(\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}\otimes_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{L}}\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}\bigr)
 \otimes_{\mathcal R_\mathrm{I}}^{\mathrm{L}}X
 \simeq X.
\]
The counit of the adjunction is therefore an isomorphism, so
\(\iota_*\) is fully faithful.

Since restriction of scalars is exact, every object in its image has
cohomology of level \(\mathrm{I}\). Conversely, suppose that every
\(\mathrm{H}^q(K)\) is of level \(\mathrm{I}\). For any such module \(N\), the same
calculation gives
\[
    \mathcal R_\mathrm{I}\otimes_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{L}}N\simeq N.
\]
For bounded \(K\), the hyper-Tor spectral sequence therefore shows
that the adjunction unit
\[
    K\longrightarrow\iota_*\iota^*K
\]
is a quasi-isomorphism. The general case follows by expressing \(K\)
as the filtered colimit of its bounded truncations; derived tensor
product and restriction of scalars both preserve these colimits.
Hence \(K\) belongs to the essential image of \(\iota_*\).
<!-- end proof-106 -->
